What this curriculum is for:
The subject, the end it serves, and the four rulings that shaped it.

**The goal, in one line: draw what is in front of you, and then draw what is not.**

The second half is the hard one and the one that matters. **Drawing from observation is a skill of looking; drawing from imagination is a skill of knowing** — and the second is built on the first. A character who does not exist still has a skull, a rib cage, a pelvis, and clothes that hang on them in a particular way. You cannot invent what you cannot construct.

---

**The practical end is Shepherds**, and the shape of the need is specific:

| From the project | What it asks of a hand |
| --- | --- |
| **`cinematic-and-dialogue-visual-system.md`, register 1** | **high-resolution pixel portraits** — *"facial detail, personality, age, clothing, and emotion beyond what gameplay sprites can carry"* |
| **Register 3** | **illustrated graphic-novel tableaux** — full illustration, not pixel art |
| **Register 4** | **act-transition cinematics**, which *"may move beyond pixel art"* |
| **§11's open art work** | *"Draw final **character, creature, terrain, building, prop, portrait, VFX** and remaining UI assets"* |
| **§6.7** | **ten named York residents whose *"final character art is not approved"*** — so their designs do not exist yet |
| **The 2026-09-22 reset** | **all art is hand-drawn now.** The generated pipeline is gone |

**And the boundary, which this curriculum does not cross: Timon has final say on design**, and draws by hand alongside Master Roachi. **This is about being able to contribute and to understand what he is doing** — not about replacing him.

---

**Four rulings shaped what follows**, all his, 14 October 2026:

| | Ruling | What it changed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Through colour, light and illustration** | **four stages that would not otherwise exist** — value, colour and light, illustration, and the painting half of stage 14. Stopping at value would have left registers 1, 3 and 4 unreachable |
| **2** | **Digital first, on the tablet** | **every exercise here is specified for a screenless tablet and a painting program**, and the no-undo constraint that paper gives for free is imposed deliberately instead |
| **3** | **The Famous Artists Course is one reference among many** | its 24 lessons are cited where they are best and nowhere else; lessons 17–24 are excluded as 1960s commercial practice |
| **4** | **No card deck** | **the second curriculum without one, after Godot.** Drawing is motor skill and judgement; the anatomy vocabulary is carried by the lessons themselves |

---

**And one rule that governs every stage: the count is the lesson's second half.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The first version of this curriculum was 64 counts with a paragraph each** | *"100 thirty-second gestures"*, *"50 spheres, 50 boxes, 50 cylinders"* |
| **Its argument was right** | **in this subject the quantity *is* the method.** Nobody has read their way to a good line |
| **Its mistake was that a count is not teaching** | *"50 ears"* does not say that an ear is a C of the outer rim with a Y inside it, or that **placement between the brow line and the base of the nose** is what decides whether one reads |
| **So every lesson here teaches the thing in full and then names the count** | and **the count is real.** Fifty blocked-in figures is not forty |

**The counts are deliberately large and deliberately boring.** That is not a flaw in the design.

**Practice.** Read `drawing.md` — the plan — and then the three Shepherds documents named above, so the end is concrete before the work starts. Then make the three pre-instruction drawings stage 17 will ask you to compare against: a self-portrait from a mirror, your own non-drawing hand, and a chair. Twenty minutes each, no reference, no undo. Date them and put them somewhere you will not look at again until the end.
The tablet, and what it actually is:
The instrument, before anything is drawn with it: what a graphics tablet reports, and why a screenless one is a different instrument from a pen display.

**What the hardware is on this machine:** a **Huion**, USB `256C:006D`, connected over USB. **Screenless** — there is no display in it. The three monitors on the rig are a Dell S2340L, an MSI MP275 and an Acer VG270, and none of them is the tablet.

---

**What a graphics tablet actually reports**, which is more than a mouse does:

| Axis | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **X and Y** | **absolute position on the tablet surface** — not movement, position |
| **Pressure** | **how hard the nib is pressed**, typically 8,192 levels on modern Huion hardware |
| **Tilt X and Y** | **the pen's angle from vertical**, on tablets that support it |
| **Button state** | the barrel buttons and the eraser end |
| **Proximity** | **whether the pen is near the surface at all**, which is how hover works |

**A mouse reports two of those: relative X and Y movement, and buttons.** Everything that makes a tablet a drawing instrument is in the rest.

---

**Absolute against relative** is the distinction that matters most, and it is worth being precise about:

| | A mouse | A tablet |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What it sends** | *"I moved 14 units left"* | *"The pen is at this point on my surface"* |
| **So the mapping is** | **relative** — the cursor continues from wherever it was | **absolute** — the top-left of the tablet is the top-left of the screen, always |
| **Which means** | **you can lift and reposition a mouse** | **you cannot lift and reposition a pen.** Lifting and putting the nib down somewhere else moves the cursor there |
| **Why that is the point** | — | **because it makes the tablet a map of the screen**, and the hand learns the map. That is how a drawn stroke can be aimed |

**A tablet in relative mode is a mouse with a pen-shaped grip.** It is worse than a mouse, because it is heavier and has no inertia.

---

**And the screenless question, which his hardware settles:**

| | A pen display (Kamvas, Cintiq) | A screenless tablet (Inspiroy, Intuos) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Where you look** | **at your hand** | **at the monitor** |
| **What you learn** | nothing extra | **hand-eye separation** — a real motor skill, taught in its own lesson later in this stage |
| **Parallax** | **a real problem** — the nib is a few millimetres from the pixel, so there is an offset that varies with viewing angle | **none.** There is nothing to misalign |
| **Your hand** | **covers the drawing** | **never covers the drawing** |
| **Cost** | several times more | — |
| **Arm position** | **hunched over a screen** | **flat, and the monitor at eye level** |

**The honest summary: a screenless tablet is harder for about three weeks and better afterwards.** The separation that makes it hard is also what stops your hand hiding the picture, removes parallax entirely, and keeps your neck straight. **Nobody who has learned it goes back for ergonomic reasons.**

**Practice.** Find the tablet's model from its box or its underside, and look up its active area in millimetres and its pressure-level count. Then work out the aspect ratio of the active area and compare it with the aspect ratio of the monitor you intend to draw on — the next lessons depend on that number. Then plug it in and move the pen without pressing, and watch whether the cursor jumps to an absolute position or creeps relatively. Then lift the pen and put it down in each of the four corners of the active area, ten times round, without looking at your hand — and note how far off the cursor lands. That error is the thing the next few lessons remove.
The driver problem on this machine:
A verified fault on this rig: the tablet reports as a mouse. What that costs, how it was diagnosed, and the fix.

**The finding.** On 14 October 2026 the tablet enumerated like this:

```
/dev/input/by-id/usb-HUION_Huion_Tablet-hidraw
/dev/input/by-id/usb-HUION_Huion_Tablet-if01-event-mouse
/dev/input/by-id/usb-HUION_Huion_Tablet-if01-hidraw
/dev/input/by-id/usb-HUION_Huion_Tablet-if01-mouse
```

**Read the names.** `event-mouse`. `mouse`. **There is no `event-tablet` node and no pen node.** The kernel has decided this is a mouse.

**And the driver binding confirms it:**

```
/sys/bus/hid/devices/0003:256C:006D.0004 -> hid-generic
/sys/bus/hid/devices/0003:256C:006D.0005 -> hid-generic
```

**`hid-generic` is the fallback driver** — the one the kernel uses when nothing more specific claims the device. It implements the parts of the HID standard that every device shares, which for a tablet means the mouse-like parts and nothing else.

---

**What that costs, concretely:**

| Lost | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| **Pressure** | **every stroke is the same width and the same opacity.** Half the exercises in stages 2, 14 and 15 are pressure exercises |
| **Absolute positioning** | **the hand cannot learn a map of the screen**, which is the whole premise of the previous lesson |
| **Tilt** | no angled chisel marks, no pencil-like edge work |
| **The eraser end** | unrecognised |
| **Proximity** | **no hover**, so no brush outline preview before the stroke |

**What remains: a heavy, imprecise mouse.**

---

**The diagnosis, as a method**, because the same five commands diagnose any input device on Linux:

```
1   lsusb                         -- is the device seen at all, and its vendor:product ID
2   ls /dev/input/by-id/          -- what KIND of device the kernel thinks it is:
                                     read the node suffixes
3   ls -l /sys/bus/hid/devices/*/driver
                                  -- which driver actually claimed it
4   lsmod                         -- which HID drivers are loaded at all
5   modinfo hid_uclogic           -- whether the right driver even supports it;
                                     search its aliases for the product ID
```

**Steps 2 and 3 are the ones that answer the question.** A node suffixed `-mouse` and a driver called `hid-generic` are the same fact stated twice.

---

**And step 5 is where this case resolved.** The driver that should claim a Huion is **`hid-uclogic`** — *"HID driver for UC-Logic devices not fully compliant with HID standard"*, which is exactly what a Huion is. It is present on disk:

```
/lib/modules/7.2.5-3-omarchy/kernel/drivers/hid/hid-uclogic.ko.zst
```

**And the device is in its table.** Of its 33 device aliases, one is:

```
alias: hid:b0003g*v0000256Cp0000006D
```

`v0000256C` is the vendor, `p0000006D` the product. **That is this exact tablet.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **So the hardware is supported** | |
| **And the driver exists** | |
| **And it is simply not loaded** | `lsmod` showed no `uclogic` at all |
| **Which makes it an autoload problem**, not a hardware problem | **and the distinction matters, because one is a one-line fix and the other is a purchase** |

---

**The fix, in order:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **`sudo modprobe hid-uclogic`** — load the driver |
| **2** | **Unplug and replug the tablet** — so the device re-enumerates and the now-loaded driver gets the chance to claim it |
| **3** | **List `/dev/input/by-id/` again** — **look for a node that is not a mouse.** A pen node is the success condition |
| **4** | **To make it stick across reboots:** a one-line file in `/etc/modules-load.d/` naming the module |
| **5** | **If it still does not bind**, the DIGIMEND driver package is the next thing to try — it covers tablets the in-tree driver does not |

**Practice.** Run all five diagnostic commands and write down each answer before changing anything. Then apply the fix and re-run commands 2 and 3. Then open any program that draws and make one stroke, pressing lightly and then hard — the test is whether the line changes width.
Pressure, tilt and the curve:
What pressure actually controls, why the default curve fights you, and the one setting worth changing before anything else.

**Pressure is a number between 0 and 1**, reported continuously while the nib is down. Modern Huion hardware resolves it to **8,192 levels**, which sounds enormous and is not the point — **what matters is the shape of the response, not its resolution.**

---

**What a painting program can map pressure to:**

| Mapped to | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Size** | **the stroke thickens as you press.** The pencil-like default |
| **Opacity** | **the stroke darkens as you press.** The airbrush-like default |
| **Flow** | how much paint is laid per dab, as distinct from the layer-level opacity |
| **Both size and opacity** | **the most natural for drawing**, and the most common setting for a sketching brush |
| **Nothing** | **a technical pen.** Correct for inking, and for stage 2's exercises |

**And tilt can map to the same things, plus rotation** — which is how a chisel or a flat brush behaves when you lean it.

---

**Now the curve, which is the thing nobody changes and everybody should.**

**By default the mapping from pressure to effect is linear**: half pressure gives half the effect. **Human hands are not linear.** Two problems follow:

| Problem | What it feels like | The fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The light end is unreachable** | **you cannot make a faint line.** The lightest touch you can control already gives 20–30% | **raise the curve's low end** so a light touch gives less |
| **The heavy end saturates early** | **the line stops getting thicker** well before you are pressing hard | **flatten the top** so the last third of your range still does something |

**In Krita: Settings → Configure Krita → Tablet Settings**, where the pressure curve is an editable graph, with a **Tablet Tester** beside it that draws your actual input so you can see the curve's effect while changing it.

---

**How to set it honestly**, which takes about five minutes and is worth doing once:

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Open the tablet tester and scribble at your natural drawing pressure.** Not your hardest — your natural one |
| **2** | **Note where that falls on the 0–1 range.** For most people it is around 0.3 to 0.5 |
| **3** | **Pull the curve so your natural pressure gives roughly the middle of the effect** — so you have room both lighter and heavier |
| **4** | **Check the extremes.** The lightest touch you can hold steady should give a visible but faint mark; your hardest press should be the maximum and not reach it early |
| **5** | **Leave it alone afterwards.** A curve you keep adjusting is a curve your hand never learns |

**That last row is the real rule.** **Your hand calibrates to the curve**, and a curve that changes weekly means a hand that never calibrates.

---

**And one warning about pressure as a crutch.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Pressure makes a bad line look better** | tapered ends read as confident even when the stroke wobbled |
| **Which is useful, and is also how a beginner hides from the problem** | |
| **So stage 2's exercises turn pressure off entirely** | **a uniform-width pen, where a wobble is a wobble** |
| **And it comes back in stage 14**, for rendering, where it is doing real work | |
| **The principle, which recurs through this whole curriculum** | **learn it without the aid, then use the aid** |

**Practice.** Set the pressure curve by the five steps above, using the tablet tester. Then draw twenty long strokes at a deliberately constant light pressure, and twenty more going light-to-heavy-to-light in one stroke. Then turn pressure mapping off entirely and draw twenty more, and note how much worse they look — that difference is what the aid was hiding.
Mapping the active area:
Three monitors, one tablet, and the geometry that decides whether a circle you draw comes out as a circle.

**The problem.** The tablet's active area is a rectangle of some aspect ratio. The screen area it maps to is another rectangle. **If the two ratios differ, the mapping distorts** — and a circle drawn by moving your hand in a circle arrives as an ellipse.

---

**The three decisions, in order:**

**1 — Which screen?** This rig has three monitors, and **a tablet mapped across all of them is almost always wrong**:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The combined desktop is very wide** | three monitors side by side |
| **So the tablet's area maps to that whole width** | **compressing it horribly** |
| **And your drawing occupies one monitor** | so most of the tablet is pointing at things you are not drawing |
| **The answer** | **map the tablet to one monitor** — the one you draw on |

**2 — Which part of that screen?** Usually all of it. But:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **If the tablet's aspect ratio does not match the monitor's** | **you must give up something** |
| **Option A: fit the whole tablet to the whole screen** | **distorts.** A circle is an ellipse |
| **Option B: keep the ratio and letterbox the tablet** | **some of the tablet is dead.** Nothing is distorted |
| **Which to pick** | **B, always.** Dead tablet area costs nothing; distortion costs every curve you draw |

**3 — How large?** Smaller than you think.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A large mapped area means a large hand movement per screen inch** | — which means **drawing from the shoulder**, which is what you want for long lines |
| **It also means fine detail needs very fine motor control** | and you will zoom in instead, which is correct |
| **The usual mistake** | **mapping a small area, so the pen is twitchy** and every small tremor becomes a big line |

---

**On Linux**, the mapping is set outside the painting program:

| Session | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| **Wayland** (which Omarchy is) | **the compositor's own input configuration** — Hyprland's tablet section, with `output` naming the monitor |
| **X11** | `xinput set-prop` with the *Coordinate Transformation Matrix* |

**And the monitor is named by its connector or its description.** The rig's own gotcha applies here: **connector names can change between boots, so match on the description** — `Microstep MSI MP275 E2 ...` rather than `DP-2`.

---

**The check that proves it is right**, and it takes ten seconds:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw a circle by rotating your whole forearm**, as fast and loose as you can | |
| **If it arrives as a circle, the mapping is proportional** | |
| **If it arrives as an ellipse, the aspect ratios do not match** and option A was chosen somewhere | |
| **Then draw a diagonal from one corner of the tablet to the other** | |
| **It should reach both corners of the drawing area** — if it stops short, the mapping is letterboxed on the wrong axis | |

**Practice.** Find the tablet's active area in millimetres and the drawing monitor's resolution and physical size. Compute both aspect ratios. Then map the tablet to that one monitor, preserving the ratio, and run the circle test and the diagonal test. Then draw fifty loose circles from the shoulder and check they are round.
Krita, and why it is the one:
The program, the reasoning behind choosing it, and the settings to change before the first stroke.

**Nothing was installed.** On 14 October 2026 the rig had **Aseprite and Blender** and no painting program at all — no Krita, no GIMP, no MyPaint, no Inkscape. The medium ruling made that a blocker rather than a preference.

**Krita 6.0.3 is in Arch's `extra` repository**, 70 MB, one `pacman -S krita`.

---

**Why Krita rather than the alternatives:**

| | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| **Krita** | **free, open source, and built for drawing and painting specifically.** Excellent tablet support, a serious brush engine, animation if it is ever wanted |
| **GIMP** | **free, and a photo editor.** Its brush engine is an afterthought and its tablet handling has historically been the worse of the two |
| **Inkscape** | **vector.** A different medium entirely — useful for UI and diagrams, not for drawing |
| **Photoshop** | the industry default, **not free**, and not on Linux without effort |
| **Aseprite** | **already installed and the wrong tool.** It is a pixel-art editor: its canvas is tens of pixels across and its whole discipline is the opposite of this one |

**And the deciding point is not the feature list: Krita's defaults assume you are drawing.** GIMP's assume you are retouching a photograph. **A program's defaults are an argument about what you are doing**, and it is easier to accept a good argument than to fight a bad one.

---

**The settings to change before the first stroke.** Krita's defaults are good; these five are not quite right for this use:

| | Setting | Change it to | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | |
| **1** | **Tablet pressure curve** | **set by the previous lesson's method** | the default is linear and your hand is not |
| **2** | **Brush smoothing / stabiliser** | **None** | **the next stage's whole argument.** It is on by default at Basic Smoothing |
| **3** | **Canvas-only mode** | **learn the shortcut, Tab** | **the interface is not the drawing.** Seeing it clean is how you judge it |
| **4** | **Mirror view** | **learn the shortcut, M** | the single most effective error-finder there is, and the subject of its own lesson |
| **5** | **The pop-up palette** | **right-click on canvas** | brushes and colours without crossing the screen, which matters when the tablet is mapped to one monitor |

---

**The four concepts Krita uses that are worth naming now**, because the manual assumes them:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Brush engine** | **the algorithm behind a brush.** Pixel, Color Smudge, Filter, Sketch and others. A "brush" is an engine plus its settings, and the engine decides what kinds of marks are possible |
| **Brush preset** | **a saved configuration of an engine.** What you actually pick from the palette |
| **Flow against opacity** | **flow is per-dab, opacity is per-stroke.** Low flow with high opacity builds up; the reverse does not |
| **Blending mode** | **how a layer or a stroke combines with what is under it.** Normal, Multiply and Erase cover nearly everything in this curriculum |

**And the resource folder** — where presets, brushes and palettes live — **is worth knowing about now**, because it is the thing to back up.

---

**One thing Krita does that no paper does, and which is a trap:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`Ctrl+Z` has a long history** | dozens of steps by default |
| **Which makes a stroke feel free** | and **it is not.** The next lesson is about exactly this |
| **And `Ctrl+Shift+Z` goes forward again** | so nothing is ever committed |
| **The habit it produces** | **drawing the same line twenty times rather than learning to draw it once** |

**Practice.** Install Krita and make a new document — A4 at 300 dpi will do for now, the next lesson argues about sizes. Then set the five settings above. Then open the brush preset list and count how many presets ship by default; pick five and make twenty strokes with each, noting what each engine makes possible. Then press Tab, M, and right-click, until all three are automatic.
The canvas, and what size to work at:
Resolution, dpi, and the decision that quietly limits what a drawing can become.

**Two numbers describe a digital canvas, and only one of them is real:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Pixel dimensions** — 3000 × 2000 | **the real number.** It is how much information the image contains |
| **dpi** — 300 | **a note about intended print size**, stored as metadata. It changes nothing about the image |

**A 3000 × 2000 image at 300 dpi and the same image at 72 dpi are the same image.** The dpi number only says how large to print it: 10 inches wide at 300, 41 inches at 72. **For work that will be seen on a screen, dpi is irrelevant.**

---

**So what decides the pixel dimensions?**

| Purpose | Size | Reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Studies and exercises** | **2000 × 1500 or so** | big enough to work loosely, small enough to be fast. Most of this curriculum |
| **Gesture drawing** | **1500 × 2000**, portrait | you will make hundreds; keep them light |
| **A finished illustration** | **4000 px on the long edge or more** | **you cannot add information later.** Upscaling invents nothing |
| **Reference for a pixel-art portrait** | **large, then reduced** | which is `hud.md`'s own rule for UI art: *"never enlarged past their useful source resolution"* |
| **Print** | **the print size in inches × 300** | and decide this before starting |

**The rule underneath all of them: it is easy to go down and impossible to go up.** Working too large costs memory and brush lag; working too small costs the drawing.

---

**And the subtler reason to work large, which is about the hand rather than the file:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **At 100% zoom on a 1080p monitor you see about 2 megapixels** | |
| **So a 4000 × 3000 canvas at 100% shows you a quarter of itself** | |
| **Which means you are always either zoomed out and seeing the whole thing small**, or zoomed in and seeing a detail large | |
| **And the trap is spending all your time zoomed in** | **rendering a face that is, at the real size, four pixels across** |
| **The habit that prevents it** | **zoom to fit, constantly.** The next lesson makes it a rule |

---

**Three Krita specifics worth knowing at the start:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Colour depth** | **8-bit per channel is correct for this work.** 16-bit matters for heavy compositing and doubles the memory |
| **Colour space** | **sRGB** unless there is a reason. Everything downstream — the web, Godot, the monitor — assumes it |
| **Background** | **a white *layer*, not a transparent canvas with white behind it.** The distinction matters the moment you export |

---

**And one thing worth setting up once: a template.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A document you save as a template** | with the size, the colour space, a white background layer and a sketch layer above it |
| **Why it matters** | **because the friction before the first stroke is what stops a daily practice** |
| **The daily habit is `brush`, every day** | and a drawing session that begins with five dialog boxes is a session that does not begin |
| **Make two** | **a study template and a gesture template**, and nothing else until you need it |

**Practice.** Make the two templates described above. Then take one old drawing and view it at 100%, at fit-to-screen, and at 25%, and note how different it looks at each. Then make three canvases — 1000 × 750, 2500 × 1875 and 5000 × 3750 — and draw the same simple object on each at the same zoom level, and notice how much your mark-making changes with the canvas size.
Brushes: the five that matter:
Why a beginner needs five brushes and not five hundred, which five, and what each one is for.

**Krita ships with well over a hundred presets.** Almost all of them are a distraction, and the reason is specific rather than puritanical.

---

**What a textured, expressive brush does to a beginner's drawing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It adds visual interest the drawing did not earn** | a scratchy charcoal preset makes a bad line look characterful |
| **Which hides the error** | **and the whole purpose of practice is to see the error** |
| **And it couples two decisions** | *"is this line in the right place"* and *"does this texture look good"* — **and you can only learn one thing at a time** |
| **The rule** | **learn the mark before the medium** |

---

**The five, and what each is for:**

| | Brush | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **A hard round, pressure to size, no texture** | **everything in stages 2 to 13.** Construction, gesture, line. The default instrument |
| **2** | **A uniform-width ink pen — no pressure at all** | **stage 2's exercises, and all inking.** A wobble cannot hide behind a taper |
| **3** | **A soft round, pressure to opacity** | **value and rendering, stage 14.** Builds tone in passes rather than in one stroke |
| **4** | **A hard eraser** | **and it is a brush**, with the same size and pressure settings. Most people never configure it and should |
| **5** | **A large soft airbrush at very low flow** | **atmosphere and large value shifts, stages 14 and 15.** Dangerous: it makes everything look smooth and finished, so use it last |

**That is the whole kit for roughly fourteen stages.**

---

**The settings that matter on brush 1**, since it does most of the work:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Pressure → size**, on the curve set two lessons ago | |
| **Opacity at 100%, flow at 100%** | **so a stroke is a stroke.** Tone comes from the drawing, not from the brush being faint |
| **No spacing gaps** | a dotted line at speed means the spacing is too wide |
| **Anti-aliasing on** | this is not pixel art, and the §10.1 rule banning it belongs to the other curriculum |
| **Size on a shortcut** | **the single most-used control.** Krita's default is `[` and `]`, and the right-drag-on-canvas gesture is faster |

---

**And one real warning about Krita's brush collection.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Its bundled presets are genuinely excellent** | and many are by working artists |
| **Which makes them tempting early** | |
| **The failure mode is brush-shopping** | **spending the drawing session choosing a brush** |
| **The test** | **if you cannot name what a brush does that your hard round cannot, you do not need it yet** |
| **When to expand** | **stage 14**, where texture and edge quality become the subject rather than a distraction |

**Practice.** Build the five brushes above as your own presets, named plainly, and put them in the pop-up palette in that order. Then draw the same simple object — a mug, from life — five times, once with each brush, and write down what each one made easy and what it hid. Then hide every other preset from your view, and leave them hidden until stage 14.
Layers, and not hiding behind them:
What layers are for, the four this curriculum uses, and the specific way they stop a beginner learning.

**A layer is a transparent sheet over the canvas.** They stack, they can be reordered, hidden, made partly transparent, and combined with blending modes. **That is the whole concept**, and it is genuinely one of the real advantages of drawing digitally.

---

**The four that earn their place:**

| | Layer | What goes on it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Background** | **a flat white or mid-grey fill.** Mid-grey is better for value work, because white is one end of the range rather than the middle |
| **2** | **Construction** | **the gesture, the boxes, the proportion marks.** Kept, at low opacity, under everything |
| **3** | **Drawing** | **the actual line.** The layer that matters |
| **4** | **Notes** | **a red layer for your own corrections**, written on top and deleted later |

**And that is enough for every exercise in stages 2 to 13.** Colour work in stage 15 adds more, and they are introduced there.

---

**Now the problem, which is real and specific.**

| How layers help | How the same thing hurts |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw the construction, then the line on top, then hide the construction** | **the line is traced.** Your hand never learned to place it without scaffolding |
| **Draw a limb on its own layer and move it when the proportion is wrong** | **you never learned to see the proportion was wrong before drawing it** |
| **Lower the opacity of a bad passage and redraw over it** | **infinite retries, so no stroke is ever committed** |
| **Keep every version** | **no decisions.** A drawing is a sequence of decisions |

**The honest statement: layers let you avoid the error instead of correcting it, and avoiding an error teaches nothing.**

---

**So the rule this curriculum applies, which is a compromise rather than a prohibition:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Stages 2 and 3** | **one layer.** No construction layer, no undo beyond a slip. The exercises are about the mark |
| **Stages 4 to 6** | **construction and drawing, two layers** — because construction is genuinely a separate pass |
| **Stages 7 to 13** | **as many as the work needs**, by which point the hand has been trained without them |
| **Throughout** | **never move, scale or transform part of a drawing to fix a proportion.** Redraw it. The transform is the one tool that most reliably prevents learning |

**That last line is the important one.** **Free Transform is the layer feature that does the most damage**, because it fixes the symptom instantly and perfectly, and the cause — that you did not see the proportion — survives untouched into the next drawing.

---

**And the two layer features that are purely good, with no cost:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Reference layers** | a photograph at low opacity, locked, to measure against — **not to trace.** The distinction is whether you look at it or draw through it |
| **The notes layer** | **correcting your own drawing in red, on top, before redrawing it.** This is the single most useful habit in the whole stage, and it is what a teacher would do |

**Practice.** Set up the four-layer template. Then take ten old drawings and critique each one on a red notes layer — circle what is wrong, draw the correct line over the wrong one, write why. Then redraw three of them from scratch, without the original visible. Then do one week of exercises on a single layer, to find out what you were leaning on.
Hand-eye separation:
The one real skill a screenless tablet demands that no drawing book covers, why it takes about three weeks, and the exercises that shorten it.

**The situation: your hand is on the desk and the mark appears on a monitor.** They are in different places, at different scales, in different planes. **Your proprioception — the sense of where your own hand is — now has to be mapped onto a surface you are not looking at.**

**This is a genuine motor skill, it is learnable, and essentially no drawing instruction addresses it**, because every drawing book assumes paper and every digital-painting course assumes you will cope.

---

**What is actually being learned:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Not hand-eye coordination** | you have that |
| **A coordinate transform** | **tablet space to screen space**, applied continuously and unconsciously |
| **Which the cerebellum learns the same way it learns a musical instrument** | by repetition with feedback |
| **And the feedback is the cursor** | which is why **hover matters** — seeing where the pen will land before it lands is most of the learning signal |
| **So a tablet with no proximity reporting is much harder to learn on** | which is one more reason the driver problem had to be fixed first |

---

**Three weeks is the normal figure**, and it decomposes:

| Stage | What it feels like |
| --- | --- |
| **Days 1–3** | **actively unpleasant.** Every stroke lands somewhere you did not intend. Many people stop here |
| **Days 4–10** | **large movements become accurate; small ones do not.** You can hit a region, not a point |
| **Days 10–21** | **the map consolidates.** You stop thinking about it, which is the actual success condition |
| **After** | **you forget it was ever hard**, which is why nobody writes about it |

**The single most important thing: do not keep changing the mapping during this period.** **Every change to the mapped area, the monitor or the scale resets the map your hand is building.** Set it once, by the previous lesson's method, and leave it alone for a month.

---

**The four exercises that shorten it**, in order:

| | Exercise | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Dot targeting.** Scatter 30 dots on the canvas. Lift the pen and land on each one in turn, **without hovering first** — put the nib straight down. Score how many you hit | **30 dots, 10 rounds** |
| **2** | **Corner finding.** Lift and land on each of the four corners of the canvas in turn, eyes on the screen, hand unwatched | **40 rounds** |
| **3** | **Blind lines.** Draw a straight line between two marked points with the monitor covered for the stroke's duration. Uncover and look | **50 lines** |
| **4** | **Scale calibration.** Draw a 10 cm line on the tablet and see what length it is on screen. Repeat until you can predict it | **20 attempts** |

**Exercise 1 is the one that does the most work**, because landing without hovering is precisely the skill — hovering is a crutch that the map eventually replaces.

---

**And two things that are not worth doing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Drawing on paper taped over the tablet** | it changes the friction, which is a real and useful thing, and it does **not** help the mapping, which is the actual difficulty |
| **Buying a pen display to avoid the problem** | **the separation is also the benefit** — no parallax, hand never covering the work, and a neutral neck position. Three weeks against years of posture |

**Practice.** Do exercises 1 to 4 above as a fifteen-minute warm-up before every drawing session for three weeks — and keep the dot-targeting score each day, because watching it climb is what gets most people through days 1 to 3. Then stop doing them, and start every session with ten minutes of exercise 1 only, indefinitely.
The flip, the zoom and the greyscale che:
Three ways of looking at your own drawing that find errors your eye cannot, and why each one works.

**The problem these solve:** you stop seeing your own drawing. **After twenty minutes your eye has accepted every error on the canvas**, and you cannot find what is wrong by looking harder.

**All three checks work the same way: they change the image enough that your eye processes it as new.**

---

**1 — The flip.** Mirror the canvas horizontally.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it reveals** | **every asymmetry and every lean.** A head you have drawn slightly tilted looks violently tilted flipped; a figure that is off balance falls over |
| **Why it works** | **your eye has learned this specific image.** Mirrored, it is a new one — and the errors are the parts that look wrong immediately |
| **Why it works on paper too** | **hold the drawing up to a mirror**, which is the traditional version of exactly this |
| **In Krita** | **`M` for mirror *view*, which flips the display and not the image.** Instant, free, and does not touch the file |
| **How often** | **every few minutes.** It should become a tic |

**And the deeper fact behind it:** you have a handedness bias in your drawing. **A right-handed artist's curves tend to favour one direction**, and the flip is how you find out that is happening.

---

**2 — The zoom-out.** View the drawing small.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it reveals** | **everything structural** — proportion, silhouette, value massing, composition |
| **Why it works** | **detail disappears and only the large relationships remain.** Which is what the viewer sees first |
| **The specific failure it catches** | **a beautifully rendered face on a figure whose head is too large.** Zoomed in, the face is lovely; zoomed out, the drawing is wrong |
| **How small** | **small enough that you cannot see detail** — thumbnail size, a few hundred pixels |
| **How often** | **after every passage.** And always before deciding a drawing is finished |

**Squinting does the same thing** and is the analogue version — it blurs high-frequency detail and leaves the value structure.

---

**3 — The greyscale check.** Remove the colour.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it reveals** | **whether the value structure works without hue doing the work** |
| **Why it matters** | **value carries form and hue carries identity** — a picture whose shapes only separate by colour collapses in greyscale, and will also collapse for a colour-blind viewer |
| **When** | **stage 15 onward**, where there is colour to remove |
| **In Krita** | a filter mask or a desaturating adjustment layer kept at the top of the stack, toggled |

**And it is the same test Shepherds' own documents apply:** *"no telegraph depends on hue alone."*

---

**The three as a single habit**, which is the point of the lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Flip** | **every few minutes** |
| **Zoom out** | **after every passage** |
| **Greyscale** | **whenever colour is involved** |
| **And a fourth, free one** | **leave it overnight.** Time does the same thing more thoroughly than any of them, and costs nothing but patience |

**Practice.** Take ten of your existing drawings and flip each one, writing down the first error you see within two seconds — that first impression is the whole value of the exercise. Then view each at thumbnail size and write down what survives. Then adopt the flip as a habit for one week by flipping at every natural pause, and count how many errors it catches.
Undo, and the rule about it:
What paper gave for free, what the tablet takes away, and the discipline this curriculum imposes to replace it.

**His ruling was digital first.** It is the right call for his purposes and it has one real cost, which this lesson exists to pay.

---

**Drawabox — the best free structured drawing course there is — is ink on paper, deliberately.** Not pencil. Its reasoning is exactly this:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A mark you cannot take back must be planned** | so you look before you draw |
| **Which forces the sequence** | **decide, aim, commit** |
| **And a mark you can take back need not be planned** | so you draw first and judge after |
| **Which produces** | **the scribble-until-it-looks-right habit**, where a line is found by averaging twenty attempts rather than by being aimed |

**The second habit is slower, produces worse lines, and does not improve with practice** — because what is being practised is scribbling.

---

**So the rule, and it applies to stages 2 and 3 absolutely:**

> **Undo is for mistakes, not for retries.**

| Allowed | Not allowed |
| --- | --- |
| **The pen slipped; the tablet glitched; you drew on the wrong layer** | **the line was wobbly and you want another go** |
| **You drew the wrong thing entirely** | **the line was in slightly the wrong place** |
| **A technical failure** | **a quality judgement** |

**The test is one question: am I undoing because something went wrong, or because I did not like the result?** The second is a retry, and a retry is the habit being trained.

---

**What replaces undo: the ghosting method**, which is Drawabox's and is the single most useful technique in this stage.

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Decide the mark.** Where it starts, where it ends, what curve it takes |
| **2** | **Ghost it.** Move the pen through the motion **above the surface**, several times, until the motion is smooth and your arm knows it |
| **3** | **Commit.** One stroke, at speed, without slowing to be accurate |
| **4** | **Live with it.** Look at what happened and let it inform the next mark |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Step 3's "at speed" is counter-intuitive and essential** | **a slow stroke wobbles.** Accuracy comes from the planning in step 2, not from careful execution |
| **And step 4 is the one people skip** | **a mark you keep is information; a mark you undo is nothing** |

**On a tablet, hover makes ghosting better than it is on paper** — the cursor shows exactly where the stroke will go while you rehearse it, which is a genuine advantage the medium gives back.

---

**And the other two aids with the same problem:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The stabiliser** | **off until stage 14.** It makes a beginner's lines look expert, which means you cannot see whether your lines are improving. Its own lesson follows in stage 2 |
| **The transform tool** | **never, for fixing proportion.** Redraw. Discussed in the layers lesson and repeated here because it is the one that does most damage |

---

**A practical compromise worth stating, since dogma helps nobody:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **During exercises — stages 2 and 3** | **the rule is absolute** |
| **During a finished illustration — stage 16** | **undo freely.** You are making a picture, not training a hand |
| **The distinction** | **a study is for you; a drawing is for the viewer** |
| **And knowing which one you are making** | **is itself a skill**, and stage 17 is partly about it |

**Practice.** Do one week of exercises under the absolute rule, counting every undo and writing the reason beside it — the count alone will change your behaviour. Then take 50 long straight lines using the full ghosting method, and 50 more without ghosting, and compare them. Then set your undo history to five steps for a month, and notice what changes.
Files, versions and the sketchbook:
Where the work goes, what to keep, and the one habit that makes a daily practice measurable.

**The Drawing habit is daily** — one of the fourteen on the dashboard, icon `brush`. **A daily practice produces hundreds of files a year**, and a practice you cannot look back through is one you cannot measure.

---

**The layout, and the reasoning:**

```
~/Admin/drawing/
    sketchbook/2026/2026-10-14/        one folder per day
    studies/<subject>/                 anatomy, heads, hands, animals
    exercises/<stage>/                 the counted work, by curriculum stage
    finished/                          the few pieces taken to completion
    reference/                         gathered reference, by subject
```

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Dated folders for the sketchbook** | **because the date is the only metadata that matters** for undirected work |
| **Subject folders for studies** | **because you will want every hand study together** when you come to draw a hand |
| **Stage folders for exercises** | **because the counts are per stage**, and counting is how you know a stage is done |
| **`finished/` is deliberately small** | and if it stays empty, that is itself the finding |

---

**File naming**, one rule: **sortable first.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`2026-10-14-gesture-01.kra`** | sorts correctly forever |
| **`gesture1.kra`** | **sorts next to `gesture10.kra` and before `gesture2.kra`** |
| **And the format** | **`.kra` while working** — it keeps layers; **`.png` to look at or share** |
| **Export the PNG** | because **you will not open a `.kra` to flick through a year of work**, and a folder of PNGs can be viewed in any image browser |

---

**What to keep, which is the question people get wrong in both directions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Keep every exercise** | **they are the evidence the counts were real**, and they are the progress record |
| **Keep every study** | they become your own reference |
| **Keep the failures** | **especially the failures.** A drawing you abandoned tells you what you cannot yet do, which is the most useful information available |
| **Delete nothing for a year** | storage is free and judgement at the time of drawing is unreliable |
| **And back it up** | one folder, one copy elsewhere |

**The contrast with Shepherds is worth noting:** its art contract says *"rejected and superseded art is deleted rather than archived"* — **because a game repository must contain only what ships.** A practice folder is the opposite kind of thing: **it exists to be looked back through.**

---

**And the habit that makes it measurable: the count log.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One plain text file** | `~/Admin/drawing/counts.md` |
| **One line per session** | the date, the stage, what was drawn, how many |
| **Why a file rather than the dashboard** | **the dashboard tracks lessons; this tracks repetitions**, and a lesson is done once while its count is done over weeks |
| **What it is actually for** | **the counts in this curriculum are large.** *"100 thirty-second gestures"* is not a thing you do in one sitting, and without a log you will not know where you are |
| **And at the end** | **stage 17's comparison needs it** |

**Practice.** Make the folder structure and the count log. Then put the three pre-instruction drawings from the first lesson into `sketchbook/` under today's date, and write the first line of the log. Then set up whatever backup you use to include the one folder. Then, for one week, write a log line after every session, however short — seven lines is the whole exercise.
What a line is:
Before any exercise: what a drawn line actually represents, and why that question is not philosophical.

**There are no lines in the world.** There are edges — where one form ends and another begins, where a surface turns away from the light, where one thing overlaps another. **A line is a convention for recording an edge**, and knowing which kind of edge it is recording decides how it should be drawn.

---

**The four things a line can be:**

| | Kind | What it records |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **A contour** | **the silhouette's boundary** — where the form turns away from you entirely |
| **2** | **An overlap** | **one form passing in front of another.** The single strongest depth cue in drawing |
| **3** | **A cross-contour** | **the surface's curvature**, drawn across the form rather than around it |
| **4** | **A division** | **a change of material or colour on one continuous surface** — a seam, a stripe, a shadow's edge |

**And the practical consequence: these should not all be drawn the same weight.** A contour and an overlap are structural; a division is surface detail. **Drawing them identically flattens the picture**, and it is the most common reason a beginner's drawing reads as a diagram.

---

**Crane's point**, from *Line and Form*, and it is the useful one: **a line is a decision about what to leave out.** The drawing is not an incomplete photograph. **It is a selection**, and the selection is the content.

---

**What makes a line good**, in the order that matters:

| | Quality | Why it is in this order |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **It is where it should be** | **placement beats everything.** A wobbly line in the right place reads; a perfect line in the wrong place is wrong |
| **2** | **It was drawn with confidence** | **a confident line is read as intentional**, and the eye forgives it |
| **3** | **It is the right weight for its job** | the four kinds above |
| **4** | **It has the right character** | **last, and it is where beginners start** |

**Stage 2 trains 2 and 3.** Placement is stages 3 to 6, because placement is a question about form rather than about the hand.

---

**And the thing to understand about confidence**, because it sounds like advice and is mechanical:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A line drawn slowly wobbles** | because **your hand corrects continuously** against what it sees, and each correction is a small deviation |
| **A line drawn at speed does not wobble** | because **there is no time to correct** — it is a single ballistic motion |
| **So a fast line is straighter and less accurate** | and **a slow line is more accurate and uglier** |
| **The resolution** | **plan slowly, execute fast.** Which is the ghosting method from stage 1 |
| **And the accuracy comes back with practice** | **the planning gets better.** The execution never gets slower |

**Practice.** Take 100 lines of about 15 cm between two marked points: 50 drawn as slowly and carefully as you can, 50 ghosted and then drawn in one fast stroke. Compare them for wobble and for accuracy, and write down which trade you prefer at this point. Then take one existing drawing of your own and mark each line as contour, overlap, cross-contour or division — and notice how many are the same weight.
The stabiliser argument:
The slider that makes a beginner's lines look like an expert's, what it costs, and when to turn it on.

**What it does.** A stabiliser averages the pen's reported positions over a short window, so the drawn line lags behind the cursor and smooths out tremor. **Krita offers four modes: None, Basic Smoothing, Weighted Smoothing and Stabilizer**, in increasing order of effect — and the default is not None.

---

**What it costs, and the argument is not aesthetic:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A wobbly line is feedback.** It tells you the stroke was unplanned or too slow | |
| **The stabiliser removes the feedback and leaves the cause** | so **you cannot tell whether you are improving** |
| **Which means the practice stops working** | — **the entire purpose of a repetition is the information it returns** |
| **And the dependency is real** | a hand trained with a stabiliser at high strength **has not been trained** |

**The analogy that fits: it is the stabiliser wheels, and the problem is that they work.** A child on stabilisers can ride for years without learning to balance, because balance is never required.

---

**And there is a second, subtler cost — it changes what you can draw.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A stabilised stroke lags** | so **fast gestural marks arrive late and short** |
| **Sharp corners round off** | because the averaging window spans the corner |
| **Small marks are disproportionately affected** | the window is a fixed length in screen space |
| **So high stabilisation makes long smooth curves easy and everything else worse** | which is why it looks so good on a line test and so bad on a gesture drawing |

---

**The ruling this curriculum applies:**

| Stage | Setting |
| --- | --- |
| **2 and 3** | **None.** Absolutely. The exercises are about the hand |
| **4 to 13** | **None**, or Basic Smoothing if the hardware reports noisily |
| **14 onward** | **whatever serves the picture.** Long rendered contours and inked line work are a legitimate use |
| **Inking specifically** | **a real and honest use.** Professional inkers use it, and inking is an execution task where the planning has already happened in the pencil |

**The principle is the same one that runs through the whole curriculum: learn it without the aid, then use the aid.**

---

**One honest qualification.** There are reasons a hand shakes that practice does not fix:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Essential tremor, medication, injury, age** | real, common, and nothing to do with skill |
| **For which the stabiliser is an accessibility tool and should be used without apology** | |
| **The test to tell them apart** | **does the wobble change with stroke speed and with planning?** A tremor does not; an untrained hand does |
| **Try the 100-line exercise from the previous lesson before concluding anything** | **most people who think they have a tremor have an unplanned stroke** |

**Practice.** Set the stabiliser to None and draw 50 long curves; then to maximum and draw 50 more; compare them and be honest about how much better the second set looks. Then leave it at None for the whole of stages 2 and 3 — and re-run the comparison at the end of stage 3 to see how much of the gap has closed.
The ghosted line:
Drawabox's central technique, in full: the four-step method that replaces drawing a line twenty times with drawing it once.

**The method, from stage 1's undo lesson, now as the exercise:**

| | Step | What is happening |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Plan.** Mark the start and the end. Decide the path between them | **the decision is made here, and only here** |
| **2** | **Ghost.** Move the pen through the motion above the surface, 3–6 times, watching the cursor | **the arm rehearses the motion until it is smooth** |
| **3** | **Execute.** One stroke, at speed, nib down, without slowing to be accurate | **ballistic — no correction mid-stroke** |
| **4** | **Look.** Do not redraw. See what happened | **the information is in the gap between plan and result** |

---

**Why each step is non-negotiable:**

| Step | If you skip it |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **the stroke has no target**, so there is nothing to be accurate against, and no information in the result |
| **2** | **the arm has not found the motion**, so the stroke is a first attempt and wobbles |
| **3** | **drawing slowly reintroduces correction**, and correction is wobble. **This is the step people cannot make themselves do** |
| **4** | **redrawing averages attempts**, which is the scribble habit — and it buries the one piece of feedback the repetition produced |

**Step 3 deserves the emphasis.** Everyone understands planning. **Almost nobody is willing to execute fast and be wrong**, because a fast wrong line looks worse than a slow wrong line. It is not worse. **It is wrong in a way you can learn from**, because the error is in the planning rather than smeared across the execution.

---

**What ghosting is really training**, which is worth understanding rather than taking on faith:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A drawn line is a ballistic movement** | planned before it starts and executed without feedback, like throwing |
| **The alternative is a feedback-controlled movement** | continuously corrected, like threading a needle |
| **Ballistic movements are fast, smooth and inaccurate until trained** | |
| **Feedback movements are slow, accurate and never become smooth** | |
| **Drawing requires the first** | **so the practice must be the first, repeated until the planning is accurate** |

**And this is why the tablet's hover is a genuine advantage over paper**: the cursor during step 2 shows exactly where the stroke will land, which paper cannot do.

---

**The exercises, in Drawabox's order:**

| | Exercise | What it isolates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Superimposed lines** — one line, then 7 more directly over it, all starting at the same point | **fraying.** The end tells you where your accuracy runs out |
| **2** | **Ghosted lines** — between two dots, every length and angle | **the full method** |
| **3** | **Ghosted planes** — four dots, then the four edges, then the two diagonals | **planning several related marks**, which is construction's precursor |

**Read the fraying honestly.** Superimposed lines fray at one end and not the other — **they fray at the end, because the start is anchored and error accumulates.** If they fray at both ends, the starting point is not being hit, which is a different and easier problem.

**Practice.** 50 sets of superimposed lines, 8 strokes each, at mixed lengths and angles. Then 200 ghosted lines between dot pairs, every angle, lengths from 2 cm to the full canvas. Then 50 ghosted planes with their diagonals. Do not redraw a single stroke, and keep every page.
Arcs, curves and the elbow:
Why a curve is harder than a straight line, which joint draws which curve, and the exercise that fixes a curve's most common fault.

**The fault first, because naming it makes it visible: a beginner's curve flattens in the middle and hooks at the ends.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Why** | **the hand decelerates towards the end of the stroke**, and a decelerating stroke curves more tightly |
| **So the curvature is not constant** | — it is loose at the start and tight at the finish |
| **And the fix is not "try harder"** | it is **to draw the curve as part of a larger circle you are not completing** |

---

**The principle: every arc is a segment of a circle, and the circle is bigger than the arc.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ghost the whole circle**, not the visible arc | |
| **Begin the stroke before the arc starts**, in the air, so the hand is already moving at speed | |
| **Lift after the arc ends**, not at its end | |
| **Which gives a constant curvature**, because the motion was never accelerating or decelerating inside the visible part | |

**This is exactly how a long straight line works too** — start moving before the nib lands — and it is the same principle generalised.

---

**Which joint draws which curve**, and this is mechanical rather than stylistic:

| Joint | Radius it naturally sweeps | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Fingers** | **1–3 cm** | **detail only.** Nothing structural |
| **Wrist** | **5–10 cm** | **medium curves**, and most lettering |
| **Elbow** | **20–30 cm** | **long arcs and the majority of drawing** |
| **Shoulder** | **40 cm and more** | **full-canvas lines, gesture, and anything that must be smooth** |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The single most common beginner fault across the whole subject** | **drawing from the fingers** |
| **What it produces** | **short, hesitant, hairy strokes**, because the fingers have the least range and the most tremor |
| **And on a tablet it is worse than on paper** | **because the mapped area is often small**, so a screen-sized line is a finger-sized movement |
| **Which is why the mapping lesson said map large** | — **a large mapped area forces the elbow and shoulder** |

---

**And the specific case that matters most later: the ellipse.** It gets its own lesson next, but the principle is here —

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An ellipse is a closed curve with no corners and constant smooth change** | |
| **So it cannot be drawn in segments** | a segmented ellipse has corners, always |
| **It must be one continuous motion**, usually drawn round two or three times | |
| **Which means it must come from the elbow or shoulder** | and **this is why people cannot draw ellipses: they are drawing them with their fingers** |

**Practice.** 100 arcs of varying radius, each ghosted as a full circle and drawn as a segment, alternating direction. Then 50 long sweeping curves across the full canvas, from the shoulder. Then deliberately draw 20 curves from the fingers and 20 from the shoulder and compare — the difference is the lesson, and seeing it once is worth more than being told.
Ellipses:
The hardest basic mark, why it matters more than it seems, and the three properties that make one correct.

**Why ellipses deserve their own lesson: every circle in three dimensions is an ellipse.** Wheels, cups, eyes, joints, barrels, the cross-sections of every cylinder, the openings of every tube. **Perspective turns every circle into an ellipse, and nothing else does the job.**

---

**The three properties, and all three must be right:**

| | Property | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Smooth and closed** | **one continuous motion, no corners, ends meeting.** Drawn through 2–3 times |
| **2** | **The correct degree** | **how open or narrow it is** — a circle seen face-on is 90°; nearly edge-on is 10°. **The degree records the angle you are seeing the circle from** |
| **3** | **The correct minor axis** | **the ellipse's narrow axis points along the axis of the form it belongs to.** A wheel's minor axis is the axle |

**Property 3 is the one that is wrong in nearly every beginner drawing**, and it is the one that makes a cup look broken. **The ellipse at the top of a cup has its minor axis vertical**, because that is the cup's axis. Tilt that and the cup is bent.

---

**How to draw one:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Ghost the motion** — a circling movement from the elbow, several times, above the surface |
| **2** | **Land without stopping**, and go round **two or three times** |
| **3** | **Lift while still moving** |
| **The two-or-three-times rule** | **gives the hand a chance to converge.** A single pass is a first attempt; the third is the one you aimed |
| **And it reads as intentional** | **a multi-pass ellipse looks like drawing, a single wobbly one looks like a mistake** |

---

**The degree, more precisely**, because it is a real variable with a rule:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A circle perpendicular to your line of sight** | **90°** — a true circle |
| **Tilted away** | **narrower, as the cosine of the angle** |
| **Edge-on** | **0°** — a straight line |
| **And along a cylinder receding from you** | **the degree WIDENS the further the ellipse is from your eye level** |

**That last point is the one that makes drawn cylinders convincing**, and it is why a stack of ellipses up a tube must change degree along its length. **A tube drawn with identical ellipses is a flat strip.**

---

**The exercises, in Drawabox's order:**

| | Exercise | What it isolates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Tables of ellipses** — a grid of boxes, each packed with ellipses touching their neighbours and the walls | **smoothness and consistency** |
| **2** | **Ellipses in planes** — an ellipse inscribed in a drawn plane, touching all four edges | **degree and axis, constrained** |
| **3** | **Funnels** — a curved axis with ellipses across it, all sharing a minor axis and changing degree along it | **the minor-axis rule**, which is the one that matters |

**Exercise 3 is the important one.** The others train the hand; the funnel trains the understanding.

**Practice.** Fill 10 full pages with tables of ellipses — this is the single largest count in the stage and it is not negotiable. Then 100 ellipses inscribed in drawn planes. Then 50 funnels, each with at least 7 ellipses sharing a minor axis. Then draw 20 cups and 20 bottles from life and check every ellipse's minor axis against the object's own axis.
Line weight, and what it is for:
Varying a line's thickness is not decoration — it is how a drawing states depth, light and importance without tone.

**Four jobs line weight does**, and knowing which one you are doing is the whole skill:

| | Job | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Depth** | **nearer forms get heavier lines.** The strongest and simplest use |
| **2** | **Overlap** | **the line of the form in front thickens where it crosses behind-form** — which states which is which in one mark |
| **3** | **Light** | **the shadow side's contour is heavier.** Light eats the edge it falls on |
| **4** | **Hierarchy** | **the silhouette heavier than internal detail.** What matters most reads first |

**And one job it does not do: making the drawing look nice.** Weight applied for appearance produces a drawing that is busy and says nothing.

---

**The overlap case worked properly, because it is the most useful:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Two forms cross. One is in front** | |
| **At the crossing, thicken the front form's contour** — just at the crossing, tapering away within a centimetre | |
| **And the behind form's line simply stops** | |
| **The result** | **unambiguous depth from two marks, with no tone and no perspective construction** |
| **Which is why it is Drawabox's main depth device** | — it works on any subject with no setup |

---

**How to produce weight on a tablet**, and there are three ways with different consequences:

| | Method | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Pressure** | **fast, natural, continuous.** And it tapers at both ends whether you want it to or not |
| **2** | **A second pass over part of the line** | **deliberate and controllable.** Drawabox's preferred method, because it forces the decision |
| **3** | **A larger brush for a separate stroke** | **the most control, the slowest** |

**Method 2 is the one to learn.** Pressure makes weight happen accidentally; **a second deliberate pass means you chose where the weight goes and why.** And the second pass must be ghosted like any other stroke — a sloppy weight pass is worse than no weight.

---

**The two failure modes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Everything weighted** | **nothing reads.** Weight is a contrast device and contrast requires something unweighted |
| **Weight applied as a final pass over a finished drawing** | **it becomes a traced outline**, and the drawing looks like a colouring book. **Weight is applied as the drawing is built**, at the moment the relationship is decided |

---

**And the thing that makes line weight feel advanced and is actually simple:** **it is the first place a drawing stops recording what is there and starts saying what matters.** A photograph has no line weight. **Every weighted line is an editorial decision**, which is Crane's point from the first lesson arriving in practice.

**Practice.** Take 30 pairs of overlapping simple forms and state the overlap with weight alone, no tone. Then take 20 of your existing line drawings and add weight in a second pass for depth and overlap only — and compare each against the original. Then draw 20 subjects where the weight states the light direction, and check by asking someone which side the light is on.
Hatching, and tone without a grey:
Building value out of line, the four hatching systems, and the one rule that keeps hatching from turning to mud.

**Why learn this when a brush can lay a flat grey?** Three reasons, and the third is the real one:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **It is how ink works**, and ink is half the drawing tradition this curriculum draws on |
| **2** | **It describes form as it darkens** — hatching follows the surface, so it states curvature and tone at once |
| **3** | **It forces you to decide the value** — **you cannot smudge your way to a tone you have not chosen.** Which is exactly the discipline stage 14 needs |

---

**The four systems:**

| | System | What it is | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Parallel hatching** | lines in one direction, spacing controlling value | **flat planes, and anything where the form should not be emphasised** |
| **2** | **Cross-hatching** | a second layer at an angle to the first | **deeper values**, built in passes |
| **3** | **Contour hatching** | lines following the surface's curvature | **curved forms.** Describes shape and value together |
| **4** | **Stippling** | dots | **texture and soft gradients.** Enormously slow and sometimes the only thing that works |

---

**The rule that prevents mud: change one variable at a time.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Value from hatching comes from spacing, not from pressure** | **keep the line weight constant and vary the gaps** |
| **Because varying both** | gives a tone you cannot control or repeat |
| **And the second layer crosses at a shallow angle** | **30° to 45°.** At 90° it makes a visible grid that reads as texture rather than tone |
| **Three layers is usually the limit** | past that it fills in and becomes a flat black with lumps |

---

**Contour hatching deserves the detail**, because it is the one that does the most work:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The lines run across the form, the way a cross-contour does** | |
| **So on a cylinder they are ellipse segments**, and on a sphere they curve in both directions | |
| **Which means the hatching states the curvature even where the value is flat** | |
| **And the error that ruins it** | **hatching a curved form with straight parallel lines** — the value is right and the form reads flat |
| **Hogarth and Bridgman both draw this way** | which is why their anatomy plates read as three-dimensional with no tone at all |

---

**On a tablet, two specifics:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Use the uniform-width pen** — brush 2 from stage 1 | **pressure variation defeats the spacing-controls-value rule** |
| **And resist the urge to use the line tool** | **mechanically perfect hatching looks mechanical.** The slight irregularity of hand-drawn hatching is what makes it read as drawing |

**Practice.** Make a 10-step value scale in parallel hatching, spacing only, each step a clear increment. Then the same scale in cross-hatching, and again in stippling. Then hatch 20 spheres and 20 cylinders with contour hatching, following the form. Then take 10 of your line drawings and render each with hatching alone, no greys.
Aiming, and hitting the point:
Accuracy as a separate skill from smoothness, why they trade against each other, and how to train the one without losing the other.

**Two different failures, and they need different fixes:**

| | Failure | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **The line wobbles** | **unplanned or too slow** | **ghosting, and speed** | |
| **The line is smooth and lands in the wrong place** | **the plan was wrong** | **aiming practice** | |

**Stage 2's earlier lessons fixed the first.** This one is the second, and it is the one that persists — **a confident line in the wrong place is still wrong**, and it is wrong in a way that looks deliberate.

---

**The trade, stated plainly:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Fast strokes are smooth and inaccurate** | |
| **Slow strokes are accurate and ugly** | |
| **Practice does not remove the trade — it moves it** | |
| **A trained hand is accurate AT SPEED**, which is a different thing from being accurate slowly | |
| **So training accuracy slowly trains the wrong skill** | and this is the lesson's whole point |

**Which means: aim practice must be done at full drawing speed, accepting the misses.** Slowing down to hit the mark defeats the exercise.

---

**The four exercises, in increasing difficulty:**

| | Exercise | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Two dots, one ghosted line.** Score a hit as landing within a nib's width of each dot | **200 lines** |
| **2** | **Three dots, two connected lines** — plan both before drawing either | **100 pairs** |
| **3** | **A dot and a direction.** Start at the dot, draw 10 cm at a stated angle, check with a straight edge | **100 lines** |
| **4** | **Dot-to-dot at distance** — points at opposite corners of the canvas, drawn from the shoulder | **100 lines** |

**Exercise 3 is the one that transfers.** Most real drawing is not connecting two visible points — **it is starting somewhere and going in a direction for a length**, which is how every construction line works.

---

**And the thing that improves aim fastest is not more lines — it is checking.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw the line. Then measure the error** | |
| **Where did it land relative to where you aimed?** | |
| **Is the error consistent?** | **it usually is.** Most people overshoot in one direction and undershoot in another, by handedness |
| **Once you know your bias, you can aim off it** | **which is a conscious correction that becomes unconscious within a few hundred lines** |
| **Without checking, 200 lines teaches nothing** | **you repeat the same bias 200 times** |

**That is the difference between practice and repetition**, and it applies to every count in this curriculum.

---

**One tablet-specific note.** Hover makes aiming easier than it is on paper, and that is fine — **but do exercise 1 sometimes without hovering**, landing the nib directly, because it tests the hand-eye map from stage 1 rather than the cursor.

**Practice.** 200 ghosted lines between dot pairs, scoring each as hit or miss at both ends, and recording the running percentage. Then 100 lines of exercise 3, checking each angle. Then work out your own directional bias from the misses and write it down. Then repeat exercise 1 for 100 lines with hover off.
Sighting and measuring:
How to get proportions right from observation without guessing: the pencil-held-at-arm's-length method, and its digital equivalents.

**The problem it solves:** your eye is unreliable about proportion and reliable about comparison. **Asked "how long is that arm?" you will be wrong. Asked "is the arm longer or shorter than the head?" you will be right.** Sighting converts the first question into the second.

---

**The traditional method, which still works:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Pick a unit.** Something in the subject — the head, a hand, a bottle's width. **Everything is measured in that unit** |
| **2** | **Hold the pen at arm's length, locked elbow**, and mark the unit against the subject with your thumb |
| **3** | **Count how many units** fit along the thing you are measuring |
| **4** | **Transfer that count to the drawing**, in whatever size the unit is on your canvas |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Arm's length and locked elbow are not fussiness** | **the measurement is an angle subtended at your eye**, so it is only consistent if the distance is consistent |
| **One eye closed**, for the same reason | |
| **And you must not move** | a different viewpoint is a different set of proportions |

---

**Measuring angles**, which is the half people skip:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Hold the pen along the edge you are judging** | |
| **Compare it with true vertical and true horizontal** — **the pen's own edge against the frame of your view** | |
| **Then reproduce that angle on the canvas** | |
| **Why it matters** | **a roof's pitch, a shoulder's tilt and a thigh's direction are all angles**, and they are what make a drawing feel observed rather than invented |
| **Edwards' name for it** | sighting, and her course spends a long time on it |

---

**On a tablet, the same methods plus three the medium gives free:**

| | Method | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **A reference layer at low opacity** | **to measure against, not to trace.** The distinction is whether you draw through it |
| **2** | **Guide lines on their own layer** | horizontals and verticals through key landmarks — deleted at the end |
| **3** | **Flipping the reference and your drawing together** | **the mirror check from stage 1, applied to observation** |

**And one honest warning: the tablet makes tracing frictionless.** The line between measuring against a reference and drawing over it is one Ctrl-click away. **A traced drawing teaches nothing and looks fine**, which is the worst combination.

---

**The two measurements that catch most errors**, if you only ever take two:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Total height against total width** | **the bounding box.** Getting this wrong makes everything inside it wrong |
| **2 — The halfway point** | **where is the vertical middle of the subject?** On a standing adult it is roughly the pubic bone, and almost everyone draws it too high |

**Practice.** Draw 30 still-life objects from life using sighting for every proportion, and write the unit you chose on each. Then draw 20 subjects measuring only the bounding box and the halfway point, and nothing else — and see how much that alone fixes. Then take 10 drawings you have already made and measure them against their references to find your consistent errors.
Negative space:
Drawing the gaps instead of the thing, why it works, and the one subject it rescues.

**The exercise: draw the shapes of the empty space around and between the parts of the subject, and let the subject appear as what is left.**

**It sounds like a gimmick and is one of the most reliable techniques in observational drawing**, for a specific reason.

---

**Why it works:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **You have a symbol for a chair** | and when you draw a chair, the symbol competes with what you see |
| **You have no symbol for the gap between a chair's legs** | |
| **So you are forced to look at it** | **and record the shape actually there** |
| **Edwards' whole argument** | **the obstacle to drawing is knowing what things are called.** Naming invokes the symbol |
| **Negative space defeats naming** | because the shapes have no names |

---

**Where it is most useful**, and it is not everywhere:

| Subject | Why negative space helps |
| --- | --- |
| **Chairs, bicycles, machinery** | **lots of enclosed gaps**, and complex positive forms your symbol-making will simplify |
| **Hands** | **the gaps between fingers are easier to see than the fingers** — and hands are stage 9's hardest problem |
| **Foliage and trees** | **the sky holes.** Harding's whole method for trees rests on this |
| **A figure with limbs crossing the body** | **the triangle between arm and torso tells you the arm's angle** immediately |
| **Foreshortened limbs** | **the gap is not foreshortened the way the limb is**, so it is more honest |

**And where it is of little use:** a single smooth solid form — a vase, a head — **has no interesting negative space**, so the technique has nothing to bite on.

---

**The method:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Frame the subject.** Negative shapes need a boundary — the edges of your canvas will do |
| **2** | **Find the biggest enclosed gap and draw it as a shape** — as if it were an object |
| **3** | **Then the next, and the next** |
| **4** | **Do not draw the subject at all.** It arrives on its own |
| **5** | **Check: do the gaps tile together correctly?** They must, because they are a partition of the space |

**Step 5 is a free error check that positive drawing does not give you.**

---

**And the version that transfers into everything afterwards: use it as a check rather than a method.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw normally** | |
| **When something looks wrong and you cannot say why** | **look at a negative shape next to it** |
| **Compare it with the real one** | |
