| **The error is almost always visible there** | **because you are not looking at the thing you have a symbol for** |
| **This is the single most useful diagnostic in observational drawing** | and it costs nothing |

**Practice.** 20 negative-space drawings of a chair, a bicycle and similar open structures — gaps only, never the object. Then 20 of your own non-drawing hand with fingers spread. Then 10 of foliage, drawing only the sky holes. Then take 10 existing figure drawings and check one negative shape in each against the reference.
Blind and modified contour:
Nicolaides' two oldest exercises, what each trains, and why the drawings they produce are supposed to be bad.

**Blind contour drawing: look only at the subject, never at the paper, and move the pen as slowly as your eye moves along the edge.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The rule** | **your eye and your hand move together, at the same speed, continuously** |
| **You do not look at the drawing.** At all | |
| **You do not lift the pen** | |
| **And the result will be distorted, overlapping and unrecognisable** | **which is correct.** The drawing is a by-product |

---

**What it actually trains**, since the output is useless:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The coupling of eye and hand** | **continuous recording rather than glance-then-draw** |
| **Looking for longer than you want to** | — beginners look at the subject perhaps 20% of the time; the proportion should be the reverse |
| **Attention to edge detail** | because you have nothing else to do while moving slowly |
| **And the removal of judgement** | **you cannot judge a drawing you cannot see**, so the self-criticism that stops people drawing is switched off |

**Nicolaides' claim is that this is the most important exercise in his book**, and that a student should do it for weeks before anything else. **That is an overstatement of a real effect.**

---

**Modified contour: the same, but you may glance at the drawing occasionally** — perhaps every few seconds, to reposition.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Produces drawings that are recognisable and still distorted** | |
| **Which makes it the usable version** | and the one to do more of |
| **The ratio to aim for** | **roughly 80% looking at the subject, 20% at the drawing** — which is the proportion the exercise is really teaching |

---

**On a tablet, one adaptation and one advantage:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The adaptation** | **you must not look at the screen**, so either cover it, close your eyes, or turn the monitor off. Closing your eyes is easiest and is enough |
| **The advantage** | **the drawing is not under your hand**, so there is no temptation to peek at it the way there is with paper |
| **And the pen has no feedback** | which makes it slightly harder and slightly more honest |

---

**Why these are in stage 2 rather than a "learning to see" stage of their own.** The first version of this curriculum opened with a whole stage on seeing, built on Edwards. **The material is good and it is not a stage** — it is four or five exercises, and they belong next to the other mark-making exercises rather than preceding them. **A beginner who spends three weeks on blind contours before learning to draw a straight line has learned to look and cannot draw.**

**Practice.** 20 blind contour drawings of your own non-drawing hand, 2 minutes each. Then 20 of complex objects — a crumpled shoe, a plant, a bunch of keys. Then 30 modified contour drawings at the 80/20 ratio, and compare them against the blind ones. Then, for one week, consciously count how often you look up at the subject during ordinary drawing.
Line economy:
Saying more with fewer marks: why a drawing with 40 lines can beat one with 400, and how to find which 40.

**The observation: beginners' drawings have too many lines.** Not badly drawn ones necessarily — **too many**, and the excess is what makes the drawing look uncertain.

---

**Where the excess comes from:**

| | Source | What it looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Searching** — drawing a line several times to find the right one | **a furry, hairy contour** |
| **2** | **Recording everything** — every fold, every hair, every edge | **a drawing with no hierarchy, where nothing matters because everything does** |
| **3** | **Not trusting the viewer** | **closing every shape, outlining every form** |
| **4** | **Not knowing what the drawing is about** | **the real cause of 1 to 3** |

---

**The fix for 1 is the ghosting method, already covered. The fix for 2 to 4 is a decision made before drawing: what is this drawing about?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A gesture drawing is about the action** | so it needs the line of action and almost nothing else |
| **A construction study is about the form in space** | so it needs the volumes and their intersections, and no surface detail at all |
| **A costume study is about the clothing** | so the face can be two marks |
| **And a drawing that is about everything is about nothing** | |

**Crane's point from the first lesson, arriving as a working method: the line is a decision about what to leave out.**

---

**Three exercises that force economy**, each a constraint:

| | Exercise | What it teaches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The fixed line budget.** Draw the subject in exactly 20 lines. Then 10. Then 5 | **which lines are load-bearing** |
| **2** | **The continuous line.** One unbroken stroke, never lifting | **connection and flow; it is also where many people first draw something they like** |
| **3** | **Timed.** 30 seconds, then 15, then 10 | **the same constraint applied by the clock rather than by counting** |

**Exercise 1 at 5 lines is the most instructive.** Five lines for a standing figure forces you to choose: the line of action, the shoulder line, the hip line, and two for the legs. **Those are the five that matter**, and discovering that by constraint is worth more than being told.

---

**And the test for whether a mark earns its place:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Remove it. Is the drawing worse?** | |
| **If not, it was decoration** | |
| **If you cannot tell, it was decoration** | |
| **The harder version** | **does it do a job no other mark does?** Two marks saying the same thing is one mark too many |

**On a tablet this test is free — hide the mark on its own layer and look.** Which is one of the places the medium is simply better.

**Practice.** 50 drawings under the 20-line budget, counting every line. Then 30 at 10 lines, and 20 at 5. Then 50 continuous-line drawings, pen never lifted. Then take 10 of your most detailed existing drawings and redraw each in under 20 lines, and decide honestly which version is better.
Warm-ups worth the time:
What to do in the first ten minutes of every session, why it is not optional, and the four that actually transfer.

**The case for warming up**, which is physiological rather than ritual:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The first lines of a session are measurably worse** | less accurate, less smooth, more hesitant |
| **Because the ballistic motor programs from stage 2's ghosting lesson need recalibrating** | **the arm's current state — temperature, fatigue, how long since you last drew — changes the mapping** |
| **And on a screenless tablet there is a second mapping to reload** | the hand-eye transform from stage 1 |
| **So the first ten minutes of real drawing are wasted anyway** | **the only question is whether you waste them on a drawing you care about** |

---

**The four, in order, ten minutes total:**

| | Warm-up | Minutes | What it reloads |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Dot targeting** — 30 dots, land on each without hovering | **2** | **the hand-eye map** |
| **2** | **Ghosted lines** — 30 lines at mixed angles and lengths | **3** | **the ballistic stroke** |
| **3** | **Ellipses** — 2 tables, or 20 funnels | **3** | **the elbow, and smooth continuous motion** |
| **4** | **Boxes** — 10 rotated boxes, freehand | **2** | **three-dimensional thinking, which is the one that needs it most** |

**Warm-up 4 is the one people drop and the one that matters most**, because **spatial thinking is a cold start even when the hand is warm.** Ten boxes before a figure drawing session measurably improves the figures.

---

**What warming up is not:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It is not practice** | **the counts in this curriculum are separate.** Thirty warm-up lines do not count towards the 200 |
| **It is not a drawing** | do not try to make it good, and do not keep it |
| **It is not an hour** | **ten minutes.** A warm-up that eats the session is avoidance |
| **And it is not a substitute for the exercises** | **a year of warm-ups is a year of not drawing anything** |

---

**And the related habit that is not a warm-up: the daily minimum.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Drawing habit on the dashboard is daily** | and the tick is binary |
| **So define the minimum that counts** | **ten minutes of warm-up plus one drawing of any kind** |
| **Why a defined minimum matters** | **because the days you do not want to draw are the days the habit is actually built**, and a minimum you can hit while tired protects the streak |
| **And on good days you will exceed it without being told** | |

**This is the one place a drawing curriculum should be lenient**, because the thing being protected — drawing most days for years — is worth more than any individual session.

**Practice.** Do the four warm-ups before every session for 30 days without exception, and log each one. Then try 10 sessions without warming up and compare the first five minutes of real work. Then settle on your own four and write them at the top of the count log.
The line checklist:
The stage closed as a list: what to check before deciding a line problem is a drawing problem.

**The diagnosis order. A drawing that looks wrong is usually wrong for one of these reasons, in this order of likelihood.**

| | Check | If yes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Are the lines furry — several attempts at one line?** | **ghosting.** Plan, rehearse, commit once, live with it |
| **2** | **Are they wobbly rather than furry?** | **too slow.** Execute at speed; accuracy comes from the plan |
| **3** | **Are they smooth but in the wrong places?** | **aiming.** Check your directional bias and correct for it |
| **4** | **Are they drawn from the fingers?** | **map the tablet larger and draw from the elbow and shoulder** |
| **5** | **Are the ellipses lumpy or segmented?** | **one continuous motion, round two or three times, from the elbow** |
| **6** | **Do the ellipses look right but the object wrong?** | **the minor axis.** It must align with the form's own axis |
| **7** | **Is everything the same weight?** | **weight for depth and overlap, applied as you build, not as a final outline** |
| **8** | **Are there too many lines?** | **decide what the drawing is about and remove what does not serve it** |
| **9** | **Is the stabiliser on?** | **turn it off and find out what your lines actually look like** |

---

**The settings this stage assumes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Stabiliser** | **None** |
| **Brush** | **the uniform-width pen for exercises; the hard round for drawing** |
| **Undo** | **mistakes only, never retries** |
| **Mapped area** | **large, one monitor, proportional — and unchanged since stage 1** |
| **Layers** | **one** |

---

**The counts this stage asks for, totalled**, since they are the actual work:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **50 sets of superimposed lines** | |
| **About 700 ghosted lines** across the aiming and line exercises | |
| **50 ghosted planes with diagonals** | |
| **100 arcs and 50 long curves** | |
| **10 pages of ellipse tables, 100 ellipses in planes, 50 funnels** | |
| **3 full value scales in hatching, and 40 hatched forms** | |
| **About 160 observational drawings** across sighting, negative space, contour and economy | |

**That is somewhere between four and eight weeks at an hour a day**, and it is the foundation everything after it stands on. **The stage is not finished when the lessons are read.**

---

**And the three ideas to carry forward:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Plan slowly, execute fast.** The single most transferable thing in the stage, and it applies to every mark in every later stage |
| **2** | **The mark is a decision about what to leave out**, not a record of what is there |
| **3** | **Checking is what turns repetition into practice.** Two hundred lines drawn without measuring the error is two hundred repetitions of the same bias |

**Practice.** Run the nine-point diagnosis on 10 of your own recent drawings and write down which number each one fails on first. Then total your counts for this stage against the list above and finish whatever is short — the stage is done when the numbers are met, not when the reading is.
Why form comes before everything:
The single idea that separates drawing from copying, and the reason this stage sits third rather than tenth.

**The claim: you are not drawing a shape on a flat surface. You are drawing a solid object that exists in a space, and recording what it looks like from where you are standing.**

**That sounds like a distinction without a difference and it is the whole subject.**

---

**What changes when you believe it:**

| | Drawing shapes | Drawing form |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What a line is** | **the boundary of a shape** | **the edge of a solid turning away from you** |
| **What you do when it looks wrong** | **adjust the shape until it looks right** | **work out where the form actually is and redraw it** |
| **Can you draw it from another angle?** | **no** — you would have to find a new reference | **yes** — you know what the thing is |
| **Can you draw it from imagination?** | **no** | **yes.** This is the entire point |
| **Can you light it?** | **no** — you would have to copy the lighting from somewhere | **yes** — you know which surfaces face where |

**The last two rows are why this stage exists.** **Character design, creature design and every illustration Shepherds needs are drawings of things that do not exist and cannot be photographed.** Shape-copying cannot produce them.

---

**And the method, which is the oldest idea in the subject:**

> **Everything is built from the box, the cylinder and the sphere.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A torso is a box** | |
| **A limb is a cylinder, or two** | |
| **A head is a sphere with the sides cut flat** | — Loomis' construction exactly |
| **A tree trunk is a cylinder; a rock is a box with the corners knocked off** | |
| **Why these three** | **because you can construct them from imagination at any angle, and once they are in place the subject is placed with them** |

**Vilppu, Loomis, Bridgman and Hogarth all teach this, in slightly different words, and they are all right.**

---

**Why it comes third, after the line and before everything else:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **After the line** | **because constructing a form requires drawing a straight line and an ellipse on purpose**, and stage 2 is that |
| **Before gesture** | **arguable, and this curriculum's choice.** Gesture is stage 5; a figure built on gesture with no construction is a flat ribbon, and a figure built on construction with no gesture is a mannequin. **You need both, and construction is the one you can check** |
| **Before anatomy** | **absolutely.** Anatomy on top of construction is detail added to a solid; anatomy without construction is a vocabulary with no grammar |
| **Before perspective** | **deliberately.** Freehand three-dimensional drawing first, constructed perspective second — because **the hand should learn space before the ruler does** |

---

**And the honest statement of what this stage costs: it is the least rewarding stage in the curriculum.** You will draw several hundred boxes. **None of them is a picture.** The reason to do it anyway is that every later stage assumes it, and the people who skip it hit a wall at the figure and cannot work out why.

**Practice.** Take 20 simple objects from around the room and draw each one twice: once by copying its outline as a shape, once by constructing it from boxes and cylinders first. Then draw each from a different angle without looking at it again, and notice which method made that possible.
The box, and three-point space:
The single most useful form to be able to draw, why it is harder than it looks, and what a correct one proves.

**A box drawn freehand in arbitrary rotation is the fundamental test of spatial drawing**, because it has twelve edges whose directions are all constrained by each other. **Get any one wrong and the box visibly bends.**

---

**What a box in space actually is:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Three sets of four parallel edges** | |
| **In perspective, each set converges to its own vanishing point** | |
| **So a box in arbitrary rotation has three vanishing points** | **and that is what "three-point perspective" means** — not a dramatic camera angle, just a box not aligned with your view |
| **The three points lie on no particular line** | the two "horizon" points plus one above or below |
| **And none of them is usually on the page** | which is why this must be done by eye |

---

**How to draw one, Drawabox's method**, which is the most reliable for freehand:

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Draw the Y.** Three lines from a single point, roughly 120° apart — the near corner and its three edges |
| **2** | **Decide how far each vanishing point is**, which is really deciding how much each pair converges |
| **3** | **Add the three edges opposite the Y's arms**, each converging slightly towards its set's vanishing point |
| **4** | **Close the box** with the last three edges, each constrained by two already drawn |
| **5** | **Check the convergence** — the next lesson is entirely about this |

**The Y start is not arbitrary.** **It fixes the rotation of the box immediately**, and every subsequent edge is then constrained rather than invented.

---

**The three errors, in order of frequency:**

| | Error | What it looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Diverging edges** — a set that spreads instead of converging | **the box flares out**, which is the single most common fault |
| **2** | **Inconsistent convergence** — one pair converges fast, its partner slowly | **the box is twisted** |
| **3** | **Converging too hard** | **a box that looks like a wide-angle photograph.** Less common and less wrong |

**Error 1 happens because the far edge is drawn without reference to its partner.** The fix is mechanical: **before drawing any edge, find the two edges it must be parallel to in 3D, and make sure your new edge converges towards their meeting point rather than away from it.**

---

**And what a correct box proves**, which is why this exercise is the one everybody does:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **That you can hold three independent directions in your head at once** | |
| **That you can draw a line towards a point that is not on the page** | |
| **That you can constrain a new mark by marks already made** | |
| **All three are the skills every constructed drawing needs** | **and the box is the smallest exercise that requires all three** |

**Practice.** 100 boxes in arbitrary rotation, freehand, no rulers, no perspective construction. Draw each with the Y method and do not correct any of them. Then take 20 and extend every edge to find where each set actually converges — the lesson is in how far off they are.
The 250-box discipline:
Drawabox's signature challenge, what the number is for, how to adapt it to a tablet, and the correction method that makes it work.

**The challenge: 250 boxes in arbitrary rotation, freehand, with every box's convergence checked and corrected in a second colour.**

**It takes most people four to eight weeks**, and it is the single most recommended exercise in free drawing instruction for a reason worth understanding.

---

**Why 250 and not 25:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The skill is not conceptual** | **you understood the previous lesson in five minutes** |
| **It is perceptual and motor** | **learning to SEE convergence and to aim a line at an off-page point** |
| **Which is trained by feedback, repeated** | and each box gives you twelve lines of feedback |
| **At 25 boxes you are still thinking about it consciously** | |
| **At 250 it has become something your hand does** | **which is the actual goal** |
| **And the improvement is not linear** | **most people report the shift somewhere around box 150**, which is precisely why stopping at 50 feels pointless |

---

**The correction method, which is what makes it an exercise rather than a chore:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Draw the box** |
| **2** | **In a second colour, extend all twelve edges backwards**, away from the box |
| **3** | **Look at where each set of four actually converges** |
| **4** | **Mark it.** A tight cluster is correct; a spread or a crossing-over is the error made visible |
| **5** | **Do not redraw the box.** Move to the next one, carrying what you saw |

**Step 5 is the hard one and the important one.** The box is not the product. **The information is the product**, and redrawing destroys the record of what you actually did.

---

**The tablet adaptation**, since the original is ink on paper:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Second colour on its own layer** | **so the extensions can be hidden to see the box cleanly** |
| **The no-undo rule applies absolutely** | this is a stage-3 exercise |
| **No line tool, no perspective guides, no vanishing-point assist** | **Krita has all three and every one defeats the exercise** |
| **Fit several boxes per canvas** | 6 to 8 — the original fits them on an A4 page, and the density matters because comparison between neighbours is useful |
| **And keep every file** | **the 250 boxes are also a progress record**, and comparing box 1 with box 250 is one of the few unambiguous measures of improvement in this whole curriculum |

---

**What to watch as you go**, because 250 boxes done without attention is 250 boxes wasted:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Which of your three sets is worst** | **it will be consistent** — most people have one axis they handle badly |
| **Whether you diverge or over-converge** | also consistent, also correctable once named |
| **Whether rotation matters** | **boxes near-aligned with the view are easy; boxes rotated hard in all three axes are the test** |
| **So deliberately draw the hard ones** | **a challenge of 250 easy boxes trains nothing** |

**Practice.** 250 boxes, every one corrected in a second colour by the five-step method, 6 to 8 per canvas, all kept and dated. Add a line to the count log after every session. At boxes 50, 150 and 250, lay the three out side by side and write down what changed.
Checking convergence:
The skill underneath the box challenge, stated separately because it transfers to everything: how to see whether lines agree about where they are going.

**The core perceptual skill in constructed drawing is judging whether two lines converge, diverge or stay parallel — and by how much.** Almost nobody can do it accurately without training, and almost everybody can after a few hundred attempts.

---

**What convergence actually encodes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Two parallel edges in the world converge in your view** | because the far one subtends a smaller angle |
| **How fast they converge records how near they are to you** | **fast convergence means close; slow means far** |
| **Which means the convergence rate IS the depth information** | |
| **And a drawing with wrong convergence is a drawing with wrong depth** | regardless of how well the shapes are drawn |

---

**The three states, and how to tell them apart by eye:**

| | State | How it reads | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Converging** | the gap narrows going away | **correct for any receding pair** |
| **2** | **Parallel** | the gap is constant | **the pair is perpendicular to your line of sight** — correct sometimes, suspicious usually |
| **3** | **Diverging** | the gap widens going away | **always wrong** for a receding pair, and it is the most common error |

**Why divergence is so common** is worth knowing: **you draw the near edge, then look at the far edge in the reference and copy its angle.** But you have not accounted for the near edge's angle, so the two are independently plausible and jointly impossible.

---

**The four checks, in increasing power:**

| | Check | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Extend the lines and look** | **the box-challenge method.** Slow, reliable, and the one that teaches |
| **2** | **Compare the near gap with the far gap** | fast, and enough for most judgements |
| **3** | **Flip the canvas** | **convergence errors are extremely visible mirrored**, and this is free |
| **4** | **Lay a straight edge along a line and see what it points at** | for a specific suspicion |

**Check 3 is underrated.** The flip from stage 1 catches convergence errors better than it catches almost anything else.

---

**And the generalisation, which is why this is its own lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The box is the training case** | |
| **The real cases are everywhere** | **a figure's shoulder line and hip line; the top and bottom of a wall; the near and far edges of a table; the two sides of a limb; a row of trees** |
| **In every one, two or more lines must agree about a point off the page** | |
| **And the error is always the same** | **each line drawn plausibly on its own and impossibly together** |
| **Which is why the fix is always the same** | **draw the second line in relation to the first, not in relation to the reference** |

**Practice.** Take 50 photographs of rectilinear objects and, on a layer over each, extend every receding edge to find the vanishing points — before drawing anything. Then 50 boxes drawn with the convergence checked by eye only, afterwards verified by extension, scoring each as converging, parallel or diverging. Then go back to 20 old drawings and extend their edges, and find out what you have been doing wrong consistently.
The cylinder:
The second primitive, the ellipse rule that governs it, and why a stack of identical ellipses is always wrong.

**A cylinder is two circles joined by a surface.** In a drawing it is **two ellipses joined by two straight lines tangent to both** — and almost everything about drawing one correctly is about the ellipses.

---

**The three rules:**

| | Rule | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Both ellipses share one minor axis**, which is the cylinder's own axis | **a cylinder whose ellipses disagree is bent** |
| **2** | **The far ellipse is NARROWER in degree than the near one** — unless the cylinder recedes away from eye level, in which case it is wider | **identical ellipses give a flat strip, not a tube** |
| **3** | **The sides are tangent to both ellipses**, not drawn to their widest points | **sides drawn to the ellipse's extremes make the cylinder pinch** |

**Rule 2 is the one that makes a drawn cylinder convincing**, and the reason is the same as the box's convergence: **a cylinder's sides converge, so the far circle subtends a smaller angle** — and for an ellipse that means a change of degree.

---

**Rule 3 deserves a diagram in words**, because it is subtle and universally got wrong at first:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An ellipse's widest point is at the end of its major axis** | |
| **But a cylinder's silhouette edge is where your line of sight is tangent to the surface** | |
| **For a tilted cylinder, those are not the same point** | |
| **So the side line touches each ellipse slightly short of its widest point** | and **the two tangent points are not opposite each other** |
| **Drawing to the widest points instead** | **gives a cylinder that bulges at the ends** |

---

**And the degree-changes-along-the-length rule, which Drawabox's cylinder challenge is built on:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Put a row of ellipses along one axis — a tube, a spring, a stack of coins** | |
| **Every ellipse shares the minor axis** | |
| **And each one's degree depends on its distance from your eye level** | **widening as it gets further from eye level in either direction** |
| **So a vertical tube running from above your eye level to below it** | **is narrowest at eye level and widens both up and down** |
| **Which is exactly what a row of lampposts or a column of barrels looks like** | and getting it right is what makes a drawn scene sit in space |

---

**Where cylinders are actually used**, so the practice has a point:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Every limb** | an arm is two tapered cylinders, a leg likewise |
| **The neck, the torso's rib cage in Vilppu's construction, fingers** | |
| **Tree trunks and branches** | |
| **Bottles, cups, barrels, wheels, columns, pipes** | — most man-made objects |
| **And the taper matters** | **a true cylinder is rare in nature; a tapered one, a cone section, is the usual case** |

**Practice.** 100 cylinders in arbitrary rotation, each with both ellipses' minor axes checked against the drawn axis. Then 50 cylinders drawn around a pre-drawn axis line, which is the harder and more useful version. Then 30 tubes with at least 7 ellipses along their length, changing degree correctly. Then draw 20 arms and 20 legs as tapered cylinders only, no anatomy.
The sphere, and why it is hardest:
The simplest form to draw and the hardest to draw convincingly: what a circle lacks, and how cross-contours supply it.

**A sphere's outline is a circle from every angle.** Which means **the outline carries no information about orientation, size or position in space** — and that is the whole problem.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A box tells you where it is** | its convergence encodes distance and rotation |
| **A cylinder tells you** | its ellipse degrees encode orientation |
| **A sphere tells you nothing** | **a circle is a circle** |

**So everything that makes a drawn sphere read as a sphere comes from outside its outline.**

---

**The four things that give a sphere its form:**

| | | What it supplies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Cross-contours** | **drawn lines across the surface**, describing curvature directly. The next lesson's whole subject |
| **2** | **Shading** | the terminator's curve states which way the surface turns. Stage 14 |
| **3** | **A cast shadow** | **states where the ground is and therefore where the sphere is** |
| **4** | **Context** | an overlap, a surrounding object, a horizon |

**Without at least one of these, a drawn sphere is a circle**, and no amount of care with the outline will change that.

---

**And the specific trap: the ellipse that is not there.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The sphere's silhouette is a circle** | |
| **The sphere's "equator" — any great circle on it — is an ellipse** | |
| **And beginners draw the equator touching the silhouette** | **which is wrong** |
| **Why** | **a great circle's silhouette tangency happens at the ends of its major axis only**, and the ellipse must sit inside the circle everywhere else |
| **An equator drawn touching the circle all round** | **makes the sphere look like a flat disc with a line on it** |

**This matters enormously later: the head is a sphere, and its construction depends on exactly this.** Loomis' ball-and-plane head draws the brow line and the centre line as great circles, and **both are ellipses that touch the outline only at their ends.**

---

**How to draw one convincingly:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Draw the circle.** Use the ellipse technique from stage 2 — continuous motion, two or three passes |
| **2** | **Decide the orientation** — where is its "north pole"? A sphere has no intrinsic one, so you are assigning it |
| **3** | **Draw the equator as an ellipse** whose minor axis is the pole axis, sitting inside the circle |
| **4** | **Add two or three more cross-contours** parallel to the equator, narrowing towards the poles |
| **5** | **A contact shadow** where it meets a surface |

**Steps 2 to 4 are the lesson.** They are also exactly how a head is constructed.

---

**And the honest note on circles themselves.** A freehand circle is hard, and **it is one of the few places where using an aid is reasonable** — in a construction drawing where the circle is scaffolding rather than content. **But do the 100 in the practice first**, because a hand that cannot approximate a circle cannot approximate a head.

**Practice.** 100 freehand circles, continuous motion, no aids, measured against a drawn circle for roundness. Then 50 spheres with assigned poles, equator and two cross-contours each, checking the equator does not touch the outline. Then 30 spheres with contact shadows on a drawn ground plane. Then draw 20 heads as spheres only, with the brow line and centre line as great circles — which is the whole of stage 10's opening.
Cross-contour:
Lines drawn across a form rather than around it: the most direct way to state curvature, and the one that exposes whether you understand a surface.

**A contour line follows the silhouette. A cross-contour runs across the surface**, the way a stripe painted around a vase would, or the way a contour line on a map follows a constant height.

---

**What it does that nothing else does:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **States the surface's curvature directly** | without tone, without colour, without context |
| **In a way that cannot be faked** | **a cross-contour drawn wrongly is obviously wrong**, where a wrongly drawn silhouette can look plausible |
| **Which makes it a test** | **if you cannot draw a cross-contour on a form, you do not understand its surface** |
| **And it is how Bridgman's and Hogarth's plates read as solid** | with no shading at all |

---

**The rules:**

| | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **A cross-contour is an ellipse or an arc**, because it is a circle or curve on a form seen in perspective |
| **2** | **Its curvature increases towards the silhouette edge** — because near the edge the surface is turning away from you fastest |
| **3** | **It must wrap.** A cross-contour that stops at the silhouette and does not imply continuing round the back states nothing |
| **4** | **Its direction tells you which way the surface bulges** — curving away from the viewer at the centre means convex, towards means concave |

**Rule 2 is the one that separates a convincing cross-contour from a flat one.** Evenly curved cross-contours make a cylinder; **accelerating ones make a sphere.**

---

**The four kinds of surface and what their cross-contours look like:**

| Surface | Cross-contours |
| --- | --- |
| **Cylinder** | **parallel ellipses, same minor axis, degree varying with position** |
| **Sphere** | **ellipses narrowing towards the poles, each inside the silhouette** |
| **Cone** | **ellipses whose size and degree both change along the axis** |
| **Saddle or cloth fold** | **curves that reverse** — convex becoming concave, which is what makes drapery hard |

---

**And the practical use, which is not decorative.** Cross-contours are mostly construction rather than finished line:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Drawn during construction and then removed or buried** | |
| **They put features on a surface correctly** | **an eye on a head, a button on a sleeve, a stripe on a limb** — place it on a cross-contour and it sits on the form rather than on the paper |
| **This is how Loomis places facial features** | the brow line, the eye line and the centre line are all cross-contours of a sphere |
| **And how a logo on a curved surface is drawn** | |
| **They are kept visible only in a technical or stylistic drawing** | where the construction is the content |

**Practice.** 50 cylinders, 50 spheres and 50 cones, each with at least 5 cross-contours, checking that curvature accelerates towards the edges. Then 30 drapery folds with reversing cross-contours. Then take 20 photographs of curved objects and draw cross-contours over them on a layer, following the real surface. Then place a feature — a circle, a stripe — on 20 forms using cross-contours to position it.
Foreshortening:
What happens when a form points at you, why it is the hardest thing in constructed drawing, and the three devices that make it work.

**Foreshortening is the compression of a form along the axis pointing towards or away from the viewer.** An arm pointing at you is nearly all hand, a little forearm, almost no upper arm.

**It is hard for a specific reason: what you know about the object contradicts what you see.** You know the forearm is long. You see a short stub. **The knowledge wins, and you draw it too long** — which is the same symbol problem the negative-space lesson named, in three dimensions.

---

**The three devices that state foreshortening:**

| | Device | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Overlap** | **the near form overlaps the far one.** The strongest and simplest. A fist drawn overlapping the forearm says the arm points at you |
| **2** | **Rapid size change** | **the near end is much larger than the far end.** The convergence lesson, applied to a limb |
| **3** | **Cross-contour** | **ellipse degree changes fast along a foreshortened form**, which states the compression directly |

**All three at once is what a convincing foreshortened limb has.** Any one alone is weak.

---

**The size change is more extreme than you think**, and this is the single most useful fact in the lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Perspective is not linear in depth** | **a form twice as close is twice as large on your retina** |
| **So a hand 40 cm from your eye and an elbow 70 cm away** | **the hand is nearly twice the size it would be at the elbow's distance** |
| **Which looks absurd and is correct** | |
| **Beginners halve it** | because the drawing looks wrong, and it is the knowledge overriding the observation again |
| **The fix** | **measure it.** Sighting, from stage 2, applied to a foreshortened limb |

---

**The cross-contour behaviour, precisely:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **On a limb pointing away from you, the ellipses narrow rapidly** | |
| **On one pointing at you, they widen rapidly** | |
| **The rate of change encodes the degree of foreshortening** | |
| **A limb drawn with slowly changing ellipses is a limb lying across your view**, whatever its outline says | |
| **Which means the ellipses can contradict the silhouette** | and when they do, **the ellipses win** — the viewer believes them |

---

**And the thing that makes extreme foreshortening possible at all: draw through the form.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Construct the whole limb as if it were transparent** | both ends of each cylinder, including the end you cannot see |
| **Place the far end in space properly**, even though it will be hidden | |
| **Then draw the visible silhouette around that construction** | |
| **Why** | **because the silhouette of a foreshortened form is unguessable** — it has to be derived from the construction, not invented |
| **Hogarth's *Dynamic Figure Drawing* is almost entirely about this** | and it is the one book here that pushes it to extremes |

**Practice.** 50 cylinders in extreme foreshortening, drawn through, with both end ellipses constructed. Then 50 arms and 50 legs pointing at and away from the viewer, using all three devices. Then take 30 photographs of foreshortened limbs and measure the near-to-far size ratio with sighting, writing each one down — the numbers are the lesson. Then draw 20 from imagination and check them against a posed reference.
Form intersections:
Where two solids meet: the line they share, why it is the hardest line in constructed drawing, and what getting it right proves.

**When two forms overlap in space, there is a line where their surfaces meet.** Drawing it correctly requires knowing both surfaces in three dimensions — **which is why it is the final test of whether a construction is real to you or merely drawn.**

---

**The four basic cases:**

| Pair | The intersection |
| --- | --- |
| **Box and box** | **straight line segments**, each lying in one plane of each box. The easiest case |
| **Box and cylinder** | **straight where the cylinder meets a flat face; curved where it wraps an edge** |
| **Cylinder and cylinder** | **a curve** — and if the radii are equal and the axes perpendicular, it is a pair of straight lines in the drawing, which surprises people |
| **Sphere and anything** | **always a circle, seen as an ellipse.** A sphere's intersection with any plane is a circle |

---

**The method that works, and it is the same every time:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Construct both forms fully, drawing through** — including the hidden halves |
| **2** | **Pick a point you are sure is on both surfaces** — usually where the silhouette of one crosses the silhouette of the other |
| **3** | **Find several more such points**, by asking at each one which part of each surface you are on |
| **4** | **Join them with a curve whose shape follows both surfaces' curvature** |
| **5** | **Check the ends** — the intersection must terminate on the silhouettes, not stop in mid-air |

**Step 2 is the whole trick.** **The silhouette crossings are free points** — you can see them, and they are definitely on both forms.

---

**And why it matters beyond the exercise**, which is not obvious until you see it:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Every joint in a figure is a form intersection** | **where the deltoid meets the arm, where the thigh meets the hip, where the neck meets the torso** |
| **Every piece of equipment meeting a body** | a strap over a shoulder, a belt round a waist, a boot on a leg |
| **Every architectural junction** | a roof meeting a wall, a chimney leaving a roof |
| **And drawing them wrong is the main reason a constructed figure looks like a mannequin** | **the parts are correct and the joins are pasted** |

**Drawabox's lesson 2 and its organic intersections exercise exist for exactly this**, and it is the point at which the box work starts paying.

---

**The two errors:**

| | Error | Why it happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The intersection drawn as a flat outline** — the far form's silhouette simply cut off at the near form's edge | **thinking in shapes.** It makes the near form look like a sticker |
| **2** | **The intersection curving the wrong way** | **not knowing which surface is in front at that point** — and the fix is to work out, at each point, which form's surface you would touch first |

---

**The organic case, which is the one figures need:** two tapered cylinders meeting at an angle, as a limb meets a torso.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The intersection is a saddle curve** | dipping on one side and rising on the other |
| **And it is almost never symmetrical** | because the forms are not the same size and the angle is not square |
| **Which is why a shoulder is hard** | and why Bridgman draws the shoulder as a wedge *between* the masses rather than as a join |

**Practice.** 100 pairs of intersecting primitives — box/box, box/cylinder, cylinder/cylinder, sphere/box — each drawn through and each intersection constructed by the five-step method. Then 50 organic intersections, tapered cylinders meeting at angles. Then 30 limb-to-torso joins drawn as pure form, no anatomy. Then take 20 photographs of real joints and draw the intersection line you can see.
Organic form:
The sausage, the tapered mass, and how the rigid primitives become the soft ones that figures and animals are made of.

**The problem with boxes and cylinders: nothing alive is one.** A limb is not a cylinder — it tapers, bends, swells at the joints and flattens at the planes. **But it is a cylinder first**, and the organic form is what you get by relaxing the primitive in controlled ways.

---

**Drawabox's "sausage" is the standard organic unit**, and its definition is precise rather than casual:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Two spheres of equal size** | |
| **Joined by a tube of constant width** | |
| **That is it.** No taper, no pinching, no change in width | |
| **Why equal and constant** | **because it keeps the form simple enough to construct reliably**, and a simple form you can place in space beats a subtle one you cannot |
| **And it bends** | **along its length, which a cylinder cannot do** |

**The sausage is the limb segment.** An upper arm is one, a forearm is one, a thigh is one. **Drawabox builds entire animals out of them**, and stage 12 does the same.

---

**Why the ends are spheres and this matters:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A sphere end gives a natural joint** | two sausages meeting at a shared sphere articulate properly |
| **It states the volume at the joint**, which is where real limbs are widest | |
| **And it makes the intersection tractable** | sphere-to-sphere is the easiest form intersection there is |
| **Compare the alternative** | **a tapered cylinder with a flat end** — which cannot bend, cannot articulate, and looks like furniture |

---

**The three controlled relaxations**, applied in order as the drawing gets more advanced:

| | Relaxation | Gives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Taper** — one end sphere smaller than the other | **a forearm, a calf, a tail** |
| **2** | **Flatten a plane** — one side of the tube made flat | **the shin's front plane, a forearm's flat inner surface** |
| **3** | **Swell** — a bulge in the tube's middle | **a calf muscle, a bicep.** This is where anatomy starts |

**Relaxation 3 is stage 7 and 8's whole subject**, and the point of doing 1 and 2 first is that **anatomy added to a correct simple form works, and anatomy added to a vague blob does not.**

---

**The cross-contour on an organic form**, which is how you check it:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A sausage's cross-contours are ellipses, like a cylinder's** | |
| **But their minor axes follow the BEND** | **so they fan rather than staying parallel** |
| **And at the bend's inside, the contours crowd together** | because the surface is compressing |
| **On the outside, they spread** | |
| **A bent limb whose cross-contours stay parallel** | **is a drawn bend on a straight form**, and it reads as rubber |

---

**And the thing to resist: drawing the organic form organically.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The temptation** | to draw a limb as a flowing silhouette, because that is what it looks like |
| **What it costs** | **you cannot foreshorten it, light it, or draw it from another angle** |
| **The order that works** | **construct the simple form, then find the organic silhouette on top of it** |
| **Which is Vilppu's whole method** | gesture to say what it is doing, construction to say what it is, anatomy to say what it is made of |

**Practice.** 200 sausages in arbitrary orientation, drawn through, with both end spheres constructed. Then 100 chains of 2 and 3 sausages articulating at shared spheres. Then 50 with cross-contours following the bend, crowding on the inside. Then draw 30 limbs from reference as sausage chains only, and 30 more adding the taper and one flattened plane.
Texture is form:
Drawabox's hardest lesson, the idea that reframes it, and why implying texture beats drawing it.

**The reframing, which is the lesson: texture is not surface pattern. Texture is small form, and small form is drawn the same way large form is — by its shadow.**

---

**What that means practically:**

| | Wrong | Right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **How you draw bark** | **outline each ridge** | **draw the shadow each ridge casts** |
| **What you are looking at** | **the pattern** | **the light** |
| **What it produces** | **a drawing that reads as a flat patterned surface** | **a drawing that reads as a rough solid** |
| **Where the marks go** | everywhere, evenly | **only where a shadow falls** |

**So texture is a lighting problem, and this is why Drawabox's texture lesson sits after its form lessons rather than before.**

---

**The method:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Decide the light direction** — texture without a light direction is pattern |
| **2** | **Identify the individual forms making the texture** — the ridges, the scales, the grains |
| **3** | **Draw only the shadow each one casts**, as a filled shape rather than an outline |
| **4** | **Let the shadows merge where the texture is dense and separate where it is sparse** |
| **5** | **Stop early** — the next point is why |

---

**Implying texture, which is the more important half:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Drawn uniformly across a surface, texture flattens it** | because **even detail reads as even**, and an even surface is a flat one |
| **So texture is drawn densely in one region and allowed to fade out** | |
| **Which does two things** | **it states the form's turn**, because texture compresses where the surface turns away; **and it directs attention**, because the eye goes to detail |
| **The practical rule** | **texture the transition between light and shadow, and leave the lit areas and the core shadow nearly bare** |
| **Which is also how a photograph looks** | texture is least visible in bright light and in deep shadow, and most visible in between |

---

**And the two failures:**

| | Failure | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Texture everywhere, evenly** | not deciding where it matters. Flattens the form and takes ten times as long |
| **2** | **Texture drawn as outline** | **the single most common one.** Outlined scales look like a net over the animal |

---

**One practical note for the tablet**, because it offers a shortcut that must be refused here:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Krita has textured brushes that stamp bark, scales and grain** | |
| **They are genuinely useful in finished work** | stage 16 |
| **And they teach nothing**, because the brush decides where the shadows fall | |
| **For this stage, the uniform pen and filled shadow shapes** | **you must know where the shadow goes before a brush can be allowed to put it there** |

**Practice.** Drawabox's 25-texture challenge: 25 textures, each drawn as a strip that fades from dense to nothing, shadows only, no outlines. Then take 20 photographs of textured surfaces and mark the light direction before drawing anything. Then draw 20 objects where the texture is concentrated only at the light-to-shadow transition. Then draw the same object twice — once textured evenly all over, once implied — and compare.
Drawing through:
Constructing the parts you cannot see, why it feels wasteful, and the three things it fixes.

**The practice: when you construct a form, draw its hidden edges too** — the back of the box, the far ellipse of the cylinder, the end of the limb behind the torso. **Treat every form as transparent while building it.**

---

**Why it feels wrong:** you are drawing lines that will not be in the finished picture, which looks like wasted effort. **It is not, and here is what it buys.**

---

**1 — It makes the form real rather than drawn.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A box with four visible edges is a shape** | |
| **A box with all twelve is a solid** | |
| **And the hidden ones constrain the visible ones** | — if the back of the box is impossible, the front is wrong, and you will see it |
| **Which means drawing through is an error check** | the cheapest one available |

**2 — It makes placement possible.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **You cannot put a leg behind a torso without knowing where the torso's back is** | |
| **You cannot put a hand on a far shoulder without the far shoulder existing** | |
| **Overlaps require both forms** | **and overlap is the strongest depth cue there is** |
| **So the drawings that need it most are the deep ones** | foreshortened, crowded, or with forms passing behind each other |

**3 — It is the only way to find a foreshortened silhouette.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The outline of a foreshortened limb cannot be guessed** | |
| **It is derived** — from where the construction's surfaces turn away from you | |
| **So the construction comes first and the silhouette is read off it** | |
| **Which is the previous foreshortening lesson's conclusion**, restated as a method | |

---

**How much to draw through, which is a real question:**

| Situation | How much |
| --- | --- |
| **An exercise in this stage** | **everything.** The construction is the point |
| **A figure construction, stages 6 to 9** | **the major masses and the joints** — not every muscle's far side |
| **A finished drawing, stage 16** | **as much as the pose needs**, on a layer that gets hidden |
| **A gesture drawing, stage 5** | **none.** Gesture is not construction and mixing them ruins both |

---

**And the tablet makes this strictly better than paper**, one of the few places where it clearly does:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Construction on its own layer, at 30% opacity** | |
| **The drawing on top** | |
| **Hide the construction to judge the drawing; show it to check the form** | |
| **On paper the construction is either erased — losing the check — or left visible** | |
| **This is the one layer use with no cost attached** | and it is worth setting up as part of the template from stage 1 |

**Practice.** Redraw 50 of your boxes from the 250 challenge with all twelve edges — and count how many of the originals turn out to be impossible solids. Then 50 cylinders and 50 sausages drawn through. Then 30 figures from reference, constructed transparently, with the far arm and far leg fully built before any silhouette is drawn. Then hide the construction on each and judge what remains.
Scale and the ground plane:
How a form gets a size: the ground, the horizon, and the one relationship that makes a drawn object sit in a world rather than float in a void.

**A form drawn alone has no size.** A box could be a die or a building. **Size is a relationship**, and this lesson is about the three that supply it.

---

**1 — The ground plane, and contact.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An object touching a drawn ground has a position** | |
| **An object not touching anything floats**, whatever else is right | |
| **The contact is stated by** | **a contact shadow**, the darkest small shape where the object meets the surface — **and it is the single cheapest way to anchor anything** |
| **Which Shepherds' own art contract requires** | its props are specified with a ground anchor and a contact shadow, for exactly this reason |

**2 — The horizon, which is your eye level.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The horizon line in a drawing is the viewer's eye height**, not a feature of the landscape | |
| **Which gives the most useful rule in the subject** | **everything the same height as you has its matching point ON the horizon** |
| **So in a street scene, every adult's eyes are on the horizon line** | regardless of how far away they are |
| **And that one fact places any number of figures correctly** | with no construction at all |
| **A low horizon means you are low** | lying down, or a child, or the camera is at the floor |

**3 — Diminution, which is comparison.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Two identical objects at different distances differ in drawn size by the ratio of their distances** | |
| **So the size difference IS the distance information** | |
| **And the error is always the same** | **not enough difference**, because the knowledge that they are the same size overrides the observation. The foreshortening lesson's problem again |

---

**The eye-level rule applied**, because it does more work than anything else in this stage:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Decide your eye height — say 1.6 m** | |
| **Draw the horizon at that height** | |
| **Any standing adult, anywhere in the scene, has their eyes on it** | |
| **A 0.8 m child's head reaches half the horizon height at the same distance** | |
| **A 3.2 m wall rises to twice the horizon height above its base** | |
| **Which means heights can be measured off the horizon**, anywhere in the picture, with no vanishing points at all | |

---

**And the thing this makes possible: drawing a scene rather than an object.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Stage 3 so far has been single forms in a void** | |
| **The ground plane is what turns them into a scene** | |
| **A box on a ground, with a horizon, at a size** — is a crate in a yard | |
| **The same box floating is a diagram** | |
| **And this is the bridge into stage 4**, which is the same ideas done with construction rather than by eye | |

**Practice.** Draw 50 scenes of 3 to 5 boxes on a ground plane with a stated horizon, each box a stated real size — a die, a crate, a shipping container — and check each against the horizon rule. Then 30 street scenes with at least 8 figures, every adult's eyes on the horizon. Then draw the same box 20 times at 20 distances and plot how its drawn height falls off. Then add contact shadows to 30 old drawings and see what changes.
Building a thing from primitives:
Putting the stage together: taking a real object, breaking it into forms, and rebuilding it from imagination at a new angle.

**This is the stage's exam.** Everything before it was a drill; this is the drill used for its purpose.

---

**The method, in five passes:**

| | Pass | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The bounding box** | **one box containing the whole object**, in the rotation you want. **Every proportion inside it is then a subdivision** |
| **2** | **Major masses** | **2 to 5 primitives**, placed inside the bounding box. Not details — the largest components |
| **3** | **Subdivision** | **divide the box and the masses to place everything else.** Halves, thirds, and diagonals |
| **4** | **Minor forms** | drawn onto the major ones, as form intersections |
| **5** | **Silhouette and detail** | **last, and derived from the construction rather than invented** |

**The order is the lesson. Beginners start at pass 5.**

---

**Pass 3, subdivision, is the one nobody is taught and everyone needs:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The diagonals of any rectangle cross at its centre** | **and this works in perspective** |
| **Which gives you the exact midpoint of a foreshortened plane**, for free, with two lines | |
| **Repeat for quarters, eighths** | |
| **And to divide into thirds** | draw the diagonals, then a line from a corner through the centre to the far edge |
| **To extend a rectangle by an equal amount** | **a diagonal through the midpoint of the far edge, extended, meets the next rectangle's corner** |
| **These four tricks place everything** | wheels on a cart, windows on a wall, buttons on a coat, eyes on a head |

**They are the reason the bounding box comes first.** **A bounding box plus subdivision replaces measuring entirely**, and it works at any rotation.

---

**What to practise on**, in order of difficulty:

| | Subject | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **A book, a brick, a box of matches** | **one primitive.** Proves the bounding box |
| **2** | **A mug, a bottle, a lamp** | **a cylinder plus small forms** |
| **3** | **A chair, a table** | **many primitives and real intersections.** The classic |
| **4** | **A hand tool — hammer, pliers, scissors** | **organic and rigid forms together** |
| **5** | **A boot, a bag, a helmet** | **soft forms with structure.** The bridge to stage 11 |

---

**And the test that proves it worked: redraw it from a different angle, without the reference.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **If you can, the construction was real** | |
| **If you cannot, you copied a shape** | |
| **There is no partial credit on this** | |
| **And it is the test every character design will face** | **a character sheet is one design drawn from several angles, and nothing else in drawing demands as much of construction** |

**Practice.** 40 objects constructed by the five passes, 8 from each difficulty tier. Then redraw every one of them from a 90° rotation without looking at the reference, and mark honestly which succeeded. Then take the 10 that failed and construct them again, with the bounding box and subdivision done more carefully. Then do 20 from imagination entirely — objects that do not exist but could.
The construction checklist:
The stage closed as a list: what to check when a constructed drawing looks wrong, and the counts the stage actually asks for.

**The diagnosis order:**

| | Check | If yes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Does the object float?** | **ground plane and contact shadow.** The cheapest fix in the stage |
| **2** | **Do any edges diverge?** | **convergence.** Extend them and look |
| **3** | **Are the ellipses' minor axes off the form's axis?** | **the cylinder rule.** This bends every tube in the drawing |
| **4** | **Do all the ellipses along a form have the same degree?** | **they must change.** Identical ellipses give a flat strip |
| **5** | **Is a foreshortened form too long?** | **almost always yes.** Measure it; the correct answer looks wrong |
| **6** | **Do the joins look pasted?** | **form intersections.** Construct them rather than cutting one silhouette off at another |
| **7** | **Is the construction hidden under the drawing or absent from it?** | **draw through.** Hidden edges constrain visible ones |
| **8** | **Did you start with a bounding box?** | **if not, the proportions have nothing holding them** |
| **9** | **Is the texture even across the surface?** | **it flattens the form.** Concentrate it at the light-to-shadow transition |
| **10** | **Can you redraw it from another angle?** | **if not, it is a copied shape, whatever it looks like** |

**Check 10 is the only one that matters absolutely.** The others are how you pass it.

---

**The counts this stage asks for:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **250 boxes**, corrected in a second colour — the largest single count in the curriculum | |
| **100 more boxes** across the earlier exercises, plus 50 redrawn through | |
| **About 250 cylinders**, including 50 around a pre-drawn axis and 30 tubes | |
| **150 circles and spheres**, with constructed equators and cross-contours | |
| **200 sausages**, plus 100 chains | |
| **150 cross-contoured forms** | |
| **100 form intersections**, plus 50 organic ones | |
| **25 textures** | |
| **40 constructed objects, each redrawn from a new angle** | |
| **About 150 scenes and placements** on a ground plane | |

**Six to twelve weeks at an hour a day**, and it is the longest stage in the curriculum by working time. **Everything after it assumes it.**

---

**And the four ideas to carry:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **You are drawing a solid seen from somewhere, not a shape on a surface.** Every other idea in the stage follows from this one |
| **2** | **Construct, then derive the silhouette.** Never the reverse, and especially not when foreshortened |
| **3** | **The bounding box plus subdivision replaces measuring**, and works at any rotation |
| **4** | **Draw through.** The hidden half is an error check, a placement tool and the only route to a foreshortened outline |

---

**One honest note on how this stage feels.** It is long, repetitive, and produces nothing worth keeping. **The 250 boxes are not a picture.** It is also the stage that most reliably separates people who can draw from imagination from people who cannot — **and the ones who cannot almost always skipped it**, because at the time it looked like the least rewarding thing available.

**Practice.** Run the ten-point diagnosis on 20 of your constructed drawings and tally which check each one fails first. Then total your counts against the list above and finish what is short. Then take the single object you construct worst and draw it 20 more times, from 20 angles, until the tenth check passes.
Why constructed perspective, after freeh:
The stage's premise: you can already draw in three dimensions by eye, and this is about the cases where the eye is not enough.

**Stage 3 built boxes freehand, judging convergence by eye.** That is the more important skill and it is not sufficient. **Three kinds of problem need construction.**

---

| | The problem | Why the eye fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Accuracy over a large scene** | **small convergence errors accumulate.** A street of twenty buildings drawn by eye drifts, and the drift is invisible until the scene is finished |
| **2** | **Things that must agree** | **a tiled floor, a brick wall, a row of identical windows.** The repetition makes any error obvious |
| **3** | **Deriving what you cannot see** | **the length of a shadow, the position of a reflection, the height of a figure 30 metres away** — these are computed, not observed |

**And one that is not a reason: making a drawing look three-dimensional.** Freehand does that. **Construction is for precision, not for conviction.**

---

**What constructed perspective actually is:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A geometric model of how light reaches one eye** | |
| **The viewer's eye is the **station point**, a single fixed point** | |
| **The **picture plane** is a sheet of glass between the eye and the world** | |
| **The drawing is what you would get by tracing the world onto that glass** | |
| **And every rule in this stage is a consequence of those three things** | |

**Which means perspective is not a convention or a style. It is a construction of a specific physical situation**, and that situation is: one unmoving eye, looking in one direction, at a flat plane.

---

**The consequences of those assumptions, which are also perspective's limits:**

| Assumption | What breaks when it is false |
| --- | --- |
| **One eye** | **you have two.** Which is why a perspective drawing never looks quite like looking |
| **Unmoving** | **you move constantly.** Real vision integrates many viewpoints |
| **A flat picture plane** | **your retina is curved.** Straight lines at the edge of a wide view really do look curved, and linear perspective says they are straight |
| **One direction of gaze** | **your eye darts.** The cone of vision lesson is about this |

**So a perspective drawing is correct for a viewer who does not exist.** It works anyway — **and knowing where the model breaks is what lets you break it deliberately** rather than by accident.

---

**And the order this curriculum chose, which is deliberate:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Freehand space in stage 3, construction in stage 4** | |
| **Because a hand that can only draw with vanishing points is useless for gesture, for figures, and for anything fast** | |
| **And a hand that draws freely but cannot construct is stuck when precision is required** | |
| **Drawabox makes the same choice** | its boxes are freehand and its perspective is taught as a sense rather than a system |
| **The classical schools made the opposite one** | and produced draughtsmen who could not sketch |

**Practice.** Draw the same room twice: once entirely freehand from observation, once constructed from a measured plan. Compare them for accuracy and for life. Then list five drawings you want to be able to make and mark, for each, whether it needs construction or not — the answer is usually no, and knowing when it is yes is the point of the stage.
The station point and the cone of vision:
The viewer's position as a geometric fact, the angle beyond which perspective distorts, and the single setting that makes a drawing look natural or wrong.

**Three things define the whole construction:**

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The station point** | **where the eye is** | a point in space |
| **The picture plane** | **the sheet of glass**, perpendicular to the direction of gaze | a plane |
| **The centre of vision** | **where the gaze meets the glass** | a point on the picture plane, on the horizon |

**And the distance from the station point to the picture plane is the one number that decides everything about how the drawing feels.**

---

**That distance, usually called the viewing distance, controls the apparent wideness of the view:**

| Viewing distance | Effect | Equivalent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Short** — eye close to the glass | **wide angle, strong convergence, dramatic** | a 20 mm lens |
| **Moderate** | **natural** | a 50 mm lens |
| **Long** — eye far from the glass | **narrow angle, weak convergence, flat** | a 200 mm lens |

**In a two-point construction it shows up as the distance between the two vanishing points**: **close together means a wide angle; far apart means a long lens.** And **beginners place them too close together**, which is why beginner perspective drawings look like fisheye photographs.

---

**The cone of vision**, which is the practical rule that follows:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Human vision is sharp only in a narrow cone** | and perspective construction is only undistorted within about **60°** |
| **Draw a circle on the picture plane centred on the centre of vision**, whose radius subtends 30° from the station point | |
| **Everything inside it looks natural** | |
| **Everything outside it stretches** | **a sphere becomes an ellipse, a box shears, a column at the edge of a wide view looks wrong** |
| **And it is not an error in the construction** | **it is correct and it looks wrong**, which is the picture-plane assumption breaking |

**The practical rule: keep the subject inside the 60° cone, and if it does not fit, move the station point back.**

---

**How the cone of vision shows up in practice:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A room drawn with the vanishing points on the page** | **is almost always too wide.** For a natural view the VPs are usually well off the paper |
| **Which is why professional perspective work is done with the VPs pinned to a board beyond the drawing** | or with a long string |
| **On a tablet** | **work on a canvas much larger than the final crop**, with the VPs out in the margin, and crop at the end |
| **Krita's perspective assistants** | can hold vanishing points outside the canvas, which is one of the few genuine advantages here |

---

**And the one thing to take away if nothing else: a drawing that looks distorted is usually a station point problem, not a drawing problem.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Figures stretched at the edges** | the subject is outside the cone of vision |
| **Everything looks like a fisheye** | the vanishing points are too close together |
| **Everything looks flat and stacked** | the vanishing points are too far apart, or the view is too narrow |
| **The fix in every case** | **move the station point and reconstruct**, rather than adjusting the drawing |

**Practice.** Construct the same cube six times with the two vanishing points at six different separations, from very close to very far apart, and write down which looks natural. Then draw a 60° cone of vision on each and see which parts of each cube fall outside it. Then take 20 photographs with a phone at its widest and its most zoomed, and find the equivalent vanishing-point separations.
One-point:
The simplest construction, what it is actually for, and the depth problem it does not solve by itself.

**One-point perspective: the subject's faces are parallel to the picture plane, so only the depth direction converges — to a single vanishing point at the centre of vision.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Horizontals stay horizontal** | |
| **Verticals stay vertical** | |
| **Only the depth lines converge, to one point** | |
| **Which point is the centre of vision** — directly ahead of the viewer, on the horizon | |

---

**What it is genuinely good for:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Interiors viewed down their length** | a corridor, a nave, a room from its doorway |
| **Roads and avenues** | |
| **Any symmetrical, frontal, formal composition** | — its symmetry is why it feels ceremonial |
| **And studies**, because it is the easiest case to construct correctly | |

**What it is bad for:** anything seen at an angle, which is most things. **A one-point drawing of a box seen cornerwise is a two-point drawing.**

---

**Now the problem it does not solve. One-point tells you where the depth lines go. It does not tell you how far along them anything is.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw a corridor's walls converging to the VP** | |
| **Where do you put the second door?** | **nothing in the construction says** |
| **Space them evenly on the page and they look wrong** | because depth compresses and even spacing does not |
| **This is the measurement problem**, and it needs one more device | |

---

**The device: the diagonal vanishing point.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A line at 45° in plan converges to a point on the horizon** | at a distance from the centre of vision **equal to the viewing distance** |
| **That point is the diagonal VP** — there is one on each side | |
| **And it works because a 45° diagonal crosses equal depths and equal widths at the same rate** | |
| **So: mark equal widths along the near edge, run diagonals to the diagonal VP, and where each crosses a depth line is the correct depth** | |

**This is the single most useful construction in one-point perspective**, and it gives you a correctly spaced tiled floor in about six lines.

---

**And the practical note that follows: the diagonal VP's position IS the viewing distance.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Close to the centre of vision** | **wide angle, strong depth compression** |
| **Far away** | **long lens, gentle compression** |
| **Which is the station-point lesson again**, arriving as a construction you can actually place | |
| **The usual mistake** | **putting the diagonal VP just off the edge of the paper because that is where there is room** — and producing a corridor that compresses absurdly |

**Practice.** Construct 20 one-point interiors with a correctly placed diagonal VP, each with a tiled floor of at least 8 × 8 tiles. Then construct the same corridor with the diagonal VP at three different distances and compare the compression. Then draw 10 rooms from photographs by finding the centre of vision first, then checking whether the real depths match your constructed ones.
Two-point:
The workhorse construction: a box seen cornerwise, where the vanishing points go, and the measuring method that makes it accurate.

**Two-point perspective: the subject's vertical edges stay vertical, and its two horizontal directions each converge to their own vanishing point on the horizon.**

**This is the default for almost everything** — a building seen from a street corner, a crate on a floor, a table.

---

**Placing the two vanishing points, which is the whole setup:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Both lie on the horizon** | |
| **Their separation is set by the viewing distance** — the station-point lesson's number | |
| **Their position relative to the subject is set by the subject's rotation** | **a box turned 45° has its VPs equidistant; a box turned slightly has one VP close and one very far away** |
| **And the geometric relationship** | **the angle subtended at the station point by the two VPs is 90°**, because the box's two directions are perpendicular |

**That last line is the rule that keeps a construction honest.** **If you place two VPs arbitrarily, the box they describe is not rectangular.** It will look like a box and its corners will not be right angles — which is invisible on one box and glaring on a street of them.

---

**Finding the station point from two VPs**, since it is the same relationship read backwards:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw a semicircle with the two VPs as its diameter** | |
| **The station point lies on that semicircle** — because an angle in a semicircle is a right angle | |
| **Directly below the centre of vision**, at the viewing distance | |
| **So given two VPs, the station point is determined**, and so is the viewing distance | |
| **Which is how you check whether your VPs are sane** | if the implied viewing distance is 15 cm, the drawing is a fisheye |

---

**Measuring: the measuring point method.** This is the part most people never learn and it is what makes two-point constructions accurate.

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Draw the near vertical edge of the box** — this is the **measuring line**, and it is in true scale because it lies in the picture plane |
| **2** | **Mark real measurements along it**, to whatever scale you like |
| **3** | **Find the measuring point for one direction**: swing an arc centred on that direction's VP, with radius equal to the distance from that VP to the station point, until it cuts the horizon |
| **4** | **Lines from your marks to that measuring point** cut the receding edge at the correct depths |
| **5** | **Repeat with the other VP's measuring point** for the other direction |

**Why it works**: the measuring point is the vanishing point of the lines that transfer true lengths from the picture plane onto the receding edge. **It is the same trick as the diagonal VP in one-point, generalised.**

---

**And the honest practical note.** Full measuring-point construction is slow, and **most drawing does not need it.**

| | Use it | Do not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A building that must be accurate** | **yes** | |
| **A tiled floor, a brick wall, a colonnade** | **yes** | |
| **A character design, a figure study, a sketch** | | **no** — the figure's own proportions matter more than the floor's |
| **A background for an illustration** | **sometimes** — construct the architecture, draw everything else by eye | |

**Practice.** Construct 20 two-point boxes with the station point verified by the semicircle test. Then 10 buildings with measuring points, every bay and storey measured rather than eyeballed. Then construct a room with a tiled floor, a brick wall and a flight of windows, all measured. Then draw 20 boxes freehand and check them afterwards against a constructed grid, to see how far your eye is off.
Three-point, and when verticals converge:
The third vanishing point: what it is for, why it is usually unnecessary, and the one case where leaving it out is wrong.

**Three-point perspective adds a vanishing point for the vertical direction**, so verticals converge too — upward for a worm's-eye view, downward for a bird's-eye.

---

**Why verticals usually do not converge in a drawing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **They converge when the picture plane is tilted** — when you look up or down | |
| **If you look straight ahead, the picture plane is vertical and parallel to the verticals** | **so they do not converge at all** |
| **Which is the normal case** | you look straight ahead most of the time |
| **So two-point is not a simplification of three-point** | **it is the correct construction for a level gaze** |

---

**When you need the third point:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Looking up at a tall building from its base** | |
| **Looking down from a height** | |
| **Any subject tall enough that its top leaves the cone of vision** | which is the real criterion |
| **And dramatic framing**, where the exaggeration is the point | |

**The criterion worth remembering: if the subject extends well outside the 60° cone vertically, you need three points** — because beyond that, two-point's parallel verticals visibly disagree with how it looks.

---

**Where the third point goes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **On a vertical line through the centre of vision** | |
| **Below the horizon for a bird's-eye view, above for a worm's-eye** | |
| **At a distance set by how steeply you are looking** | **steep gaze means a close third point and strong convergence** |
| **And usually a very long way off the page** | far further than beginners place it |

**Three-point drawings with the third VP just off the paper are the signature of comic-book dynamism**, and they are geometrically a view from about two metres away looking almost straight up. **Which is legitimate as a style and should be a choice.**

---

**Measuring in three-point is genuinely hard**, and this is worth saying plainly:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The measuring-point method extends to it** | and the construction is laborious |
