| **There is no true-scale line anywhere**, because no edge is parallel to the picture plane | |
| **So most three-point work is done by eye, with the construction only setting the three convergences** | |
| **Which is a reasonable compromise** | **and it is what Drawabox's freehand boxes are, every one of them** |

---

**And the thing that makes three-point feel wrong when it is right:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A building drawn in correct three-point from the ground looks like it is falling over** | |
| **Because it is** — that is what looking up at a building is like | |
| **And the viewer, who is used to photographs taken with the camera level, reads it as distortion** | |
| **Architectural photographers correct for exactly this** with a shift lens, producing parallel verticals that are geometrically a two-point view | |
| **So the choice is between correct and expected** | and that is a picture decision rather than a drawing one |

**Practice.** Construct 20 three-point boxes with the third VP at varying distances, and find the separation where it stops looking exaggerated. Then construct the same tower in two-point and in three-point and compare. Then photograph a tall building from its base and construct over the photograph to find where its third vanishing point actually is.
Measuring heights anywhere:
The one technique that places every figure, door and wall correctly in a scene, using nothing but the horizon.

**The rule, from stage 3, now used as a construction: the horizon is at the viewer's eye height, and anything at that height anywhere in the scene touches it.**

**From that single fact, every height in a picture can be derived.**

---

**The basic case — figures on a flat ground, viewer standing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Your eye height is, say, 1.65 m** | |
| **So every standing adult of your height has their eyes exactly on the horizon** | |
| **At any distance** — near figures are large, far figures small, and **both have their eyes on the line** | |
| **Which means a crowd is placed by drawing the horizon through everyone's eyes** | and nothing else |
| **A taller figure's eyes sit above the horizon; a shorter figure's below** | by the real difference, scaled |

**This is the fastest useful construction in the whole stage**, and it needs no vanishing points.

---

**The general case — any height, anywhere: the measuring pole.**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Establish one object of known height** somewhere in the scene — a figure, a door |
| **2** | **To place the same height elsewhere, draw a line from the base of the known object to the base of the new position**, and find where it meets the horizon — that is its vanishing point |
| **3** | **Draw a line from the top of the known object to that same vanishing point** |
| **4** | **Where it crosses the vertical at the new position gives the same real height there** |

**This transfers any height to any point on the ground plane**, and it is how a scene full of figures at different distances is kept consistent.

---

**Heights that are not on the ground:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Measure to the ground first** | drop a vertical from the object to the ground plane |
| **Transfer the ground point** | using the method above |
| **Then measure up from there** | |
| **Which is why the ground plane matters so much** | **it is the reference surface for every measurement in the scene** |
| **And an object with no derivable ground contact cannot be measured** | which is one more reason stage 3 insisted on contact |

---

**And the diagnostic use, which is how to check someone else's picture — or your own:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Find the horizon by extending any two known-parallel receding lines** | |
| **Check where it crosses the figures** | |
| **If it crosses one at the eyes and another at the chest** | **one of them is the wrong size**, or standing on different ground |
| **This is the error that makes a crowd scene feel wrong without anyone being able to say why** | |
| **And it is visible in seconds once you know to look** | |

**Practice.** Draw 20 scenes with 6 or more figures each, placed by the horizon rule alone, and check every one. Then draw 10 scenes with figures of three different heights — adults, a child, a mounted rider — using the measuring-pole transfer. Then take 20 photographs with people at different distances, find the horizon in each, and verify it crosses every adult at the same body level.
Dividing and multiplying:
The diagonal methods: halving, thirds, equal repetition and extension, all without measuring anything.

**The whole family rests on one fact: the diagonals of a rectangle cross at its centre, and this remains true in perspective.**

**Perspective preserves straight lines and incidence** — it does not preserve length, angle or parallelism, but **a point that is the intersection of two lines stays the intersection of those two lines.** Every construction here follows.

---

**1 — Halving.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw both diagonals of the plane. They cross at its centre** | |
| **A line through that centre, towards the appropriate vanishing point, divides the plane in half** | |
| **Repeat for quarters, eighths, sixteenths** | |
| **Works on any plane at any rotation**, floors, walls and ceilings alike | |

**2 — Equal repetition: extending a bay.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Given one rectangle — a fence panel, a window bay — and you want the next one, equal in real size** | |
| **Find the midpoint of the far vertical edge** (by diagonals, or by the midline already drawn) | |
| **Draw a line from the near top corner through that midpoint** | |
| **Where it meets the receding bottom line is the far corner of the next bay** | |
| **Repeat indefinitely** | **this is how a colonnade, a picket fence or a row of sleepers is drawn correctly** |

**3 — Thirds and other odd divisions.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Halving gives only powers of two** | |
| **For thirds: draw both diagonals, then a line from each near corner through the centre to the opposite far edge** | |
| **The crossings mark the thirds** | |
| **Or use a measuring line**: divide the true-scale near edge into three with a ruler, and transfer with the measuring point | |
| **The second is more general and slower** | |

**4 — Dividing a receding edge into equal real lengths**, which is the common hard case:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw a line from the near end of the receding edge at any convenient angle** | |
| **Step off equal divisions along it with a ruler** — it is not in perspective, so they are true | |
| **Join the last division to the far end of the receding edge** | |
| **Lines parallel to that one, through each division, cut the receding edge correctly** | |
| **This is the standard construction and it works on any line, in or out of perspective** | |

---

**Why these matter more than the measuring-point method:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **They need no station point, no measuring point and no scale** | |
| **They work from what is already drawn** | |
| **So they can be used in a freehand drawing** | which the full construction cannot |
| **And they are how you place things on a form** | **buttons down a coat, windows up a tower, the eyes on a head** — stage 10 uses method 1 constantly |

**Practice.** Construct 20 planes and divide each into halves, quarters and eighths by diagonals. Then draw 10 fences and 10 colonnades of at least 12 equal bays by the extension method, checking that the spacing compresses smoothly. Then divide 20 receding edges into 5 and into 7 equal parts. Then place 20 sets of features on curved and flat forms using diagonals alone.
Circles in perspective:
Constructing an ellipse rather than guessing it: the enclosing square, the eight points, and why a constructed wheel beats a drawn one.

**A circle in perspective is an ellipse** — stage 2 established how to draw one. **This is how to find the right one.**

---

**The method, in four steps:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Construct the square that encloses the circle**, in perspective, on the correct plane |
| **2** | **Draw its diagonals and midlines.** The midlines meet the square's edges at four points — **these are four of the circle's points**, because a circle touches its enclosing square at the midpoints of the sides |
| **3** | **Find four more on the diagonals.** The circle crosses each diagonal about **seven-tenths of the way from the centre to the corner** — precisely 0.707, which is 1/√2 |
| **4** | **Draw a smooth ellipse through all eight points**, in one continuous motion as stage 2 taught |

**Eight points is enough to pin an ellipse accurately.** Four is not — four points admit many ellipses.

---

**The two things this gets right that eyeballing gets wrong:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The ellipse is not centred in the square.** **Its centre is nearer the far edge than the perspective centre of the square**, because the far half is compressed. Drawing an ellipse centred on the diagonals' crossing is the classic error | |
| **2 — The minor axis is not perpendicular to the drawn square's edges**, in general. It aligns with the axis of the cylinder or the normal of the plane, which is a 3D direction and not a 2D one | |

**Error 1 is worth dwelling on.** The square's centre in perspective — where the diagonals cross — **is not the ellipse's centre.** The ellipse's major axis passes slightly nearer the viewer than that crossing. **Which is why a wheel drawn centred on the hub looks wrong, and the hub is genuinely not at the ellipse's centre.**

---

**Where this is used:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Wheels** — the canonical case, and a cart has four | |
| **Arches, vaults and round windows** | **York's architecture**, which is stage 11 and 13's subject |
| **Cups, bowls, barrels, wells** | |
| **Round tables and the objects on them** | |
| **And anything circular on a tilted plane** | where eyeballing is hopeless |

---

**The practical compromise, which is what most working artists do:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Construct the first circle properly** | one careful eight-point ellipse |
| **Draw the rest by eye, matching its degree and axis** | |
| **Because once one is right, the others are a comparison** | and comparison is what the eye is good at |
| **And for a drawing where no circle is prominent, construct none** | |

**Practice.** Construct 30 circles by the eight-point method on floors, walls and tilted planes. Then draw 20 of the same circles by eye first and construct them afterwards, measuring how far off your ellipse centre was. Then draw 10 carts or wagons with 4 wheels each, the first constructed and the rest matched. Then construct 10 arches and 10 round windows in a wall.
Inclined planes:
Roofs, ramps and stairs: where a sloping surface's vanishing point goes, and the vertical line that finds it.

**A sloping plane does not vanish on the horizon.** Its vanishing point sits above or below — and finding it is one construction, used constantly, that almost nobody is taught.

---

**The rule:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Take the slope's horizontal direction** — the way the roof ridge or the ramp runs in plan | |
| **Find that direction's vanishing point on the horizon**, as normal | |
| **Draw a vertical line through it** — the **vertical trace** | |
| **The slope's vanishing point lies on that vertical line** | |
| **Above the horizon for a rise, below for a fall** | and further from the horizon the steeper the slope |

**That is the whole construction.** A roof's two pitches have two vanishing points, one above and one below the horizon, **both on the same vertical line** — because both share the building's horizontal direction.

---

**Why it works:** the sloping lines are still parallel to each other in 3D, so they still converge to a point. **That point is where a line through the station point parallel to the slope pierces the picture plane** — and because the slope's horizontal component is the known direction, the point lies directly above or below that direction's vanishing point.

---

**Three cases worth having in hand:**

| Case | Construction |
| --- | --- |
| **A gabled roof** | **both pitches share one vertical trace.** The up-slope VP above the horizon, the down-slope VP below, equidistant if the pitches are equal |
| **A ramp or a road on a hill** | **one slope VP.** Everything on the ramp — kerbs, markings, a cart's wheels — uses it |
| **A staircase** | **the nosings of the steps lie on a sloping plane**, so the stair as a whole has a slope VP; the treads and risers use the ordinary horizontal VPs |

**The staircase case is the one that makes stairs drawable at all.** **Construct the sloping plane first, divide it for the steps, then build the treads and risers inside it.** Drawing stairs step by step without the enclosing slope accumulates error immediately.

---

**And the check that catches a wrong roof instantly:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Extend the ridge and the eaves** | **they must meet at the horizon VP**, because both are horizontal |
| **Extend the two sides of one pitch** | **they must meet above or below**, on the vertical through that same point |
| **If the ridge and the eaves do not converge to the same point** | **the roof is not sitting on the building** |
| **This is the most common architectural drawing error** | and it is visible in one line |

---

**York's architecture, which is what this is for:** steep pitched roofs, gables, dormers and jettied upper storeys. **Every one of those is an inclined plane problem**, and a drawn building whose roof slopes are guessed looks subtly wrong in a way no amount of texture will fix.

**Practice.** Construct 20 gabled buildings with both pitch vanishing points found properly on a shared vertical trace. Then 10 flights of stairs, each built inside a constructed sloping plane first. Then 10 ramps with objects sitting on them. Then take 20 photographs of roofs, extend their lines, and find the actual vanishing points.
Shadows in perspective:
Where a shadow falls, constructed rather than guessed: the two vanishing points a shadow needs, and the difference between sun and lamp.

**A cast shadow is a projection**, and it can be constructed exactly. **Two pieces of information place every shadow in a scene.**

---

**For sunlight — parallel rays:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The light's vanishing point**, where the sun's rays converge. **It is the sun itself** if the sun is in front of you, and the anti-sun point below the horizon if it is behind you | |
| **2 — The shadow's vanishing point**, on the horizon, **directly below or above the light's VP** | |
| **Because the shadow directions on the ground are the horizontal components of the rays** | so they vanish on the horizon, on the same vertical |

**The construction for one point:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **From the object's base point**, draw a line to the shadow VP on the horizon |
| **2** | **From the object's top point**, draw a line to the light's VP |
| **3** | **Where they cross is the shadow of that top point** |
| **4** | **Repeat for every corner, and join them** |

**That is it.** A box's shadow is six or seven such points.

---

**Sun in front against sun behind**, which changes the picture completely:

| | Sun in front of the viewer | Sun behind the viewer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The light's VP** | **above the horizon** — the sun, visible or not | **below the horizon** — the anti-sun point |
| **Shadows** | **come towards the viewer**, splaying | **go away from the viewer**, converging |
| **The scene** | **contre-jour: rim-lit, dramatic, shapes read as silhouettes** | **fully lit, shadows pointing into depth, forms read clearly** |

**And one trap: when the sun is behind you, the shadow VP on the horizon is where the shadows converge** — which looks like a second vanishing point and is not related to the box's geometry at all.

---

**For a lamp — radiating rays:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The rays are not parallel, so there is no vanishing point** | |
| **Instead: the lamp itself is the centre of projection** | |
| **And the point directly beneath the lamp on the ground plays the role of the shadow VP** | |
| **So: a line from the ground point beneath the lamp through the object's base, and a line from the lamp through the object's top, cross at the shadow's end** | |
| **Shadows splay outward from the lamp** | and they get longer very fast with distance, which is what makes lamplight read as lamplight |

---

**And the practical note, because full shadow construction is slow:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Construct the shadow of the main form** | |
| **Draw the rest by matching its direction and its rate of lengthening** | |
| **And always get these two right by eye if nothing else** | **shadows all run in the same direction**, and **a shadow starts at the object's contact point** |
| **Those two alone fix most shadow errors in a drawing** | |
| **The third most common error** | **shadows that do not lie on the ground's shape** — a shadow crossing a step must bend at the step |

**Practice.** Construct 20 box shadows with the sun in front and 20 with it behind, finding both vanishing points each time. Then 10 scenes lit by a lamp, with the shadows radiating correctly. Then construct the shadow of a figure across uneven ground — a kerb, a step, a slope. Then take 20 photographs in sunlight and find the shadow VP in each by extending the shadows.
Reflections:
Water, mirrors and polished floors: why a reflection is not a copy, and the one measurement that places it.

**A reflection in a flat surface is the subject mirrored through that surface — the same distance behind it as the subject is in front.** Everything else follows from that one fact.

---

**For a horizontal surface — water, a wet street, a polished floor:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The reflection of a point is directly below it** (in the picture, along the vertical), **as far below the surface as the point is above it** | |
| **Measured in 3D, not in drawn length** — so the measurement is done along the vertical, using perspective | |
| **The reflection shares all the subject's vanishing points** | because mirroring vertically does not change horizontal directions |
| **And the reflection of the waterline is the waterline** | **points on the surface reflect to themselves** |

---

**The construction:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Find where the object meets the reflecting surface** — the waterline, the floor contact |
| **2** | **For each point of the object, drop a vertical to the surface** and note where it crosses |
| **3** | **Continue the same distance below**, measured in perspective — using the measuring techniques from earlier in the stage |
| **4** | **Join the reflected points, using the same vanishing points as the original** |

---

**Three facts that surprise people:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — An object not touching the water reflects from further away.** A bird above a lake reflects well out from the shore, not at the shoreline. **Its reflection is as far below the surface as it is above**, which puts it deep and therefore distant in the picture | |
| **2 — You see different faces in the reflection.** The reflection shows the underside, because you are effectively viewing from below the surface. **A boat's reflection shows its hull** | |
| **3 — The reflection is not a flipped copy of the drawn image.** Flipping the picture vertically is only correct when the surface is exactly at the bottom of the object and the view is level — which is almost never | |

**Fact 3 is the one worth holding**, because the flip is the shortcut everyone takes and it is right rarely.

---

**For a vertical mirror**, the same rule with the mirror's plane:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Distance behind the mirror equals distance in front** | |
| **The reflected scene has its own vanishing points** — **mirrored through the mirror's plane** | |
| **For a mirror parallel to the picture plane, the reflection's VPs are the same as the scene's** | which is the easy case |
| **For an angled mirror, they are not**, and the construction is genuinely laborious | |

---

**And disturbed water, which is the common case and is simpler than it looks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ripples break the reflection into horizontal bands** | |
| **Each band is displaced sideways by the local slope of the water** | |
| **So the reflection stretches towards the viewer** and breaks up | |
| **The practical method** | **construct the still reflection, then disturb it** — horizontal strokes, displaced, with the displacement increasing towards the viewer |
| **Never draw the ripples first** | the reflection's structure has to be there to break |

**Practice.** Construct 20 reflections in still water, including at least 5 objects not touching the surface. Then 10 reflections showing undersides, checked against photographs. Then take 20 photographs of reflections and measure whether the reflection is a vertical flip — it will not be. Then draw 10 disturbed-water reflections, constructing the still version first.
Freehand against constructed:
When to build and when to draw: a decision procedure, and the hybrid that almost all real work uses.

**The stage has taught a system. This lesson is about not using it.**

---

**The honest situation:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Full construction is slow** — a measured two-point interior is an hour before anything is drawn | |
| **Freehand is fast and accurate enough for most subjects** | |
| **And the two are not alternatives** | **almost all professional work is a hybrid** |
| **Which is a thing that courses rarely say** | because each tends to be selling one or the other |

---

**The decision procedure:**

| Question | If yes |
| --- | --- |
| **Does the picture contain repeated regular elements?** — tiles, bricks, bays, columns, windows | **construct.** Repetition makes error visible |
| **Must it match a plan, a blueprint or an existing place?** | **construct** |
| **Is architecture the subject rather than the setting?** | **construct** |
| **Is the subject a figure, a creature, or anything organic?** | **freehand.** Construction will not help and will slow you to a stop |
| **Is it a sketch, a study or a gesture?** | **freehand, always** |
| **Is the perspective extreme — very wide, very steep?** | **construct**, because the eye has no experience to draw on |
| **None of the above?** | **freehand, and check with construction afterwards** |

**That last row is the most common case and the most useful habit: draw it, then verify it.**

---

**The hybrid that most illustration actually uses:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Thumbnail freehand**, to find the composition. No construction at all |
| **2** | **Establish the horizon and one or two vanishing points** on the chosen thumbnail |
| **3** | **Construct only the elements that need it** — the main architectural mass, the floor grid |
| **4** | **Draw everything else by eye**, using the construction as a scaffold |
| **5** | **Check the suspicious parts** by extending lines afterwards |

**Loomis works exactly this way in *Successful Drawing*, and so does every background painter.**

---

**And the thing construction does that is not about accuracy:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It tells you what you are looking at** | **a scene constructed is a scene understood** |
| **So even when the final drawing is freehand, constructing it once teaches the space** | |
| **Which is why the exercises in this stage are worth doing even if you never construct a finished picture** | |
| **The analogy** | **a musician learning harmony to improvise better, not to write it out** |

---

**On the tablet, two specifics:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Krita's perspective assistants** snap strokes to vanishing points, including points off the canvas | |
| **Which is genuinely useful for architecture and genuinely harmful as a default** | |
| **The rule, consistent with the whole curriculum** | **learn it without the aid, then use the aid.** Not before stage 13 |
| **And a constructed grid on its own layer**, hidden and shown, is the cleanest version of the hybrid method | |

**Practice.** Take 10 scenes and draw each twice — once fully constructed, once freehand — and time both. Then draw 20 more by the five-step hybrid. Then take 20 freehand drawings you have already made and check them by extending lines, recording how far off each was. Then decide, for the next 10 things you want to draw, which method each needs, and write the reason.
Perspective's failures:
Where the system produces something correct and wrong: four cases, what causes each, and what working artists do instead.

**Linear perspective is a model of one unmoving eye looking at a flat plane. Where reality departs from that, the construction gives answers that are geometrically right and visually wrong.** Knowing the four cases is what lets you depart deliberately.

---

**1 — Marginal distortion.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Outside the 60° cone of vision, forms stretch** | |
| **A sphere becomes an ellipse. A column at the edge of a wide interior becomes a slab** | |
| **And it is correct** — that is what projecting a wide view onto a flat plane does | |
| **Photographers meet it as "volume anamorphosis"** at the edges of wide-angle shots | |
| **What to do** | **narrow the view, or draw the spheres round anyway and accept the inconsistency.** Painters have done the second since the Renaissance |

**2 — The too-close station point.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Vanishing points placed close together imply an eye a few centimetres from the subject** | |
| **Which gives violent convergence** | |
| **Common in beginner work because the VPs have to fit on the page** | |
| **What to do** | **work bigger than the final crop and put the VPs outside it** |

**3 — Verticals that should not converge.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Correct three-point makes a tall building lean** | |
| **Viewers read photographs, and architectural photographs are corrected to parallel verticals** | |
| **So the correct drawing looks wrong and the "wrong" one looks right** | |
| **What to do** | **decide which you want.** This is a picture decision, and both answers are defensible |

**4 — Curved lines in wide views.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Your retina is curved; the picture plane is flat** | |
| **In a very wide view, straight lines really do appear curved** — look along a long wall and the top edge bows | |
| **Linear perspective says they are straight, and over 60° that becomes visibly false** | |
| **What to do** | **curvilinear perspective, which bends the lines towards up to five vanishing points** — used by Hogarth, and visible in fisheye photography |
| **Its cost** | **it looks like a lens effect**, which is a strong stylistic statement |

---

**And the general principle, which is the lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Perspective is a tool for making a picture, not a law the picture obeys** | |
| **Every great perspective painting departs from the construction somewhere** | |
| **The departures are invisible when deliberate and glaring when accidental** | |
| **Which is the only real argument for learning the system** | **you cannot break a rule you do not know, you can only fail to follow it** |

**Practice.** Construct one very wide interior — 90° or more — and find every element outside the 60° cone, then redraw those parts as they "should" look and compare. Then draw one tall building 3 times: two-point, correct three-point, and a compromise. Then photograph 5 long walls and check whether their edges bow. Then find 10 paintings you admire and look for where the perspective is deliberately wrong.
The perspective checklist:
The stage closed as a list: what to check in a constructed drawing, and the counts it asks for.

**The diagnosis order:**

| | Check | If wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Is there a horizon, and is it at a sensible eye height?** | **everything else depends on it** |
| **2** | **Do the two horizontal VPs imply a sane station point?** | **semicircle test.** A 15 cm viewing distance is a fisheye |
| **3** | **Is the subject inside the 60° cone?** | **if not, it will distort, correctly** |
| **4** | **Do all the figures meet the horizon at the same body level?** | **the fastest check in the stage, and the most often failed** |
| **5** | **Do the roof's ridge and eaves converge to the same horizon point?** | **the roof is not on the building** |
| **6** | **Are the slope VPs on a vertical through their horizontal VP?** | **inclined planes** |
| **7** | **Are repeated elements spaced by construction or by eye?** | **by eye, they will drift** — use the diagonal extension |
| **8** | **Are circles constructed or guessed?** | **check the ellipse's centre against the square's diagonal crossing — they differ** |
| **9** | **Do all shadows run to one shadow VP?** | and **does each start at its object's contact point?** |
| **10** | **Is the reflection a vertical flip?** | **then it is wrong**, except in one special case |

---

**The counts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **About 60 constructed boxes** across one-, two- and three-point | |
| **20 one-point interiors** with tiled floors | |
| **10 measured buildings** with measuring points | |
| **30 scenes placed by the horizon rule**, with 6+ figures each | |
| **About 80 divisions and multiplications** — fences, colonnades, receding edges | |
| **30 constructed circles**, plus 10 carts and 20 arches and windows | |
| **40 inclined-plane constructions** — roofs, stairs, ramps | |
| **50 constructed shadows** | |
| **30 reflections** | |
| **20 hybrid drawings** and 20 freehand drawings checked afterwards | |

**Three to six weeks**, and much less tiring than stage 3 because the results are pictures.

---

**And the four ideas to carry:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The horizon is your eye height, and everything at that height touches it.** The single most useful fact in the stage, needing no construction at all |
| **2** | **The station point decides how the drawing feels** — vanishing-point separation is a lens choice |
| **3** | **Diagonals divide and multiply anything**, in perspective, with no measuring |
| **4** | **Construct what repeats; draw the rest.** The hybrid is what real work uses |

---

**One note on what comes next.** Stage 5 is gesture, and **it uses none of this.** That is not a contradiction: **perspective governs where things are, and gesture governs what they are doing**, and a figure needs both without either being applied to the other. **Do not construct a gesture drawing.**

**Practice.** Run the ten-point diagnosis on 10 constructed drawings and 10 freehand ones. Then total your counts against the list and finish what is short. Then construct one full scene — a York street with buildings, roofs, figures, shadows and a puddle — using every technique in the stage, and keep it as the stage's single finished piece.
What gesture is:
The thing a figure drawing is actually about, why it cannot be constructed, and why this stage sits between perspective and the figure.

**Gesture is what the figure is doing.** Not its outline, not its anatomy, not its proportions — **the action, the intent, the direction of its energy.**

---

**The clearest way to see what it is: a gesture drawing of a person lifting a crate and a construction drawing of the same person are both correct and only one of them is about lifting.**

| | A construction drawing | A gesture drawing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Records** | **where the masses are in space** | **what the body is doing** |
| **Made of** | **boxes, cylinders, intersections** | **a few long sweeping lines** |
| **Time taken** | **ten minutes to an hour** | **thirty seconds** |
| **If it is wrong** | **the figure is misshapen** | **the figure is dead** |
| **Can be checked** | **yes, geometrically** | **no.** You can only feel it |

**And a finished figure drawing needs both.** Construction without gesture is a mannequin; gesture without construction is a ribbon.

---

**Why it cannot be constructed**, which is the hard thing about this stage:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Everything in stages 3 and 4 was checkable** | extend the lines, measure the convergence, verify the ellipse |
| **Gesture has no such test** | |
| **The only check is whether the drawing reads as the action** | which is a judgement, made by looking |
| **So the practice is different** | **volume plus honest comparison, rather than volume plus measurement** |
| **And this is why it is taught by exercise rather than by rule** | Nicolaides, Vilppu and Mattesi all teach it by making you do hundreds |

---

**Why this curriculum puts it fifth, after perspective:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Most courses put gesture first** | Nicolaides does, Proko does, and the first version of this curriculum did |
| **The argument for first** | **gesture is where the life is, and starting with construction produces stiff draughtsmen** |
| **The argument for fifth, which this curriculum takes** | **gesture drawn by a hand that cannot make a confident long line is scribble**, and stage 2 is what makes that line possible |
| **And the compromise that matters** | **gesture must come before ANATOMY**, which it does — stages 7 and 8 are after it |

**The ordering mistake that actually damages people is anatomy before gesture**, not construction before gesture. **A figure built on correct muscles and no gesture is a diagram**, and it is very hard to unlearn.

---

**What a gesture drawing is for**, in practice:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The first 30 seconds of any figure drawing**, which then gets constructed on top | |
| **Thumbnailing a pose** before committing to it | |
| **Finding a character's attitude** — stage 16's character design uses this constantly | |
| **Animation keys** — Williams' *Survival Kit* is gesture drawing applied to time | |
| **And as a daily warm-up forever** | which is what most working artists use it for |

**Practice.** Take 20 figure photographs and, for each, draw two things: a 30-second gesture and a 10-minute construction. Then show both to someone and ask which one tells them what the person is doing. Then take 10 of your existing figure drawings and ask honestly whether they have any gesture in them at all.
The line of action:
The single line that carries a pose, how to find it, and the two rules that make it work.

**The line of action is one long curve running through the figure, from the head through the spine and out to whichever limb is carrying the action.** It is drawn first, in one stroke, before any part of the figure.

---

**What it does:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **States the pose's direction and energy in one mark** | |
| **Fixes the relationship between the head, the torso and the legs** | |
| **Gives everything drawn afterwards something to hang on** | |
| **And if it is wrong, nothing drawn on it will be right** | which is why it is first |

---

**The two rules:**

| | Rule | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **It is a C or an S. Never a straight line, never a Z** | **a straight line of action is a figure standing to attention** — the only pose with no action. **And a Z has corners, which bodies do not** |
| **2** | **It runs edge to edge** — from the top of the head to the foot, or to the hand if the hand is the action | **a short line of action describes part of a figure, which is not what it is for** |

**Rule 1's C-or-S is not a stylistic preference.** The spine has four curves and the body balances by opposing them; **a real standing figure is always a shallow S.** A pose with no curve is a pose with no weight shift.

---

**How to find it on a reference:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Ask what the figure is doing.** In words. "Reaching up and to the left", "slumping", "bracing against a push" |
| **2** | **Find where the action starts and ends** — usually the head and the weight-bearing foot, or the head and the active hand |
| **3** | **Draw one curve between them, through the body**, at speed, in one stroke |
| **4** | **Do not correct it.** A second attempt averages, and the average has no energy |

**Step 1 is the one people skip, and it is the lesson.** **You cannot draw an action you have not identified.** Saying it in words takes two seconds and changes the drawing completely.

---

**And the thing that makes a line of action strong: push it further than the reference.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A photograph flattens action** — a frozen moment of a dynamic movement looks less dynamic than the movement felt | |
| **So a gesture drawn exactly as photographed is weaker than the real pose** | |
| **The correction is to exaggerate the curve** | **further than you think, by a noticeable amount** |
| **How much** | **enough that it feels slightly too much while drawing.** It will look right on the page |
| **And this is the one place in the curriculum where accuracy is not the goal** | stage 6 restores it |

---

**The common failures:**

| | Failure | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Line of action through the outline rather than the body** | drawing the silhouette instead of the action |
| **2** | **Several short lines instead of one** | not committing; the ghosting method from stage 2 fixes it |
| **3** | **A straight line** | the pose was not identified, or it genuinely has no action |
| **4** | **The line stops at the hips** | **the legs carry most poses**, and a gesture that ignores them is a portrait |

**Practice.** 200 lines of action, one per reference, nothing else drawn — 30 seconds each, and say the action out loud before each one. Then 100 more where you draw the line of action and then the figure's two or three main masses on it. Then take 50 and compare your curve with the reference's actual curve, and measure how much you exaggerated — most people exaggerate far less than they think.
Thirty seconds:
The standard gesture exercise: what the time limit is for, what to draw inside it, and why longer is worse.

**The exercise: a figure reference appears, you have 30 seconds, you draw, it changes.** Repeat for an hour.

---

**What the limit is actually doing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Removing the option to render** | **you cannot draw an outline in 30 seconds**, so you must draw something else |
| **Forcing a decision about what matters** | which is the line-economy lesson, enforced by clock |
| **Preventing correction** | there is no time to go back, so each mark stands |
| **And generating volume** | **120 drawings an hour**, which is the only way a judgement-based skill improves |

**The constraint is doing the teaching.** Nobody draws better because of the specific number 30; they draw better because the number is small enough to forbid everything except the essential.

---

**What to draw in 30 seconds**, in order:

| Seconds | What |
| --- | --- |
| **0–3** | **Look. Say the action.** Do not draw |
| **3–8** | **The line of action.** One stroke |
| **8–18** | **The three masses** — head, rib cage, pelvis — as simple shapes on the line |
| **18–28** | **The limbs**, as single lines or sausages, in their direction of action |
| **28–30** | **Stop.** Do not tidy |

**The 3 seconds of looking are not wasted.** A gesture drawn without identifying the action is 27 seconds of guessing.

---

**Why longer is worse**, which is counter-intuitive:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **At 2 minutes you start drawing the outline** | |
| **At 5 you start rendering** | |
| **And both are stage 6 and stage 14's work, done badly, instead of this stage's work done at all** | |
| **The progression that works** | **30 seconds until it is comfortable, then 15, then 10** |
| **Not** | **30 seconds, then 1 minute, then 2** — which is how most people drift out of the exercise entirely |

**Line of Action, Quickposes and SketchDaily all default to escalating session lengths.** Override them. **The short end is the useful end.**

---

**What a good 30-second gesture looks like**, so you know what you are aiming at:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Five to fifteen marks** | |
| **No outline anywhere** | |
| **The action unmistakable** — someone else could name it | |
| **Proportions roughly wrong** — and that is fine, stage 6 fixes proportion | |
| **And it looks nothing like a finished drawing** | which is why people stop doing them, and why they should not |

---

**On the tablet**, one setup note that removes all the friction:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One canvas, one layer, the hard round brush, large** | |
| **Clear the canvas between poses** rather than making a new file — or use one long canvas and move along it | |
| **No undo at all** | |
| **And export the session as one image** at the end, for the log — **a sheet of 60 gestures is a far better record than 60 files** | |

**Practice.** 500 thirty-second gestures, in sessions of 60. Then 200 at 15 seconds. Then 100 at 10 seconds — at which point only the line of action and one or two masses will fit, which is the point. Keep every sheet and date it.
Force, and directional energy:
Mattesi's contribution: reading a pose as a flow of energy rather than as a shape, and the two rules that follow.

**Mattesi's *Force* makes one argument: a body in a pose is subject to forces — gravity, muscular effort, momentum — and a drawing that records those forces reads as alive, while one that records the shapes does not.**

**It is the same territory as gesture, approached differently and usefully.**

---

**The central idea: directional force.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Every part of a pose has a direction of energy** | pushing, pulling, falling, resisting |
| **A line that follows that direction is a force line** | |
| **And the body reads as one connected flow**, not as assembled parts | |
| **Which is why a gesture drawing of a limb should not stop at the shoulder** | **the force passes through** |

---

**The two rules, and they are specific enough to apply:**

**1 — Force is directional and applies to a surface.** One side of a form is the *applied* force; the other is the *resisting* edge.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **So the two sides of a limb are not symmetrical** | one is the active curve, the other receives it |
| **Drawing both sides as equal parallel curves** | **makes the limb a tube, which is stage 3's job, not this one** |
| **Which gives the practical mark** | **a curve on one side, a straighter line on the other** |

**2 — Straight against curve.** This is the rule that transfers most directly:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Opposite sides of a form alternate between straight and curved** | |
| **A thigh: curved on the outside, straighter on the inside — and the next segment reverses it** | |
| **Why** | **because muscles on one side contract while the other side stretches**, so the two sides are genuinely different |
| **And the effect** | **the alternation makes the form read as moving**, where two curves read as inflated and two straights as wooden |

**"Straight against curve" is the single most portable idea in this stage**, and it applies to limbs, torsos, drapery, animals and plants.

---

**Rhythm, which is Mattesi's third idea:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The curves of a figure pass energy from one to the next** | |
| **So the curve of the far shoulder continues into the near hip, and out to the opposite foot** | |
| **These are the rhythm lines**, and they cross the body diagonally | |
| **Finding them is what makes a figure feel connected** | |
| **And they are invisible in the reference** — they are a reading, not an observation | |

---

**Where Force and classical gesture differ**, since both are on the shelf:

| | Vilppu and Nicolaides | Mattesi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The subject** | **the action, described** | **the energy, felt** |
| **The marks** | **line of action, then masses** | **force curves, one into the next** |
| **Strength** | **structure that construction can build on** | **vitality, and the straight-against-curve rule** |
| **Risk** | **becoming a mannequin** | **becoming a decorative swoosh with no anatomy under it** |

**Use both.** The line of action gives you the pose; force gives you the life in it. **And the straight-against-curve rule is worth adopting permanently regardless of which language you think in.**

**Practice.** 200 gestures drawn as force — one side curved, the other straighter, on every limb and the torso. Then take 100 of your earlier gestures and redraw each with straight-against-curve applied, and compare. Then 50 drawings where you mark only the rhythm lines crossing the body diagonally. Then draw 30 poses from imagination using force alone.
Weight and balance:
Why most gesture drawings look like they are floating, and the three things that put a figure on the ground.

**The commonest fault in figure drawing is not proportion. It is that the figure has no weight.** It is standing without pressing on anything.

---

**What weight actually requires:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — A centre of gravity**, somewhere around the pelvis | |
| **2 — A base of support**, which is the area enclosed by whatever is touching the ground | |
| **3 — The first vertically above the second** | **or the figure is falling** |

**That third line is the rule.** **Drop a vertical from the pit of the neck: it must land inside the base of support.** If it lands outside, the figure is mid-fall — which is fine if it is falling and wrong if it is standing.

---

**The three things that put weight into a drawing:**

| | | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The weight-bearing side** | **the hip on the loaded leg rises; the shoulder on that side drops.** Opposed tilts — contrapposto |
| **2** | **The straight supporting line** | **the loaded leg is straighter and more vertical than the free leg**, and it takes a straight force line |
| **3** | **Ground contact** | **the foot flattens and spreads under load.** A foot drawn as a wedge touching at one point carries nothing |

**Rule 1 is contrapposto and it is nearly universal in standing figures.** Shoulders and hips tilt in opposite directions. **A figure with parallel shoulder and hip lines is standing on both legs equally** — which is a rest pose, and rarer in life than in drawings.

---

**Reading a pose for weight**, in three questions, which takes about two seconds:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Which foot carries the weight?** | |
| **Where is the pelvis in relation to it?** | |
| **Which way do the shoulders tilt?** | |
| **Answer those and the gesture's structure is decided before any mark** | |

---

**And weight in motion**, which is the harder and more useful case:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A walking figure is falling forwards and catching itself** | **the centre of gravity is outside the base of support for most of the cycle** |
| **A running figure more so** | both feet off the ground at the extremes |
| **A figure lifting something heavy counterbalances** | leaning away from the load |
| **A figure pushing braces** | a straight line from the hands through the body to the back foot |
| **In every case the drawing must state what the weight is doing** | **not merely where the limbs are** |

**Williams' *Animator's Survival Kit* is the best book here on this**, because animation forces the question: a character that does not shift its weight is a character that floats, and that is visible in motion in a way it is not in a still.

---

**The Shepherds connection**, since it is concrete: **§5's animation contract requires weight-bearing poses, and the approved idle reference holds a pose for part of its cycle.** A held pose that is not balanced reads as a mistake for the whole hold.

**Practice.** 100 gestures where you mark the weight-bearing foot, the centre of gravity and the vertical between them, before anything else. Then 50 contrapposto standing figures, with shoulder and hip lines drawn explicitly and opposed. Then 50 figures in motion — walking, running, lifting, pushing — where the centre of gravity is deliberately outside the base. Then take 20 of your own old figure drawings and drop the vertical on each.
The three masses:
Head, rib cage and pelvis: the three solids that carry a pose, and why everything else is attached to them.

**A figure's structure is three rigid masses joined by two flexible links.**

| Mass | Shape | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The head** | **a sphere with flattened sides**, or an egg | **points.** Its direction is most of the figure's attention |
| **The rib cage** | **an egg, or a barrel flattened front to back** | **rigid.** It does not bend — the spine around it does |
| **The pelvis** | **a wedge, or a shallow box** | **carries the weight into the legs** |

**And the links: the neck, and the lumbar spine.** Everything a figure does with its torso happens at those two places, because **the rib cage and the pelvis are each a single unit.**

---

**Why this is the most useful simplification in figure drawing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Three forms is a tractable number** | you can place three solids in space |
| **Their relative tilt IS the pose** | — and reading it is one glance |
| **They are rigid, so they cannot be drawn wrong by bending** | |
| **And everything else hangs off them** | arms from the rib cage via the shoulder girdle, legs from the pelvis |

---

**The three tilts, which is what to read:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The head's tilt and turn** | |
| **The rib cage's tilt and turn** | |
| **The pelvis's tilt and turn** | |
| **Six numbers describe almost any standing pose** | and the differences between them are contrapposto |
| **In gesture, draw them as three simple shapes on the line of action** | and the pose is already there |

---

**The shoulder girdle, which is not one of the three and is why arms are hard:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The clavicles and shoulder blades sit ON the rib cage and slide over it** | |
| **So the shoulders are not part of the rib cage's shape** | they are a yoke lying across it |
| **Which means a raised arm raises the whole shoulder** — the rib cage does not move | |
| **And a figure drawn with the shoulders as part of the torso** | **cannot raise its arm properly** |
| **Bridgman draws this better than anyone** | the shoulder as a separate wedge between masses |

---

**How to use it in a gesture, in sequence:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Line of action** |
| **2** | **Rib cage and pelvis as two shapes on it**, with their tilts |
| **3** | **Head**, with its direction |
| **4** | **A line for the shoulder girdle across the rib cage** |
| **5** | **Limbs from those attachment points** |

**Five steps, and it fits in 30 seconds with practice.** It is also exactly the opening of a constructed figure in stage 6 — **which is why this stage, done properly, makes stage 6 much faster.**

---

**And the error this fixes: the bending rib cage.** A figure drawn as a continuous flowing torso will bend in the middle of the chest, where no spine bends. **The bend belongs at the waist, between the two masses** — and once you are drawing two separate solids, it cannot go anywhere else.

**Practice.** 200 gestures drawn as three masses on a line of action, nothing else. Then 100 where you also mark the shoulder girdle as a separate line across the rib cage. Then take 50 reference photographs and mark only the tilt of each of the three masses, as three short lines, and see how much of the pose that captures. Then draw 50 torsos from imagination by choosing three tilts at random.
Exaggeration, and how far:
Pushing a pose beyond the reference: why it is necessary, the four things to push, and where the limit is.

**The problem: a drawing made exactly as the reference looks weaker than the reference.** This is consistent, it affects everyone, and it has causes worth knowing.

---

**Why accuracy under-reads:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A photograph is a frozen instant of a continuous movement** | and the instant you see is less dynamic than the movement felt |
| **A drawing has no motion blur, no context, no before and after** | so it must carry the action in the pose alone |
| **The eye compensates when looking at a real body** | it integrates over time, and a drawing gives it one frame |
| **So "accurate" is a loss**, and exaggeration is a compensation for the loss | |

**This is not a licence to distort for style. It is a correction**, and the amount is roughly fixed.

---

**The four things to push:**

| | What | How far |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The line of action's curve** | **noticeably further.** The most important one |
| **2** | **The tilt differences between the three masses** | **more opposition** — a bigger shoulder-hip contrast |
| **3** | **The straight-against-curve contrast** | **straighter straights, curvier curves** |
| **4** | **Foreshortening** | **more compression and more size difference**, because this is the one that under-reads most |

**And the four not to push, in a gesture:** **proportions, anatomy, the direction of a limb, and which foot carries the weight.** Those are facts; the four above are emphasis.

---

**Where the limit is**, which is the real question:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The test** | **can the pose still be read as the same action?** |
| **Push until it is slightly uncomfortable while drawing** | **it will look right on the page** |
| **Push until it is uncomfortable to look at** | **too far** |
| **And the asymmetry worth knowing** | **under-exaggeration is far more common than over.** Almost nobody pushes too hard; almost everybody pushes too little |

---

**The two kinds of exaggeration**, and only one is this lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Corrective** — restoring what the medium lost. **What this lesson is about**, and it applies to every drawing including the most realistic | |
| **Stylistic** — pushing beyond that for character. **Caricature, cartooning, Hogarth's heroic figures.** A legitimate choice, made deliberately, and not what a study is for | |
| **The failure is confusing them** | a figure study exaggerated stylistically has no reference value, and a character design exaggerated only correctively is bland |

---

**And the one honest warning:** exaggeration compounds with error.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **If your proportions are off and you exaggerate the pose** | **you cannot tell which is which afterwards** |
| **Which is why this lesson sits in the gesture stage and not in stage 6** | **gesture tolerates wrong proportion; a constructed figure does not** |
| **The working rule** | **exaggerate in gesture, measure in construction**, and let the construction pull the exaggeration back where it has gone too far |

**Practice.** Take 50 references and draw each twice — once as accurately as you can, once pushed on all four axes — and compare. Then 100 gestures where you deliberately push until it feels like too much, and look at them the next day. Then take 20 drawings that feel stiff and find which of the four you failed to push.
Gesture of an action, not a pose:
Drawing what the body is doing rather than what it looks like at one instant, and the three questions that get you there.

**A pose is a configuration. An action is a process.** A drawing of the configuration is correct and inert; a drawing of the process has life. **The difference is almost entirely in what you decide before drawing.**

---

**The three questions:**

| | Question | What it gives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **What is this body doing?** | **the action, in words.** Lifting, reaching, bracing, collapsing, listening |
| **2** | **What was it doing a moment ago, and what next?** | **the direction of the movement**, which the frozen instant does not show |
| **3** | **What is it feeling?** | **effort, ease, tension, exhaustion** — which changes every curve in the body |

**Question 2 is the one that transforms a gesture drawing**, and it costs nothing but a second of thought.

---

**How the answers change the marks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A figure mid-way through sitting down** | **draw it still descending** — the weight still falling, the hands not yet bearing |
| **A figure at the top of a reach** | **draw the stretch**, the ribs lifted, the far side extended |
| **A figure exhausted** | **everything sags towards the ground**, and the line of action collapses rather than curves |
| **A figure braced** | **straight lines, a force path from hands to back foot** — curve would read as softness |

---

**Where this matters for Shepherds specifically:** **§5 requires anticipation, active frames, impact, release and recovery**, and **all five are the same pose at different moments of one action.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Anticipation** | **the body loading** — moving opposite to the coming action |
| **Active** | **the movement itself**, usually the fastest and least visible frames |
| **Impact** | **the moment of contact**, with the whole body committed |
| **Recovery** | **the settle**, overshooting and returning |
| **Drawing these requires thinking in actions rather than poses** | **and an animator who draws only poses produces an animation that is a slideshow** |

**Williams' *Survival Kit* is this lesson's natural companion**, and it is the reason the book is on the shelf.

---

**The exercise that teaches it fastest: draw the pose before and the pose after.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Given one reference, draw three gestures** | the moment before, the reference, and the moment after |
| **The first and third are invented** | which forces you to understand the action |
| **And the middle one gets better** | because you now know what it is part of |
| **This is also exactly how animation keys are drawn** | and how a character sheet's action poses are chosen |

---

**And the related habit: name the drawing.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Write the action on each gesture, in two or three words** | |
| **It takes two seconds and it forces question 1 to have been answered** | |
| **And reviewing a sheet of 60 named gestures is far more useful than reviewing 60 unnamed ones** | **because you can see which actions you cannot draw** |

**Practice.** 100 gestures, each named in two or three words before drawing. Then 50 sets of three — before, during, after — from single references. Then 30 drawn from a verbal description alone, with no reference: "a man catching a falling crate", "a woman turning to listen". Then take 20 of Muybridge's sequences and draw the anticipation, the action and the recovery from each.
Gesture in animals:
Applying the stage to four legs: what transfers directly, what does not, and the two things that make an animal gesture read.

**Everything structural transfers.** An animal has a line of action, three masses, weight and balance, force and rhythm. **What changes is the arrangement.**

---

**The three masses, for a quadruped:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Head** | as before, and usually carried forward rather than above |
| **Rib cage** | **much larger relative to the body than a human's**, and the deepest part of the animal |
| **Pelvis** | **smaller, higher or lower depending on species** |
| **And the link between them is longer** | **a horizontal spine, which is the main difference** |

**The line of action for a quadruped usually runs along the spine, from nose to tail** — which makes it longer, flatter, and more about undulation than about a single C.

---

**The two things that make an animal gesture read:**

**1 — The weight distribution between front and back.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A horse carries about 60% of its weight on the forelegs** | |
| **A cat is more even and can shift violently** | |
| **A sheep is front-heavy and low** | |
| **The gesture must state where the weight is** | **a drawn quadruped with weight evenly spread looks like a toy** |
| **And the readable sign is the angle of the spine and the bend of the legs** | |

**2 — The rhythm along the spine.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A galloping animal's spine flexes and extends — it is the main source of the stride** | |
| **A stalking cat's spine is level and the legs do the work** | |
| **A grazing animal's spine curves down to the ground** | |
| **So the spine's curve is the action**, more than the limbs are | |
| **Which is the opposite emphasis from a human**, where the limbs usually carry it | |

---

**The digitigrade problem**, which is where almost everyone goes wrong and which stage 12 covers properly:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A dog, cat, deer or fox walks on its toes** | |
| **So the joint half-way up the back leg that bends backwards is the ANKLE, not the knee** | |
| **The knee is higher, tucked against the body** | |
| **Draw it as a backwards knee and the animal reads as broken** | **and it is the single most common animal-drawing error** |
| **In gesture this matters less than in construction** | but getting the leg's two bends in the right places even in a 30-second drawing makes it read |

---

**The Shepherds cast**, which is what this is for: **a sheep, a dog, a deer and a fox** in the Prologue.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Sheep** | **low, front-heavy, almost no visible leg articulation under the fleece.** The gesture is the body's mass and the head's position |
| **Dog (Pip)** | **the most expressive** — tail, ears and spine all carry emotion |
| **Deer** | **high centre of gravity, long legs, alert head.** Gesture is in the neck and the leg angles |
| **Fox** | **low, long, with a heavy tail that counterbalances** — and §6.5 fixes its lunge at 0.22 s and its rear at 0.62 s |

**Practice.** 200 animal gestures at 30 seconds, from free timed reference — 50 each of a quadruped with hooves, a cat-type, a dog-type and a bird. Then 100 of the four Shepherds animals specifically. Then 50 where you mark only the spine's curve and the weight distribution. Then draw 30 from Muybridge's animal sequences, where you can see the whole stride.
Gesture failures:
The six ways a gesture drawing dies, what causes each, and the fix.

**This lesson is a diagnostic, because gesture cannot be checked geometrically and the failures are therefore learned by recognition.**

---

| | Failure | What it looks like | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The outline** | a thin contour of a person, correct and inert | **drawing what you see instead of what is happening** | **say the action first; draw the line of action before anything** |
| **2** | **The noodle** | flowing curves with no structure, like a ribbon | **gesture without the three masses** | **place the rib cage and pelvis as solids** |
| **3** | **The mannequin** | correct masses, no life | **construction applied in a gesture drawing** | **this stage's exercises; and do not construct a 30-second drawing** |
| **4** | **The floater** | a figure not standing on anything | **no weight-bearing decision** | **mark the loaded foot and the vertical through the centre of gravity** |
| **5** | **The hesitation** | furry multi-stroke lines | **no commitment** | **stage 2's ghosting, applied at speed** |
| **6** | **The stiff symmetry** | shoulders and hips parallel, limbs matched | **drawing the idea of a body rather than the one in front of you** | **contrapposto: oppose the tilts; make the two sides different** |

---

**Failure 1 is by far the most common**, and it is worth understanding why it persists:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The outline is what you can see** | |
| **The action is an interpretation** | |
| **So drawing the outline feels like accuracy and drawing the action feels like making things up** | |
| **It is the reverse** | **the outline is a projection artefact of one viewpoint; the action is the thing that is actually true about the body** |
| **The symptom to watch for** | **starting at the head and working down the edge.** If you are tracing a boundary, you are drawing an outline |

---

**Failure 3 is this curriculum's specific risk**, because it puts construction before gesture:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Having spent stage 3 on boxes and cylinders, the hand wants to use them** | |
| **And in a 30-second gesture they produce a stiff, blocky, lifeless figure** | |
| **The rule** | **gesture and construction are separate passes with separate purposes** |
| **Gesture first, always, even in a long drawing** | |
| **And never at the same time** | a drawing that tries to be both at once is neither |

---

**The self-review method**, which is how to use this list:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Take a sheet of 60 gestures at the end of a session** | |
| **Mark each one with the number of its dominant failure** | |
| **Count them** | |
| **One number will dominate** — and that is what to work on, rather than "getting better at gesture" | |
| **Repeat weekly** | the distribution shifts, and watching it shift is the clearest progress signal in this stage |

**Practice.** Mark up 5 sheets of 60 gestures by the six failure numbers and tally each. Then do 200 gestures aimed only at your dominant failure. Then re-mark a new sheet and compare the distribution. Then take 20 of your best gestures and work out what they have in common.
The gesture checklist:
The stage closed as a list: the sequence, the counts, and what carries into the figure.

**The 30-second sequence, which is the stage in one table:**

| Seconds | What |
| --- | --- |
| **0–3** | **Look. Name the action in words** |
| **3–8** | **The line of action** — one stroke, C or S, edge to edge, exaggerated |
| **8–18** | **The three masses** — rib cage, pelvis, head, with their tilts opposed |
| **18–22** | **The weight** — which foot, and the shoulder line |
| **22–28** | **The limbs**, as force lines with straight against curve |
| **28–30** | **Stop** |

---

**The checks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Can someone else name the action?** The only test that matters |
| **2** | **Is there a line of action, and is it a C or an S?** |
| **3** | **Are the shoulder and hip lines opposed?** |
| **4** | **Does a vertical from the pit of the neck land inside the base of support?** |
| **5** | **Is any limb drawn with two parallel curves?** Straight against curve |
| **6** | **Is the rib cage bending?** It cannot |
| **7** | **Is it an outline?** |
| **8** | **Did you push it far enough?** Almost certainly not |

---

**The counts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **500 thirty-second gestures**, plus 200 at 15 seconds and 100 at 10 | |
| **200 lines of action alone**, and 100 with masses | |
| **200 force gestures** with straight against curve | |
| **200 three-mass gestures** | |
| **100 weight and contrapposto studies** | |
| **200 animal gestures**, plus 100 of the Shepherds four | |
| **100 named gestures** and 50 before-during-after sets | |
| **About 350 across exaggeration, failure review and imagination** | |

**Well over 2,000 drawings, and that is the correct order of magnitude.** At 30 seconds each that is about 17 hours of actual drawing, spread over weeks. **Nobody has ever got good at gesture in fewer.**

---

**What carries into stage 6:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The line of action**, which becomes the spine of the constructed figure | |
| **The three masses**, which become the constructed torso | |
| **The weight decision**, which becomes the figure's balance | |
| **The exaggeration**, pulled back by measurement but not removed | |
| **And the habit of naming the action**, which stops a constructed figure being a mannequin | |

**The relationship to state plainly: stage 6 builds on the gesture, it does not replace it.** A constructed figure drawing begins with a 30-second gesture, and **if that gesture is dead, ten minutes of accurate construction on top of it will not revive it.**

---

**And one note on where this never stops.** Gesture is the one thing in this curriculum that stays a daily warm-up forever. **Ten minutes before every session, for years.** It is also the cheapest — any free timed-reference site, no setup, no materials.

**Practice.** Run the eight checks on 5 sheets of your gestures. Then total your counts against the list above and finish what is short. Then adopt 10 minutes of gesture as the start of every drawing session, indefinitely, and add it to the warm-up routine from stage 2.
From gesture to construction:
How the two passes join: what the gesture supplies, what construction adds, and the order that keeps both alive.

**The sequence for a full figure drawing**, and it is the same whether the drawing takes five minutes or five hours:

| | Pass | Time | What it decides |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Gesture** | **30 seconds** | **the action, the line of action, the three tilts, the weight** |
| **2** | **Construction** | **5–20 minutes** | **the masses as solids in space, proportion, the limbs' volumes** |
| **3** | **Anatomy** | stages 7–8 | **the forms on top of the construction** |
| **4** | **Contour and finish** | | **the silhouette, derived; and the rendering** |

**The rule that makes it work: each pass is complete before the next begins, and none of them is a correction of the one before.**

---

**Why not construct from the start?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Because the gesture decides things construction cannot** | **how far to push the pose, where the energy goes, what the figure is doing** |
| **And construction decided first locks proportion before action** | **giving a correctly proportioned figure doing nothing** |
| **The gesture is the drawing's intention** | |
| **The construction is its accuracy** | |
| **And intention has to come first** | because accuracy has nothing to be accurate about otherwise |

---

**What survives from the gesture into the construction, concretely:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The line of action becomes the spine** | not literally — the spine is a shallower curve — but its direction and energy carry |
| **The three mass tilts become the rib cage's and pelvis's orientations in 3D** | |
| **The weight decision becomes which leg is straight** | |
| **The exaggeration stays**, pulled back where measurement contradicts it | |
| **And what is discarded** | **the gesture's limb lines, which were force indicators rather than placements** |

---

**The practical method on a tablet, which is where layers finally earn their place:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Gesture on layer 1**, at speed, 30 seconds | |
| **Drop it to 25% opacity** | |
| **Construct on layer 2**, referring to it constantly | |
| **Drop that to 25%** | |
| **Draw on layer 3** | |
| **And at any point, hide layers 1 and 2 to see what you actually have** | |

**This is the one workflow where the tablet is clearly better than paper**, and it is worth setting up as a template — which stage 1 anticipated.

---

**The failure mode to watch for: construction killing the gesture.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It happens when the construction is drawn by measuring from the reference rather than by building on the gesture** | |
| **The symptom** | **the finished figure is accurate and stiff, and the 30-second gesture underneath is better** |
| **Which is a real and common experience**, and it is worth taking seriously when it happens | |
| **The fix** | **construct ON the gesture rather than beside it** — the gesture's curves are the targets, and the reference is a check |
| **And if the finished drawing is worse than the gesture, keep the gesture** | |

**Practice.** 50 figures drawn in the two passes, with the gesture kept on its own layer. Then for 20 of them, show the gesture and the finish side by side and judge honestly which is better. Then 30 where you deliberately construct without a gesture first, and compare the stiffness. Then 30 where you spend 2 minutes on the gesture instead of 30 seconds.
Proportion, and which canon:
The head-count systems, what each is for, and the handful of measurements that actually matter.

**Proportion in figure drawing is expressed in head-heights** — the head's length used as a unit for the whole body. **Which canon you use decides what kind of figure you draw.**

---

**The canons:**

| Heads | Figure | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **7** | **average real adult** | **honest observation.** Most people are between 7 and 7.5 |
| **7.5** | **Loomis' "ideal"** | **illustration.** Slightly flattering, still believable |
| **8** | **Loomis' "idealised"** | **fashion, heroic illustration, classical sculpture** |
| **8.5–9** | **heroic / comic-book** | **Hogarth's figures, superhero art** |
| **5–6** | **children, dwarves, stylised characters** | **and the ratio is what makes them read as such** |

**The single most useful fact: real people are about 7.5 heads and most beginners draw 6.** The head is drawn too large, consistently, by nearly everyone.

---

**The landmarks that matter more than the total**, because they are what is actually wrong when a figure looks off:

| | Landmark | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The halfway point of the whole figure** | **the pubic bone — roughly the crotch.** Not the waist, which is where almost everyone puts it |
| **2** | **The nipples** | about 2 heads down |
| **3** | **The navel** | about 3 heads |
| **4** | **The fingertips of a hanging arm** | **mid-thigh** |
| **5** | **The elbow** | **level with the waist / the bottom of the rib cage** |
| **6** | **The knee** | **just above the halfway point between hip and floor** |
| **7** | **The foot** | **about one head long** |

**Landmark 1 is the one to internalise.** A figure whose halfway point is at the waist has legs that are too short, and it is the commonest proportion error in the subject.

---

**Two measurements that are not head-counts and are more reliable:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Shoulder width** | **about 2 heads for a man, slightly less for a woman** |
| **The hand** | **from wrist to fingertip, about the same as the face from chin to hairline.** Which is why a hand covers a face |

**The hand-equals-face rule is worth more than most of the canon**, because hands are drawn too small by almost everyone and this fixes it in one check.

---

**And the honest position on canons**, which matters because they are often taught as law:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A canon is a default, not a measurement** | |
| **Real people vary enormously** — in head size, limb length and torso proportion | |
| **So for observation, measure the actual figure** (stage 2's sighting) **and let the canon catch gross errors** | |
| **For imagination, pick a canon and hold it** | **consistency matters more than which number** |
| **And for character design, the deviation from the canon IS the character** | — a 6.5-head figure reads as stocky, a 9-head one as elongated, and both are decisions |

**Practice.** Measure 30 figure photographs in head-heights and record the actual numbers — the spread will surprise you. Then draw 50 figures at 7.5 heads from imagination, checking all seven landmarks on each. Then draw the same character at 6, 7.5 and 9 heads and note what each reads as. Then take 20 old figure drawings and measure their halfway point.
The Loomis mannequin:
The simplified figure that makes construction possible: what the parts are, how they attach, and why this specific simplification won.

**Loomis' mannequin reduces the body to a handful of simple solids that can be drawn from any angle and in any pose.** It is not the only such system and it is the one most widely used, because its parts correspond to real anatomy closely enough to carry detail later.

---

**The parts:**

| Part | Form |
| --- | --- |
| **Head** | **a ball with the sides flattened**, plus a jaw block |
| **Neck** | **a cylinder**, tilted forward |
| **Rib cage** | **an egg or a flattened barrel** — wider than deep |
| **Pelvis** | **a box, or a shallow bucket** |
| **Upper arm, forearm** | **tapered cylinders** |
| **Thigh, calf** | **tapered cylinders**, the thigh much larger |
| **Hands, feet** | **wedges and boxes**, detailed in stage 9 |
| **And the joints** | **spheres** — shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee, ankle |

---

**The two connections that do the work:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Rib cage to pelvis** | **by the spine, which is a flexible link** — the only place the torso bends |
| **Shoulder girdle to rib cage** | **a yoke lying across it, free to slide and rotate** |
| **Everything else is a hinge or a ball joint** | and knowing which is which is what stops a figure bending where it cannot |

**Which joints are which, since it is short and useful:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ball joints** — rotate in every direction | **shoulder, hip** |
| **Hinges** — one axis only | **elbow, knee, finger joints** |
| **Complex** | **wrist and ankle**, which do most things but not rotation about the limb's axis |
| **And the forearm's rotation is not at the wrist** | **it is the two forearm bones crossing**, which stage 8 covers and which changes the forearm's whole shape |

---

**How to draw it, in order:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The gesture, already done** |
| **2** | **Rib cage and pelvis as two solids**, with their tilts in 3D — using cross-contours to state their orientation |
| **3** | **The line between them** — the spine's curve |
| **4** | **The head and neck** |
| **5** | **The shoulder girdle across the rib cage**, and the hip line across the pelvis |
| **6** | **Limbs as tapered cylinders with sphere joints**, drawn through |
| **7** | **Check the proportions** against the landmarks |

---

**What makes it a construction rather than a diagram: the cross-contours.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A rib cage drawn as an egg shape is a shape** | |
| **A rib cage drawn with a centre line down the sternum and a cross-contour at the bottom of the ribs is a solid in a known orientation** | |
| **Those two lines are the whole difference** | |
| **And they are what lets you put a nipple, a belt or a strap on it correctly** | which is stage 11's problem |

---

**Where the mannequin stops being enough:** it has no anatomy, so **it cannot show muscle, fat, or the specific landmarks that make a figure look like a person.** That is stages 7 and 8, and **they are drawn on top of this** — never instead of it.

**Practice.** 100 mannequins from imagination, at varied angles, every one with cross-contours on the rib cage and pelvis. Then 100 built on gestures from reference. Then 50 in extreme foreshortening, drawn through. Then take 30 and check each against the seven proportion landmarks, correcting on a notes layer rather than redrawing.
The rib cage and pelvis:
The two solids that decide a torso: their real shapes, their orientations, and the relationship between them that makes a pose.

**Almost everything about a torso is the relationship between these two masses.** Getting their shapes and tilts right is most of figure drawing.

---

**The rib cage, as a form:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An egg, tilted** — narrower at the top, widest about two-thirds down | |
| **Flattened front to back**, so it is wider than deep | |
| **The bottom edge is not level** — it rises at the sides and dips at the front, forming the **thoracic arch**, an inverted V below the sternum | |
| **And it is rigid** | the ribs move for breathing and the shape does not change |
| **Its visible landmarks** | **the pit of the neck, the sternum's line, and the bottom edge of the ribs**, all of which show on most bodies |

**The thoracic arch is the single most useful landmark on the torso**, because it tells you exactly where the rib cage ends and the soft waist begins.

---

**The pelvis, as a form:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A box, or a bucket tipped forward** | |
| **Wider than it is tall** | |
| **Its top edge is the iliac crest** — which you can feel on yourself, and which is the key landmark | |
