| --- | --- |
| **The gastrocnemius has two heads — inner and outer** | |
| **The inner head is LARGER and extends LOWER** | |
| **So the calf is asymmetrical, with the bulge sitting lower on the inside** | |
| **And below them the soleus shows at the sides**, continuing down to the Achilles | |
| **The Achilles tendon** — **the narrowest point of the leg**, flat and broad, running to the heel | |

**The inner-lower, outer-higher asymmetry is the calf's defining fact**, and a symmetrical calf reads as wrong immediately even to a viewer who cannot say why.

---

**The shin:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The tibia's front edge is directly under the skin, the whole way down** | |
| **So the shin is a hard, straight, flat ridge** — the only place on the body where bone forms the silhouette over a long distance | |
| **It runs slightly diagonally**, from the tibial tuberosity down to the inner malleolus | |
| **Muscle sits on the OUTER side of it only** | the tibialis anterior, which makes the outer shin fuller |
| **Which gives the lower leg's cross-section**: **flat on the inner front, full on the outer front, round behind** | |

---

**The ankle and the foot's attachment:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The two malleoli, inner high and forward, outer low and back** | |
| **Between and below them the foot attaches** — and **the leg does not sit on top of the foot**, it enters it behind the mid-point | |
| **So the foot projects much further forward than back** | roughly 3:1 |
| **And the Achilles runs down behind the ankle to the heel**, which projects backwards | |
| **The heel is the only part of the foot behind the leg's axis** | and it is what stops you falling over backwards |

---

**The whole leg's rhythm**, which is how to remember all of this:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Outer thigh: high and flat.** Inner thigh: low and full | |
| **Outer calf: high.** Inner calf: low | |
| **Outer ankle: low.** Inner ankle: high | |
| **Which alternates all the way down** | and is the straight-against-curve rule from stage 5, arriving as anatomy |
| **This alternation is why a leg looks like a leg** | and drawing both sides the same is the error that makes it a tube |

**Practice.** Draw 50 knees from front, side and three-quarter with all four front forms. Then 50 calves with the inner head lower and larger. Then 50 lower legs with the tibia's flat ridge forming the inner silhouette. Then draw 30 whole legs marking the alternating high-low rhythm down both sides.
Muscle in action:
What a muscle looks like when it is working, when it is stretched, and the rule that makes the difference drawable.

**A muscle has exactly two states that matter for drawing: contracted and stretched.** Learning what each looks like is more useful than learning another twenty muscle names.

---

**Contracted:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Shorter and thicker** — the volume is conserved, so shortening means bulging | |
| **The bulge moves towards the middle of the muscle belly** | |
| **Its outline becomes CONVEX and its edges sharper** | |
| **And it becomes harder, so the skin over it tightens** — fewer folds, more definition | |

**Stretched:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Longer and thinner** | |
| **The outline flattens, becoming STRAIGHT or even slightly concave** | |
| **The muscle's own form nearly disappears** | |
| **And the structures under it show through** — bone, tendon, and the forms beneath | |

---

**Which gives the rule that makes limbs readable:**

> **Every joint has an inside and an outside. The contracted side bulges and curves; the stretched side flattens and straightens.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A bent elbow** | **biceps bunched and round on the inside; triceps flat and long on the outside** |
| **A bent knee** | **hamstrings bunched behind; quadriceps stretched and flat in front** |
| **A raised arm** | **deltoid bunched on top; latissimus and pectoral stretched below** |
| **And this is stage 5's straight-against-curve**, now with a physical cause | |

**Which is the point worth making: the straight-against-curve rule is not a stylistic device. It is what muscles actually do.**

---

**The second effect: displacement.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A contracting muscle pushes the soft tissue around it out of the way** | |
| **So a flexed bicep displaces the skin and fat over it, and the forms either side change too** | |
| **Which means you cannot draw one muscle's contraction in isolation** | |
| **The region responds** | and this is why a drawn figure with one carefully rendered flexed muscle on an otherwise relaxed arm looks pasted |

---

**The third: compression at the joints.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A fully bent elbow or knee compresses the flesh on the inside** | |
| **Producing a fold, a crease, or a roll** — on every body, at every weight | |
| **And a gap or hollow on the outside** | |
| **Drawing a bent limb with a smooth inner curve** | **misses the compression entirely**, and it is one of the clearest signs of a figure drawn from knowledge rather than observation |

---

**And the thing to look for in reference, which turns photographs into study material:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **For every limb, ask which muscle is working** | |
| **Then check: is its outline convex and is its opposite flat?** | |
| **If both sides of a limb look the same in the reference, the limb is relaxed** — and draw it that way | |
| **This single question extracts more from a photograph than an hour of copying it** | |

**Practice.** Draw 50 pairs of the same limb, relaxed and working, with the convex/flat contrast explicit. Then 50 bent joints with compression folds on the inside. Then take 30 reference photographs and mark, on each limb, which muscle is working. Then draw 30 figures from imagination where the action decides which side of each limb bulges.
The limbs checklist:
The stage closed as a list: the construction order, the checks, and the counts.

**The order for a limb:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The bones' axis** — including the femur's inward slant and the arm's carrying angle |
| **2** | **The joint landmarks** — elbow's three, knee's three, wrist's two, ankle's two |
| **3** | **The masses**, as tapered forms with the correct cross-sections |
| **4** | **Which muscle is working** — and therefore which side bulges |
| **5** | **The alternating rhythm** down both sides |
| **6** | **Compression folds**, where joints are bent |

---

**The checks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Is the elbow point on the forearm?** It belongs to the ulna |
| **2** | **Does the brachioradialis ridge point at the thumb?** |
| **3** | **Does the deltoid end in a V part-way down the arm?** |
| **4** | **Is only the working muscle defined?** |
| **5** | **Does the femur slant inward from hip to knee?** |
| **6** | **Is the inner malleolus higher and the outer lower?** |
| **7** | **Is the inner calf head lower and larger than the outer?** |
| **8** | **Is the outer thigh flat, from the IT band?** |
| **9** | **Does the shin's inner silhouette read as a hard straight bone edge?** |
| **10** | **Does the alternation — outer high, inner low, repeating — run down the limb?** |

---

**The counts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **50 arm skeletons, 50 leg skeletons**, from memory | |
| **150 forearms** across supination, pronation and mid | |
| **100 upper arms** in push and pull | |
| **50 deltoids** at varied positions | |
| **80 thighs**, front, side and seated | |
| **150 lower legs** — knees, calves, shins | |
| **100 action pairs** — the same limb relaxed and working | |
| **50 compression studies** at bent joints | |
| **Plus the landmark hunt on your own body**, for all of them | |

**Four to six weeks**, alongside continued gesture.

---

**And the four ideas to carry:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Contracted bulges and curves; stretched flattens and straightens.** One rule, and it covers every limb in every pose |
| **2** | **The limbs alternate** — outer high and inner low, repeating down their length. A symmetrical limb is a tube |
| **3** | **The forearm's twist is readable from the thumb**, via the brachioradialis |
| **4** | **Joint landmarks are bone and do not move.** Everything soft is placed against them |

---

**What this stage completes.** With stages 6, 7 and 8 done, **you can construct a figure in any pose from imagination and put correct surface form on it.** That is the hardest technical problem in the subject, and everything after it — heads, hands, drapery, animals, composition, colour — is either a specialised case of it or a different subject entirely.

**The two remaining things the figure needs are the head and the hands**, which are stages 9 and 10, and they are separated out because **each is as hard as the whole rest of the body.**

**Practice.** Run the ten checks on 20 limb drawings. Then total the counts and finish what is short. Then draw 20 complete figures from imagination with full anatomy, and check each against reference afterwards — listing what you got wrong, which is the study plan for the next month.
Why hands are hard:
The part everyone hides: why it is genuinely difficult, and the simplification that makes it tractable.

**Hands are hidden in beginners' drawings — behind backs, in pockets, cropped out of frame — and the reason is that they are legitimately the hardest part of the body.**

---

**Why, specifically:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Twenty-seven bones and more than thirty joints**, in a small space | |
| **Every finger has three segments and three joints**, each with its own angle | |
| **The thumb opposes**, which means it moves on a different plane from everything else | |
| **It is small**, so errors are proportionally large | |
| **It is enormously expressive**, so a wrong hand reads as a wrong emotion | |
| **And everyone knows what hands look like**, so errors are obvious to every viewer | |

**That last point is the same problem faces have, and it is why hands and the head get their own stages.**

---

**The simplification that makes it possible: the hand is a box and a wedge.**

| | Part | Form |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The palm** | **a flattened box** — wider than deep, with a slight curve across it |
| **2** | **The thumb mass** | **a wedge attached to the box's side**, with its own base |
| **3** | **The fingers** | **four chains of three segments**, attached along the box's far edge |

**Three parts. Everything about hand drawing is getting those three into the right relationship before any finger is drawn.**

---

**The proportions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The hand is as long as the face** — chin to hairline. **Stage 6's rule, and the single most useful hand fact** | |
| **The palm is roughly half the hand's length**, the fingers the other half | |
| **The middle finger is the longest**, and its length is about the palm's length | |
| **The thumb's tip reaches roughly the middle knuckle of the index finger** | |
| **And the palm is wider than it is deep** | which means it has a front, a back, and two narrow edges |

---

**The knuckle arc**, which is the detail that makes a hand read:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The knuckles where the fingers meet the palm do not form a straight line** | |
| **They form an ARC**, with the middle-finger knuckle highest | |
| **And the fingertips form a second, deeper arc** | |
| **Both arcs curve the same way** | |
| **Drawing the knuckles in a straight line is the most common hand error** | and it is also the easiest to fix |

---

**And the one strategic point: a hand is read by its gesture, not by its detail.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A hand drawn with correct overall shape and no finger detail reads fine** | |
| **A hand drawn with every knuckle rendered and the wrong overall shape does not** | |
| **So the order is: mass, then plane, then gesture, then fingers, then detail** | |
| **And most drawings should stop at gesture** | |
| **Which is also why hands at small sizes are three or four marks** | — and at 80 pixels, one |

**Practice.** Draw 100 hands as a box plus a wedge plus four chains, no detail. Then 50 with the knuckle arc and the fingertip arc explicit. Then measure your own hand against your own face. Then draw your non-drawing hand 50 times from life, in 50 positions, at two minutes each.
The hand's structure:
The bones that matter, the three arches, and the way the palm is not flat.

**The bones, simplified to what changes the surface:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Five metacarpals** — in the palm, one per finger. **They are part of the palm, not the fingers** | |
| **Fourteen phalanges** — three per finger, two in the thumb | |
| **And the carpals** — eight small bones at the wrist, which for drawing is one block | |

**The crucial structural fact: the knuckles you see when you make a fist are the HEADS of the metacarpals** — so **the fingers begin further back than they appear.** The first finger segment is partly inside the palm.

---

**The three arches**, which is why the palm is not a flat board:

| | Arch | Direction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The transverse arch at the knuckles** | **across the hand** — the one the knuckle arc shows |
| **2** | **The transverse arch at the wrist** | **across, deeper** — making the palm concave |
| **3** | **The longitudinal arch** | **along the hand**, from wrist to fingers |

**The palm is a shallow dome, concave on the inside.** Which is why a hand can cup, and why the palm's drawn surface is never flat.

---

**The two mobile sides:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The thumb side and the little-finger side both fold inward** | |
| **The index and middle metacarpals are nearly fixed** | |
| **So the hand curls from the outside in** | and a cupped hand is deepest on the little-finger side |
| **Which is why the hand's silhouette changes so much** | — the mobile edges move while the middle stays |

---

**The thumb**, which is the hardest part and the most important:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Its metacarpal is OUTSIDE the palm's box**, attached at the wrist, free to swing | |
| **Which means the thumb has three segments visible, not two** — the metacarpal shows as part of the thumb's mass | |
| **It sits at roughly 90° to the other fingers' plane** | so **the thumbnail faces sideways when the fingernails face back** |
| **Its base is a triangular mass** — the thenar eminence, the fleshy pad | |
| **And its opposition is what makes a hand a hand** | |

**The 90° rotation is the fact to hold.** **A thumb drawn in the same plane as the fingers is the second-commonest hand error**, and it makes the hand read as a paddle.

---

**The back against the palm:**

| | Back | Palm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Surface** | **bony** — tendons and metacarpals visible | **fleshy** — three pads and a hollow |
| **Landmarks** | **the knuckles, the tendons fanning from the wrist** | **the thenar (thumb) and hypothenar (little finger) pads, and the creases** |
| **How it reads** | **structural, angular** | **soft, with creases describing the folds** |
| **Which to draw when** | **the back is easier and more often seen** | the palm needs the creases to read |

**Practice.** Draw 50 hands with the three arches explicit, including a cupped hand seen end-on. Then 50 with the thumb's plane at 90° to the fingers', checked by the nail directions. Then 50 backs of hands with tendons, and 50 palms with the pads and creases. Then make 20 shapes with your own hand and draw each from three angles.
Fingers, and the gesture of a hand:
How fingers actually bend, the arcs they move in, and the thing that makes a drawn hand look alive rather than assembled.

**The fingers' joints:**

| | Joint | Movement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Knuckle (MCP)** | where finger meets palm | **bends, and spreads sideways** |
| **Middle (PIP)** | | **bends only** — a pure hinge |
| **End (DIP)** | | **bends only**, and is partly coupled to the middle joint |

**The coupling is a useful fact: you cannot easily bend the end joint without the middle one.** Which means **a finger's two outer segments move roughly together**, and drawing them independently looks wrong.

---

**The segments' proportions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Each segment is shorter than the one before it** | |
| **Roughly: the first is the longest, the second about two-thirds of it, the third about two-thirds again** | |
| **Which is why a bent finger spirals inward** rather than curling evenly | |
| **And a fully curled finger's tip points back at its own knuckle** | |

---

**The fingers do not bend in parallel:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **When the hand closes, the fingers converge** — they point towards the base of the thumb, not straight back | |
| **Because they are arranged on an arch and bend towards a common point** | |
| **Which is why a fist's fingers are not four parallel tubes** | |
| **And why a relaxed hand's fingers are slightly fanned** | the little finger furthest out |

---

**Now the gesture of a hand**, which is what makes it live:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A hand at rest has all its fingers at slightly different angles** | |
| **Never equal, never parallel, never symmetrical** | |
| **The usual relaxed posture** — **a gentle curl, with the index least curled and the little finger most** | |
| **And a hand doing something has one or two active fingers and the rest following** | |
| **Drawing four fingers in the same position** | **is the thing that makes a hand look like a glove** |

---

**The three gestures worth knowing as defaults:**

| | Gesture | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Relaxed hanging** | **a soft curl, fingers staggered**, thumb forward of the palm | |
| **Gripping** | **fingers wrapped round the object, thumb opposing**, and **the object's shape visible in the hand's form** | |
| **Pointing or gesturing** | **one or two fingers extended, the rest curled**, the extended ones straighter than feels natural | |

**And the rule for all three: draw the hand's overall mass and direction first, then the fingers as a group, then individual fingers last.**

---

**Hogarth's *Drawing Dynamic Hands* is the book**, and the reason it is better than the alternatives is that **it organises hands by action rather than by anatomy** — which is the right organisation for drawing them.

**Practice.** Draw 100 hands in the three default gestures, mass first and fingers last. Then 50 fists, with the fingers converging towards the thumb's base rather than parallel. Then 50 hands gripping objects of different shapes, where the object is visible in the hand's form. Then draw your own hand 100 times in 100 different positions, two minutes each.
Feet, and standing:
The other end: the foot as a wedge and an arch, why it is easier than the hand, and what shoes do to it.

**Feet are much easier than hands** — fewer positions, less expression, usually covered — **and they are drawn badly for a different reason: nobody looks at them.**

---

**The structure:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The foot is a wedge** — thick at the heel and ankle, thin at the toes | |
| **With an arch along the inside**, lifting the inner edge off the ground | |
| **So the foot touches the ground at three points** — **the heel, the ball of the big toe, and the outer edge** | |
| **And the outer edge touches along its length** while the inner does not | |
| **Which means the foot is asymmetrical from front to back and from side to side** | |

---

**The proportions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **About one head long** | |
| **The ankle is NOT at the middle** — **the foot projects roughly three times as far forward as back** | |
| **The toes occupy about a quarter of the length** | |
| **And the big toe is much larger than the others**, which taper quickly | |
| **The second toe is often the longest** | depending on the individual |

**The ankle's position is the fact that fixes a drawn foot.** Placing the leg at the foot's centre produces the flipper that is the commonest foot error.

---

**From the three main views:**

| View | What defines it |
| --- | --- |
| **Side, inner** | **the arch** — a clear curve lifting off the ground. The most characteristic view |
| **Side, outer** | **flat along the ground**, almost no arch, the little toe's base visible |
| **Front** | **foreshortened and hard** — the toes stack, and the ankle's two malleoli frame it |
| **Back** | **the Achilles and the heel**, narrow above and wide below |

---

**What the foot does in a pose:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Bearing weight** | **the arch flattens slightly, the foot spreads, the toes grip** |
| **Free** | **the arch is higher, the toes relax and curl slightly** |
| **On tiptoe** | **the arch is maximal, the metatarsals angle steeply, the toes bend at their bases** |
| **And the ankle tilts** | **inward or outward with the leg's weight shift**, which is visible and almost never drawn |

---

**Shoes**, which is what you will actually draw most of the time:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A shoe is a form over a form** — it takes the foot's shape and adds its own | |
| **The arch is usually hidden** and the sole's shape replaces it | |
| **The ankle's position relative to the shoe stays the same** | which is the key to drawing it correctly |
| **And the shoe's toe box determines the silhouette** — a period boot, a modern trainer and a bare foot have very different outlines | |
| **For York, the relevant forms are turnshoes and ankle boots** | soft-soled, close-fitting, with little structure — and **Grafton's and Tierney's plates are the reference** |

**Practice.** Draw 50 bare feet from all four views with the three ground contact points marked. Then 50 with the ankle placed at the correct third rather than the middle. Then 30 weight-bearing and 30 free, showing the arch's change. Then draw 50 shoed feet, the foot constructed first and the shoe over it.
Hands and feet at small sizes:
What survives when a hand is five pixels across: the hierarchy of hand information, and why learning the detail still matters.

**The practical situation: in most of the drawings this curriculum leads to, a hand is small.** In an illustration it is a centimetre; in a Shepherds sprite it is two or three pixels.

---

**The hierarchy, in order of what survives longest:**

| | Information | Survives to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The hand's overall direction and angle** | **everything.** Even at 2 pixels |
| **2** | **Open or closed** | **almost everything** |
| **3** | **The silhouette's mass** — mitten-shaped, splayed, fisted | **small sizes** |
| **4** | **The thumb's separation** | **medium sizes** |
| **5** | **Individual fingers** | **large only** |
| **6** | **Knuckles, creases, nails** | **study size only** |

**So at small sizes a hand is: a direction, a state, and a mass.** Three decisions.

---

**Which raises the obvious question: why learn the detail at all?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Because the silhouette you draw at small size is a simplification OF something** | |
| **And a simplification of a correct form reads correctly** | |
| **While a simplification of a vague idea reads as a blob** | |
| **The specific test** | **does the small hand's mass have the right proportions, the right angle at the wrist, and the thumb in the right place?** Those three survive, and they are only right if you know the structure |
| **This is the same argument as stage 7's "what shows at a distance"** | and it is the curriculum's recurring one |

---

**The practical rules for small hands:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw the mass, not the fingers** | |
| **State open or closed unambiguously** — an ambiguous hand reads as a mistake | |
| **Keep the thumb visible if possible** — it is what makes a shape read as a hand rather than a paddle | |
| **Make the wrist's angle clear** | **it carries the gesture** |
| **And at the smallest sizes, let the silhouette do everything** | which is stage 9 of the Aseprite curriculum's argument exactly |

---

**And the specific case this curriculum serves: an 80-pixel character.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A hand at that scale is about 3 × 4 pixels** | |
| **Which is one value, maybe two** | |
| **So the hand is: a direction, and whether it holds something** | |
| **And what it holds is usually larger and more readable than the hand** | — the crook, the sling, the lantern |
| **Which means the equipment carries the hand's meaning**, and the hand carries its angle | |
| **§9's signature equipment rule, arriving from the other side** | |

---

**The study that transfers**, since it is a different exercise from the ones above:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw a hand large and correctly** | |
| **Then draw the same hand at 3 cm, at 1 cm, and at 3 mm** | |
| **Each time deciding what to keep** | |
| **The reduction is the skill**, not the enlargement | |
| **And doing it ten times teaches more about small hands than a hundred small hands drawn directly** | |

**Practice.** Take 30 hands and draw each at four sizes, deciding the reduction each time. Then draw 100 small hands directly, at about 1 cm, aiming only for direction, state and mass. Then draw 20 figures at 5 cm tall where the hands read correctly. Then draw 20 hands holding objects where the object does the work.
The hands and feet checklist:
The stage closed as a list: the construction order, the checks, and the counts.

**The order for a hand:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The wrist's angle** — the hand's gesture starts here |
| **2** | **The palm as a flattened box**, with its plane stated |
| **3** | **The thumb's wedge**, at 90° to the fingers' plane |
| **4** | **The knuckle arc** across the box's far edge |
| **5** | **The fingers as a group**, converging, staggered |
| **6** | **Individual fingers**, last, and only if the size warrants |

---

**The checks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Is the hand as long as the face?** |
| **2** | **Do the knuckles form an arc rather than a line?** |
| **3** | **Is the thumb's plane perpendicular to the fingers'?** |
| **4** | **Do the fingers converge towards the thumb's base when closing?** |
| **5** | **Are all four fingers at different angles?** |
| **6** | **Is the palm drawn as an arched surface rather than flat?** |
| **7** | **Is the foot about a head long, with the ankle at the back third?** |
| **8** | **Does the foot touch the ground at three points?** |
| **9** | **Is the inner arch lifted and the outer edge flat?** |
| **10** | **At the size this will be seen, is the hand's direction and state unambiguous?** |

---

**The counts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **200 hands** as box, wedge and chains | |
| **100 with the two arcs**, 50 with the arches, 50 thumb-plane studies | |
| **100 in the three default gestures**, 50 fists, 50 gripping | |
| **100 of your own hand from life** | |
| **130 feet** across the four views, weight states and shoes | |
| **120 small-hand studies** and 30 four-size reductions | |

**Three to four weeks**, and it is the stage people most often cut short — which is why hands stay bad.

---

**And the three ideas to carry:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The hand is a box, a wedge and four chains.** Everything else is detail on those |
| **2** | **The thumb is on a different plane.** This single fact separates a hand from a paddle |
| **3** | **Hands are read by direction and state, not by detail** — at every size, including large |

---

**One honest note about this stage's difficulty.** **Hands take longer to learn than anything else in the figure**, and the usual experience is that they stay noticeably worse than the rest of your drawing for a long time. **That is normal and it is not a reason to stop drawing them.** The alternative — hiding them — produces a body of work where every figure has its hands behind its back, which is far more conspicuous than a slightly wrong hand.

**Practice.** Run the ten checks on 20 hand drawings. Then total the counts and finish what is short. Then commit to drawing one hand from life every day for a month, and compare the first with the last.
Why the head is hardest:
The one part of the body every viewer is an expert on, and the three consequences for how it must be drawn.

**Humans have dedicated neural machinery for faces.** You can recognise a face from a few pixels, at a glance, in bad light, at an odd angle — and you can tell when one is slightly wrong without being able to say what.

**Which means a drawn head is judged by a specialist**, and every other part of the body is not.

---

**The three consequences:**

| | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Small errors are large.** A nose two millimetres too long on a 10 cm head is immediately visible; a forearm two millimetres too long is not |
| **2** | **Accuracy is not enough.** A head can have every feature correctly placed and still fail to look like the person, or fail to look alive |
| **3** | **Symbols interfere more than anywhere else.** You know what an eye looks like, and the thing you know is an almond with a circle in it, which no real eye resembles |

---

**The symbol problem, specifically**, because it is the main obstacle:

| | The symbol | The reality |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Eye** | **an almond with a circle** | **a sphere in a socket, covered by two thick lids with visible edges, set back under a brow** |
| **Nose** | **a hook and two dots** | **a wedge with a bony top, cartilaginous end, and two wings** |
| **Mouth** | **two curved lines** | **two soft forms wrapped round a cylinder of teeth, with no outline at all** |
| **Ear** | **a C** | **a C of the outer rim with a Y inside it**, deeply three-dimensional |

**Drawing the symbols produces a face that reads as a drawing of a face.** Stage 2's negative space and contour exercises exist partly for this.

---

**What makes this tractable: the head is a simple solid with features placed on it by rule.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The skull is a predictable shape with very little individual variation in its structure** | |
| **The features' positions are governed by proportions that hold across almost everyone** | |
| **And likeness is mostly in the PROPORTIONS, not in the features' shapes** | |
| **Which means a head can be constructed** | and that is what this stage teaches |

---

**The order, which is Loomis' and is still the best:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The ball and plane** — the skull's basic solid |
| **2** | **The guide lines** — brow, eye line, nose, mouth, centre line |
| **3** | **The features' boxes** — where each one sits, before any detail |
| **4** | **The planes** — how the surface turns |
| **5** | **The features themselves** |
| **6** | **Hair, as a mass** |
| **7** | **Detail and rendering** |

**Steps 1 to 3 decide whether the head works. Steps 5 to 7 decide how finished it looks, and no amount of 5 to 7 rescues a failure at 1 to 3.**

**Practice.** Draw 30 faces entirely from memory, with no reference, before reading further — and keep them. Then draw the same 30 after this stage and compare. Then take 20 reference photographs and, for each, write down what the eye, nose, mouth and ear actually look like rather than what you know they are.
The ball and plane:
Loomis' construction: a sphere with its sides cut off, a jaw hung from it, and the three lines that make it a head rather than a shape.

**The construction, in four steps:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Draw a sphere.** This is the cranium |
| **2** | **Cut off the sides** — slice a flat plane off each side, parallel, leaving a shape wider than it is deep... **no: narrower across than front-to-back is wrong.** The cut sides make the ball narrower across, which is what a skull is |
| **3** | **Draw the centre line and the brow line** as great circles on the ball — **both ellipses, touching the silhouette only at their ends** |
| **4** | **Hang the jaw** from the side plane, below and in front |

**That is the whole thing**, and it is the most widely used head construction because the sphere is easy to draw at any angle and the cut planes make its orientation visible.

---

**The proportions of the construction:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The ball's diameter is the head's width across the temples** | |
| **The side cuts are at about 1/4 of the diameter in from each side** | |
| **The brow line is the ball's "equator"** — roughly its widest circle in the vertical direction | |
| **And the jaw's bottom is about 1/3 of the ball's diameter below it** | |
| **Which makes the whole head about 1.3 ball-diameters tall** | |

---

**The three lines, which do all the work:**

| | Line | States |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Centre line** | down the face, over the ball and the jaw | **the head's TURN** — left and right |
| **Brow line** | across, at the ball's equator | **the head's TILT** — up and down |
| **Jaw line** | from the ear down to the chin | **the jaw's position and the head's bottom** |

**Those two great circles on the ball specify the head's orientation completely.** Everything else is placed from them.

---

**And the critical detail from stage 3's sphere lesson**, which is where most ball-and-plane heads fail:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The centre line and the brow line are ELLIPSES, not straight lines** | |
| **They touch the ball's silhouette only at their two ends** | |
| **Everywhere else they are inside it** | |
| **A centre line drawn as a straight line down the face flattens the head completely** | |
| **And a brow line drawn straight does the same** | |

**This is the single most useful correction in the whole stage**, and it is also why stage 3's sphere work was worth doing.

---

**Where the ear goes**, because it is the one feature placed from the construction rather than from the face:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Behind the side plane's centre, at the back of the jaw's hinge** | |
| **Between the brow line and the base of the nose**, vertically | |
| **Which means the ear's position is fixed by the construction**, not by the face | |
| **And it is the landmark that makes a three-quarter head sit correctly** | |

---

**The alternatives on the shelf**, since Loomis is not the only system:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Hogarth** — a more angular construction with explicit planes from the start. **Better for understanding the surface, harder to draw quickly** | |
| **Reilly** — an abstract system of rhythmic lines over the face. **Excellent for likeness, and it assumes you can already construct a head** | |
| **Hamm** — diagrammatic and fast, good as a check | |
| **Use Loomis to construct, Hogarth to understand the planes, and the others later** | |

**Practice.** Draw 200 ball-and-plane heads at every angle, with the centre line and brow line as correct ellipses every time. Then 50 with the ear placed from the construction. Then 50 looking up and 50 looking down, where the brow line's ellipse changes degree. Then take 30 reference photographs and draw the construction over them on a layer.
The skull:
What is underneath: the bones that show through on every face, and why learning them fixes more than learning features does.

**The skull is mostly bone directly under skin.** More of the head's surface is bone-determined than any other part of the body — which makes it the one place where learning the skeleton pays off immediately.

---

**The forms that show on every face:**

| | | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The brow ridge** | above the eyes, stronger in men |
| **2** | **The temple** | a flat or hollow plane at the side of the forehead |
| **3** | **The cheekbone — the zygomatic** | **the widest point of the face**, and its arch runs back to the ear |
| **4** | **The eye socket** | a deep bony cavity — **the eye sits well back inside it** |
| **5** | **The nasal aperture** | a hole; the nose's bony part is only its top third |
| **6** | **The upper jaw** | carrying the top teeth, curving forward |
| **7** | **The jaw** | the mandible — its angle at the back is a strong character marker |
| **8** | **The chin** | a separate projecting form on the mandible |

---

**The three that decide a face's character:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The cheekbone's width and prominence** | **the face's widest point, and the single biggest factor in face shape** |
| **The jaw's angle** — square and wide, or narrow and sloping | |
| **The brow's projection** — heavy or flat | |
| **Change those three and you have a different person**, with identical features | |
| **Which is why likeness is structural rather than featural** | and the next lessons build on it |

---

**The eye socket, which is the fact that fixes eyes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It is a deep cone in the skull, not a shallow dish** | |
| **The eyeball sits INSIDE it, set back, with the brow overhanging** | |
| **So the eye is in shadow from above on nearly every lighting** | |
| **And the lids wrap round a sphere** rather than being flat shapes | |
| **Drawing the eye on the surface of the face** | **is the error that makes a face look like a mask** |

---

**The teeth and the mouth's underlying form:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The upper and lower jaws carry the teeth in two arches** | |
| **Which form a CYLINDER, curving back at the sides** | |
| **So the mouth wraps round that cylinder** — the lips are not flat on the face | |
| **And the corners of the mouth are further back in space than its centre** | |
| **Which is why a mouth drawn as a flat line across the face reads wrongly on a three-quarter view** | |

---

**And the proportion the skull gives for free:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The eyes are at the vertical MIDDLE of the head** | not two-thirds up, which is where everyone puts them |
| **Because the cranium is large and the face occupies the lower half** | |
| **This is the single most commonly violated proportion in portrait drawing** | |
| **And the reason is that we attend to the face and ignore the cranium** | so we draw the part we look at too large |

**Practice.** Draw the skull from memory 50 times, from front, side, three-quarter, above and below. Then 50 faces with all eight bony forms marked before any feature. Then 30 where you vary only the cheekbone width, jaw angle and brow projection, keeping features identical, and see how many different people you get. Then check the eye-at-the-middle rule on 30 photographs.
The head's proportions:
The measurements that hold across almost everyone, and the four that matter most.

**The classical divisions**, with the head seen from the front:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The head divides in half at the EYES** | |
| **The lower half divides in thirds** — **brow to nose base, nose base to chin, with the mouth about a third of the way down the last third** | |
| **The upper half is cranium** — forehead and hair | |

---

**The full set, worth knowing as defaults:**

| | Measurement | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Eyes** | **halfway down the head** |
| **2** | **Eye width** | **the face is five eyes wide** — and the gap between the eyes is one eye |
| **3** | **Nose base** | **halfway between the brow and the chin** |
| **4** | **Mouth** | **about a third of the way from the nose base to the chin** |
| **5** | **Ears** | **between the brow line and the nose base** |
| **6** | **Head width** | **about two-thirds of its height** |
| **7** | **The mouth's width** | **the corners fall under the pupils**, roughly |
| **8** | **The nose's width** | **the wings fall under the inner corners of the eyes**, roughly |

---

**The four that matter most**, because they are the ones most often wrong:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Eyes at the halfway point.** Drawn too high by almost everyone | |
| **2 — Five eyes wide.** The eyes are drawn too large and too close together | |
| **3 — Ears from brow to nose base.** Drawn too small and too high | |
| **4 — Head width two-thirds of height.** Drawn too narrow | |

**Those four alone fix most proportion errors in a drawn face.**

---

**The profile, which has its own proportions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The head is as deep as it is tall**, roughly — **it fits in a square** | |
| **The ear is at the horizontal MIDDLE of that square**, or slightly behind | |
| **The back of the skull projects much further than people draw** | |
| **And the face occupies only the front third** | |
| **The commonest profile error** | **a head too shallow front-to-back**, because the cranium behind the ear is underdrawn |

---

**And the honest qualification, as with the figure's canon:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **These are averages and real heads vary considerably** | |
| **Their use is as a CHECK, not a template** | |
| **Measure the actual head you are drawing** — sighting, from stage 2 | |
| **And the deviations from the average ARE the likeness** | **a person with eyes slightly above the midline and a long lower face looks like themselves because of it** |
| **So: construct with the canon, then measure, then adjust** | and the adjustments are the person |

**Practice.** Draw 50 heads to the canon exactly, from memory. Then measure 30 reference photographs against all eight rules and record the deviations — that table is your evidence that the canon is an average. Then draw 30 portraits where you deliberately exaggerate each person's deviations. Then check your own face in a mirror against all eight.
The planes of the head:
Where the surface turns: the plane breaks that make a head read as a solid, and why this is what lighting needs.

**A head is not a smooth egg.** It has distinct planes meeting at edges, and **the edges are where value changes** — which is why understanding them is what makes a head shadeable.

---

**The major plane breaks:**

| | Break | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Front to side of the forehead** | a corner running up from the outer brow |
| **2** | **The temple** | a flat or slightly hollow plane |
| **3** | **The brow's underside** | **turning sharply down into the eye socket** |
| **4** | **The cheekbone's front and side** | the face's widest corner |
| **5** | **The side of the nose** | **three planes — front, two sides — plus the underside** |
| **6** | **The upper lip's plane** | **angled back and down** from the nose |
| **7** | **The chin's front and underside** | |
| **8** | **The jaw's side plane**, running back to the ear | |

---

**The simplification worth memorising: the head has a front, two sides, a top and a bottom.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The front** — the face's flat-ish frontal plane | |
| **The sides** — from the cheekbone back to the ear | |
| **The top** — the cranium's dome | |
| **The bottom** — under the jaw and the chin | |
| **And every feature sits on one of them**, or spans a break | |

**A head lit from above and to one side has: a lit top, a half-lit front, a shadowed side, and a dark underside.** Four values, which is exactly Shepherds' §10.1 — and the reason that constraint works at all is that the head really does have four main planes.

---

**The nose's planes, which are the clearest example:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Four planes: front, two sides, and the underside with the nostrils** | |
| **Drawn as a wedge** | |
| **The front plane catches the most light and is usually the face's brightest area** | |
| **The underside is usually the face's darkest** | |
| **And the side planes turn sharply** — the nose is not a rounded tube | |
| **Which is why a nose drawn as an outline with two nostril dots cannot be lit** | |

---

**Why planes matter more than contours:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A contour drawing of a head states its silhouette** | |
| **A plane drawing states its form** | |
| **And form is what you light, shade and render** | |
| **So a portrait drawn from contours cannot be finished** — there is nothing to shade | |
| **Hogarth's *Drawing the Human Head* is built on exactly this** | planes first, features second |

---

**The exercise that teaches it: the planar head.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw the head as flat facets only**, like a cut gem — no curves anywhere | |
| **Every surface a flat plane with a hard edge** | |
| **Which forces you to decide where every break is** | |
| **Then shade each plane with one flat value** | according to its angle to the light |
| **And the result looks like a head** | which proves the planes were the information |

**The Asaro head — a sculpted planar head — is the standard reference object for this**, and drawing from one or from photographs of one is the fastest way to learn the breaks.

**Practice.** Draw 100 planar heads — flat facets only, no curves — at varied angles. Then shade 50 of them with four flat values from one light direction. Then draw 50 noses as four-plane wedges. Then take 30 portrait photographs and mark every plane break on a layer before drawing anything.
The eye:
A sphere in a socket, the two lids with thickness, and the six things that are wrong with the symbol.

**The symbol is an almond with a circle in it. Here is what is actually there.**

---

**The structure:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A sphere**, about 24 mm across, sitting in a bony socket | |
| **Two lids wrapping round it** — curved sheets, not flat shapes | |
| **Each lid has THICKNESS** — the lower one's thickness is visible as a pale edge, always | |
| **The brow above, overhanging** | |
| **And the whole thing set back in shadow** | |

---

**The six corrections to the symbol:**

| | Symbol | Reality |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **the eye is on the surface** | **it is recessed, in a deep socket, usually in shadow** |
| **2** | **the lids are lines** | **they have thickness.** The lower lid's edge is a visible pale band |
| **3** | **the two corners are the same** | **the inner corner is lower and has the tear duct; the outer is higher and tucks under the lid** |
| **4** | **the iris is a full circle** | **the upper lid always covers part of it**, except in surprise or fear |
| **5** | **the eye is symmetrical** | **the upper lid's highest point is towards the inner side; the lower lid's lowest is towards the outer.** The eye's shape is a skewed curve |
| **6** | **the lids are the same** | **the upper lid is larger, more curved, and casts a shadow on the eyeball** |

**Correction 4 is the one that fixes dead eyes.** **A fully visible iris reads as staring**, and it is why drawn characters often look alarmed.

---

**The surrounding forms, which are most of what you actually draw:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The brow ridge**, and the crease beneath it | |
| **The upper lid's fold** — present on most adults, varying hugely by individual and ethnicity | |
| **The lower lid's bag or furrow** | |
| **The inner corner's recess**, which is darker than everything near it | |
| **And the eyebrow** — which is a mass sitting on the brow ridge, not a line | |

**At a distance, those surrounding forms carry more than the eye itself does.**

---

**Both eyes together**, which is where three-quarter views fail:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **They sit on the same cross-contour of the head's ball** | |
| **So on a turned head, the far eye is foreshortened and sits HIGHER on the page** if the head is tilted | |
| **The far eye's visible width is compressed, and part of it may be hidden by the nose** | |
| **They are always the same size in 3D**, so the drawn size difference is pure perspective | |
| **And the gap between them is one eye's width**, which holds even in three-quarter | |

---

**What survives at small sizes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **At portrait size** — everything above | |
| **At figure size** — **a dark socket shape and a lighter eyeball.** Two marks | |
| **At thumbnail** — **a dark smudge** | |
| **At 80 pixels** — **one pixel, or none** — which is why Shepherds' §9 says a sprite's identity is silhouette rather than features | |

**Practice.** Draw 100 eyes from reference, with the lid thickness and the asymmetric corners on every one. Then 50 pairs in three-quarter view, both on the same cross-contour. Then 50 with the iris correctly covered by the upper lid, and 10 deliberately staring to see the difference. Then draw your own eye in a mirror 20 times.
The nose and the mouth:
The two features that carry the most character, their underlying forms, and the outlines that must not be drawn.

**The nose first, since it is the simpler.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A wedge projecting from the face** | |
| **Its top third is bone** — fixed, and the bridge's width is a strong character marker | |
| **Its lower two-thirds are cartilage** — the ball at the tip, the two wings, and the septum between the nostrils | |
| **The ball at the tip is a distinct spherical form** | and finding it is what makes a nose read as solid |
| **The wings are separate forms** that wrap round from the ball | |

**The four planes from the previous lesson — front, two sides, underside — are the construction.** Draw the wedge, find the ball, add the wings, state the underside.

---

**What varies between people:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The bridge's height and width** | |
| **The profile's line** — straight, convex, concave, or a combination | |
| **The tip's angle** — up, down, or level | |
| **The wings' flare** | |
| **And the underside's visibility**, which depends on the tip's angle and the viewing height | |
| **These five are most of a nose's individuality** | and they are all structural |

---

**The mouth**, which is harder:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The lips wrap round the teeth's cylinder** — so they curve back at the corners, in 3D | |
| **The upper lip is usually DARKER than the lower**, because it angles down and away from the light | |
| **The lower lip is fuller and catches light** — often the brightest point of the lower face | |
| **The upper lip has three parts** — two halves and the central tubercle, with the philtrum's groove above | |
| **And the corners are not points** | they are small recessed pockets |

---

**The outline that must not be drawn:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The lips have no outline.** Their edge is a change of colour and a soft change of plane | |
| **The one line that IS dark is the mouth's opening — between the lips** | |
| **Which is the only line a mouth needs** | |
| **Drawing both lips' outer edges as lines** | **produces the sticker-mouth**, and it is the single most common mouth error |
| **The correct construction** | **the dark line of the opening, plus the forms of the two lips as shading** |

---

**The mouth's expressive range**, which is why it matters so much:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The corners' position and direction carries most of a face's expression** | |
| **Up, down, pulled back, pushed forward, tightened, slack** | |
| **And it works at tiny sizes** — a mouth corner's direction is readable when nothing else is | |
| **Which makes it the most important feature for small-size character work** | and Faigin's book is almost entirely about it |

---

**The relationship between them**, which is the construction detail:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The upper lip's plane angles back and down from the nose's base** | |
| **So in a three-quarter view the mouth's far corner is further from the nose than the near one** | |
| **And the philtrum connects them**, centring both on the head's centre line | |
| **If the nose and mouth do not share the centre line** | **the face is broken**, and it is the first thing to check on a failed portrait |

**Practice.** Draw 100 noses as four-plane wedges with the ball and wings found. Then 50 profiles varying only the bridge and tip. Then 100 mouths with no outer outline — opening line plus shading only. Then 50 three-quarter mouths wrapping the teeth cylinder, with both corners correctly placed in depth.
The ear, and hair:
Two things everyone draws badly: the ear's actual structure in one rule, and hair as a mass rather than as strands.

**The ear, in one rule: it is a C of the outer rim with a Y inside it.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The C** — the helix, the outer rim, running round from the top to the lobe | |
| **The Y** — the antihelix, inside it, forking at the top | |
| **The bowl** — the concha, the deep hollow in the middle, leading to the canal | |
| **The tragus** — the small flap in front of the opening | |
| **And the lobe** — attached or free, depending on the individual | |

**Five parts. The C and the Y alone make a drawn ear read.**

---

**Placement, which matters more than structure:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Vertically: between the brow line and the base of the nose** | |
| **Horizontally: at the back of the jaw, behind the side plane's centre** | |
| **Angled: tilted back**, roughly parallel to the jaw's angle, not vertical | |
| **And in profile: at the middle of the head's square**, or slightly behind | |

**A crudely drawn ear in the right place passes. A beautiful one in the wrong place looks like a mistake.** Which is the whole lesson, and it is true of ears more than of any other feature — **because nobody looks at ears, so only their placement registers.**

---

**The ear's size**, which is the common error:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Drawn too small, by nearly everyone** | |
| **The brow-to-nose-base span is a third of the head's height** | |
| **Which is a large feature** | |
| **And ears grow throughout life**, so on an older face they are proportionally larger still | |

---

**Now hair**, which is the thing most likely to ruin an otherwise good head.

**The rule: hair is a mass with a form, not a collection of strands.**

| | Draw | Do not draw |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The mass's silhouette**, which is the head plus a thickness | **individual strands across the whole mass** | |
| **The large groups** — the parting, the main locks, the direction of flow | **every lock equally** | |
| **Where it catches light** — usually a band following the skull's roundness | **texture evenly all over** | |
| **The edge where it meets the face** — the hairline, which is soft | **a hard outline round the whole hair** | |

---

**The three facts that make hair read:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — It has volume.** **The hair's silhouette is the skull's shape plus 1–3 cm all round.** Drawing it flat to the skull is the commonest error, and drawing it as an undifferentiated cloud is the second | |
| **2 — It grows from a point or a parting and flows.** **The direction of flow is the structure**, and it is consistent across the whole head | |
| **3 — It is darker than you think at the roots and lighter at the edges** — **the silhouette's edge catches light and breaks up**, which is what makes it read as hair rather than as a helmet | |

---

**And the simplification for any size below portrait:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One silhouette, two values, and the direction of flow** | |
| **At figure size: a shape and a value** | |
| **At 80 pixels: a shape and one accent** | |
| **Which is where hair's colour does the work of its texture** | |

**Practice.** Draw 100 ears as C-plus-Y, placed from the construction rather than from the face. Then 50 heads where the ear is deliberately drawn large enough to span brow to nose base. Then 100 heads of hair as masses — silhouette, flow direction, one light band, no strands. Then take 20 portraits and reduce each one's hair to three values.
Likeness:
What makes a drawn head look like a specific person: the measurements that carry identity, and why the features are not where it lives.

**The central finding, and it is counter-intuitive: likeness is in the proportions, not in the features.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **You can draw a person's eyes, nose and mouth perfectly and have it not look like them** | |
| **And you can draw crude features in exactly the right places and have it unmistakable** | |
| **Which is why caricature works at all** — it exaggerates proportions and simplifies features | |
| **And why a police sketch assembled from accurate features often looks like nobody** | |

---

**The measurements that carry identity, in order:**

| | Measurement | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The head's overall shape** — the skull's width, height and the jaw's angle | **the silhouette is read first and recognised fastest** |
| **2** | **The distance between the eyes** | **a very strong identity signal**, and one people are acutely sensitive to |
| **3** | **The vertical position of the features** — how far down the eyes, the nose base, the mouth | |
| **4** | **The cheekbones' width and height** | **the face's widest point** |
| **5** | **The ratio of face to cranium** | |
| **6** | **The brow's heaviness** | |
| **7** | **The chin's projection and shape** | |

**Features' own shapes come eighth and below.**

---

**The method for a likeness:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Construct the head generically** — ball and plane, canon proportions |
| **2** | **Measure the actual person** against the canon, by sighting |
| **3** | **Write down the deviations** — "eyes slightly closer together", "long lower face", "jaw narrower than average" |
| **4** | **Rebuild the construction with those deviations** |
| **5** | **Add features last**, generically at first |
| **6** | **Check by flipping** |

**Step 3 is the whole technique.** **The deviations from the average are the person**, and naming them in words makes them drawable.

---

**The check that works best: the squint test.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Squint at your drawing and at the reference** | |
| **Detail disappears; the large shapes and values remain** | |
| **If the likeness survives squinting, it is structural and will hold** | |
| **If it only works when you look closely, it is in the features and will not** | |
| **Which is the same zoom-out principle from stage 1** | applied to the hardest case |

---

**And the one thing that defeats likeness even when the proportions are right: a wrong expression.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A face at rest is not expressionless** — everyone has a characteristic resting set of the mouth and brows | |
| **Getting that wrong makes the drawing look like a different person in a mood** | |
| **So the resting expression is part of the likeness** | |
| **And it is the thing that makes drawing someone from several photographs hard** | each one has a different expression |

---

**For character design**, which is what this curriculum serves, the same principle inverts usefully:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **To design a character who looks like someone specific**, decide their deviations first | |
| **"Wide jaw, close-set eyes, heavy brow, short lower face"** — four decisions, and the character is distinguishable | |
| **Rather than designing features and hoping** | |
| **And it makes the character redrawable**, because the deviations are written down | |
| **Which is exactly what a character sheet has to guarantee** | **the same person from eight angles** |

**Practice.** Draw 30 portraits by the six-step method, writing the deviations in words before drawing. Then squint-test each against its reference. Then take 10 faces and caricature them by doubling every deviation. Then design 10 characters by choosing four deviations each, and draw each one twice a week apart to see if they survive.
Age, and the face over time:
What changes in a face between five and eighty, in the order it changes, and the three forces behind all of it.

**Three forces, and everything else follows:**

| | Force | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The skull grows, unevenly** | **the face enlarges relative to the cranium**, through childhood |
| **2** | **Soft tissue descends** | **gravity, over decades** |
| **3** | **Volume is lost** | **fat and muscle thin; the bone shows more** |

---

**Childhood, where force 1 dominates:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A baby's cranium is huge and its face is small** | |
| **The eyes are BELOW the halfway line of the whole head** | |
| **The nose is small and the bridge barely exists** | |
| **The jaw is tiny and the chin recedes** | |
| **Cheeks are full with fat pads** | |
| **And there are no visible bony landmarks at all** | — the whole face is soft forms |

**The drawable rule: for a young child, place the eyes low, make the cranium large, soften every landmark, and keep the features small and central.**

---

**Adolescence to adulthood:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The jaw and chin grow forward and down** — the largest single change | |
| **The nose's bridge develops and the nose lengthens** | |
| **The brow ridge develops**, more in men | |
| **Cheek fat reduces, so the cheekbones appear** | |
| **And the eyes arrive at the halfway line** | which is where the adult canon puts them |

---

**Middle age and older, where forces 2 and 3 dominate:**

| | Change | Where it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The nasolabial fold deepens** | nose to mouth corner — **the first and most universal sign** | |
| **The jaw's line softens** | the jowl, as tissue descends past the jaw's edge | |
| **The upper eyelid hoods** | tissue descends over the lid | |
| **Under-eye bags form** | | |
| **The lips thin** and the upper lip lengthens | | |
| **The nose and ears appear larger** | cartilage continues growing | |
| **The temples hollow** and the cheekbones become more prominent | | |
| **And the skull's forms show through everywhere** | | |

---

**The mistake to avoid: drawing age as wrinkles.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Wrinkles are the least important age signal** | |
| **A face aged only by adding lines reads as a young face with lines on it** | |
| **The signals that work are STRUCTURAL** — descended tissue, lost volume, changed proportions | |
| **Which is why an aged character can be drawn at small size and still read old** | |
| **And why a wrinkled 80-pixel sprite reads as noise** | |

---

**For Shepherds specifically**, where `characters.md` gives ages for the cast: **the three or four structural signals above are what make an older resident read as older at figure size**, and the wrinkles would be invisible. **Age is drawn in the silhouette of the jaw and the set of the shoulders**, not in the face's surface.

**Practice.** Draw one character at 4, 12, 25, 50 and 75, keeping the skull's proportions consistent and applying only the three forces. Then draw 30 older faces using only structural signals, no wrinkles. Then take 20 photographs of people of known ages and mark which signals are present. Then draw 20 aged figures at 5 cm tall and check they still read as old.
Expression:
Faigin's subject: the muscles behind each emotion, the ones that cannot be faked, and what survives at small sizes.

**Expression is muscular and specific.** Each emotion is produced by a known set of facial muscles, it is largely universal across cultures, and **once you know which muscles do what, expressions become constructible rather than guessed.**

---

**The muscles that matter:**

| | Muscle | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Frontalis** | **raises the brows** — surprise, fear, and the inner-brow raise of sadness | |
| **Corrugator** | **draws the brows together and down** — anger, concentration, pain | |
| **Orbicularis oculi** | **squeezes the eye shut** — and **the crow's-feet of a genuine smile** | |
| **Zygomatic major** | **pulls the mouth corners up and back** — the smile | |
| **Levator labii** | **raises the upper lip and wrinkles the nose** — disgust | |
| **Depressor anguli oris** | **pulls the mouth corners down** — sadness | |
| **Mentalis** | **pushes the chin up, wrinkling it** — doubt, suppressed crying | |
| **Platysma** | **tenses the neck, pulling the lower face down** — strain, fear, effort | |

---

**The six basic expressions, and their signatures:**

| | Expression | Signature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Happiness** | **mouth corners up and back; crow's-feet; lower lids raised** | |
| **Sadness** | **inner brows raised and drawn together; mouth corners down** | |
| **Anger** | **brows down and together; lower lids tensed; lips compressed or square** | |
| **Fear** | **brows raised AND drawn together; upper lids raised; mouth stretched wide** | |
| **Surprise** | **brows raised and curved; eyes wide; jaw dropped** | |
| **Disgust** | **nose wrinkled; upper lip raised; lower lids raised** | |

---

**The ones that cannot be faked**, which is Faigin's most useful material:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A genuine smile uses the orbicularis oculi** — the eye muscle — producing crow's-feet and raised lower lids | |
| **A posed smile uses only the mouth** | |
| **Which is why a drawn smile with untouched eyes reads as insincere**, and the viewer knows without knowing why | |
| **Similarly, the inner-brow raise of genuine sadness** is hard to produce voluntarily | |
| **So drawing those involuntary components is what makes an emotion read as real** | |

**For a drawn character, this is a decision: do you want the smile to be genuine? Then draw the eyes.**

---

**The structural effects**, which is what actually gets drawn:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Expressions move volume around** — they are not lines added to a resting face | |
| **A smile pushes the cheek mass up**, which narrows the eye from below and deepens the nasolabial fold | |
| **A frown compresses the brow**, creating vertical furrows and a shelf over the eyes | |
| **And the folds that appear run PERPENDICULAR to the muscle's direction of pull** | which is the rule for placing any expression wrinkle |

---

**What survives at small sizes**, in order:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The brows' angle** — the single most readable expressive element at any size |
| **2** | **The mouth's corner direction** |
| **3** | **The eyes' openness** |
| **4** | **The head's tilt and the shoulders** — **body language, which outranks the face when the face is small** |
| **Everything else needs portrait size** | |

**Which gives the practical rule for character work: at figure size, expression is brows, mouth corners, and posture.** Three decisions, and they carry further than any amount of facial detail.

**Practice.** Draw the six basic expressions on the same constructed head, 20 times each, naming the muscles each time. Then 30 pairs of genuine and posed smiles. Then 50 faces at 2 cm where only the brows, mouth corners and head tilt carry the emotion. Then draw 30 figures where the body language contradicts the face, and see which the viewer believes.
Heads at every size:
The reduction, applied to the head: what survives at each size, and the four marks a face needs at the smallest.

**The same exercise as stages 7 and 9, applied to the hardest case.**

| Size | What carries |
| --- | --- |
| **Portrait, 20 cm** | **everything in this stage** — planes, features, likeness, expression |
| **Figure in an illustration, 2 cm** | **the head's silhouette, the hair's mass, the eye sockets as shapes, the mouth's line, the jaw's angle** |
| **Thumbnail, 5 mm** | **the head's shape, the hair, and whether it is turned or facing** |
| **80-pixel sprite head, ~20 px** | **silhouette, two or three values, and the hair's accent colour** |
| **Distant figure, 3 px** | **a shape** |

---

**At 2 cm — the most common case in illustration — a face is about six marks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The eye sockets** — two dark shapes, not two eyes |
| **2** | **The nose's underside shadow** — one small mark |
| **3** | **The mouth's opening line** — one mark, with its corners' direction |
| **4** | **The jaw and chin's silhouette** |
| **5** | **The hair's mass and its edge against the face** |
| **6** | **The neck's shadow**, which separates head from body |

**Six marks, and the head reads, has an age, a build and an expression.** Adding more at that size makes it worse, not better.

---

**The counter-intuitive fact: a small face with fewer marks reads better than one with more.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Because at small size, each mark is proportionally huge** | |
| **So a drawn pupil at 2 cm is a large dark blob** | |
| **And two eyes, two eyebrows, two nostrils, two lips and an ear is eight competing marks in a space 1 cm across** | |
| **Which reads as noise, not as a face** | |
| **The eye assembles a face from very little** | and giving it less is giving it more |

---

**The specific case of the pixel-art portrait**, since Shepherds' register 1 calls for *"high-resolution pixel portraits… facial detail, personality, age, clothing, and emotion beyond what gameplay sprites can carry"*:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A portrait at, say, 64 × 64 pixels is between the 2 cm case and the portrait case** | |
| **It can carry: the planes, the eye sockets with visible eyes, the nose's three planes, the mouth's two forms, the hair's groups, and an expression** | |
| **It cannot carry: individual lashes, wrinkles, skin texture, or subtle likeness** | |
| **So the portrait's job is age, build, costume and attitude** — which is exactly what the document asks for | |
| **And the drawing that feeds it is a plane drawing**, not a rendered one | |

---

**The exercise that teaches all of this**, and it is the stage's most useful:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw one head at 20 cm, fully** | |
| **Then the same head at 5 cm, 2 cm, 1 cm and 5 mm** | |
| **Deciding at each step what to drop** | |
| **And checking at each step that it is still the same person** | |
| **The reduction is the skill**, and it is the one that transfers into every piece of character art | |

**Practice.** Take 20 heads and draw each at five sizes, same person each time. Then draw 100 faces at 2 cm using only the six marks. Then draw 20 at 64 × 64 as plane drawings, deciding what each can carry. Then take 10 of your most detailed portraits and reduce them to 1 cm, and see which survive as the same person.
The head checklist:
The stage closed as a list: the construction order, the checks, and the counts.

**The order:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The ball, with its side planes cut** |
| **2** | **Centre line and brow line, as ellipses** |
| **3** | **The jaw, hung from the side plane** |
| **4** | **The proportion divisions** — eyes at the halfway point, lower half in thirds |
| **5** | **The plane breaks** |
| **6** | **The features' boxes**, placed before any detail |
| **7** | **The features**, generically |
| **8** | **The deviations that make it this person** |
| **9** | **Hair as a mass** |
| **10** | **Expression, and detail** |

---

**The checks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Are the eyes at the vertical middle of the head?** |
| **2** | **Is the face five eyes wide, with one eye's gap between them?** |
| **3** | **Are the centre line and brow line ellipses rather than straight lines?** |
| **4** | **Do the ears span from the brow line to the nose's base?** |
| **5** | **In profile, does the head fit a square, with the ear at its middle?** |
| **6** | **Is the eye recessed in a socket rather than sitting on the surface?** |
| **7** | **Is the upper lid covering part of the iris?** |
| **8** | **Is the mouth drawn without outer outlines?** |
| **9** | **Does the hair have volume beyond the skull?** |
| **10** | **Does the likeness survive squinting?** |

---

**The counts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **200 ball-and-plane heads**, plus 100 looking up and down | |
| **50 skulls** from memory, 50 faces with bony forms marked | |
| **100 planar heads**, 50 shaded with four values | |
| **100 eyes, 100 noses, 100 mouths, 100 ears** | |
| **100 heads of hair as masses** | |
| **30 likeness portraits** by the six-step method | |
| **120 expression studies** across the six basics | |
| **100 faces at 2 cm**, and 100 reduction sets | |
| **Plus 50 heads from imagination, from each of the eight directions** | |

**Six to ten weeks**, and it is the stage where the gap between a beginner's work and a competent drawing is most visible.

---

**And the four ideas to carry:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The eyes are halfway down the head.** One rule, and it fixes the commonest error in portraiture |
| **2** | **The centre line and brow line are ellipses on a sphere.** Drawing them straight flattens the head |
| **3** | **Likeness is proportion, not features.** Name the deviations in words and draw those |
| **4** | **At small sizes a face is six marks.** Fewer reads better |

---

**What this completes.** With stages 6 to 10 done, **the whole human figure is constructible from imagination** — body, limbs, hands, feet and head. The remaining figure-related work is **clothing it (stage 11)**, and everything after that is either other subjects or the business of making pictures.

**Practice.** Run the ten checks on 20 heads. Then total the counts and finish what is short. Then draw one invented character's head from all eight directions, on shared guide lines, as the stage's finished piece — and keep it beside the figure from stage 6.
The six folds:
Hogarth's classification: the only systematic treatment of cloth on the shelf, and why naming the fold is what makes it drawable.

**Cloth looks chaotic and is not.** Fabric does a small number of things, determined by where it is supported and which way gravity pulls. **Hogarth names six.**

---

| | Fold | Where it occurs | What it looks like |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Pipe** | **hanging from one support** — a curtain, a sleeve from a shoulder | **vertical tubes**, roughly parallel, widening downward |
| **2** | **Zigzag** | **in a bent limb, on the slack side** | **angular, alternating** — the fold at the inside of an elbow or knee |
| **3** | **Spiral** | **wrapping a cylindrical form** | **curving round a limb**, following its cross-contour |
| **4** | **Half-lock** | **where cloth changes direction sharply** | **a sharp angular break**, like a hinge |
| **5** | **Diaper** | **suspended between two points** | **diagonal, radiating from both supports** |
| **6** | **Drop** | **hanging freely over an edge** | **loose, irregular, falling** |

**Plus one more that is worth adding: the inert fold** — cloth lying on a surface, with no tension, forming soft random shapes.

---

**Why naming them matters:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Cloth drawn by observation alone is copied** | **and cannot be redrawn from another angle or invented** |
| **Cloth drawn by naming its folds is constructed** | |
| **And the construction is fast** | **"this sleeve is spiral folds round the upper arm and zigzag at the elbow"** is a complete plan |
| **Which is what lets you draw clothing on an invented character** | — the thing stage 16 needs |

---

**The two rules that govern all six:**

**1 — Every fold starts at a point of support or tension.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Find the supports first** — shoulders, elbows, a belt, a hip, a knee | |
| **The folds radiate from them** | |
| **And cloth between two supports forms diaper folds across the gap** | |
| **So the drawing order is: body, supports, folds** | never folds first |

**2 — Folds point at their cause.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A fold's direction tells you where the tension is** | |
| **Which means folds are informative** — they state the body's position underneath | |
| **And a fold pointing nowhere is wrong** | it is decoration, and it reads as noise |

---

**The error this fixes: the random wrinkle.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Beginners add wrinkles to clothing to make it look like cloth** | |
| **Scattered, equal, pointing in all directions** | |
| **Which flattens the figure and hides the form** | |
| **Whereas the correct number of folds is small** | — perhaps six to ten on a whole figure |
| **And each one is doing a job** | |

**Practice.** Draw 20 examples of each of the six folds from reference, 120 in total, naming each one. Then 50 clothed figures where you mark the supports before any fold. Then take 30 photographs of clothed figures and label every fold by type. Then draw 30 figures from imagination, choosing the folds by name rather than inventing them.
Cloth over form:
The relationship that makes drapery work: the body underneath, where cloth touches it, and where it hangs free.

**The principle: cloth describes the form it covers. If it does not, it is a sheet.**

---

**The three zones on any clothed figure:**

| | Zone | What cloth does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Contact** | **the cloth touches the body and takes its shape** — shoulders, chest, the front of a thigh, a knee |
| **2** | **Tension** | **the cloth is stretched between two contacts** — across the back when the arms come forward, across the hips when sitting |
| **3** | **Free** | **the cloth hangs away from the body** — under the arm, below a belt, between the legs |

**The craft is knowing which zone each part of the garment is in, and drawing accordingly.**

---

**What each zone looks like:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Contact** | **the body's form, shown directly.** Few folds, and the cloth's surface follows the anatomy |
| **Tension** | **straight or gently curved folds running between the two support points** — the diaper fold |
| **Free** | **pipe or drop folds, hanging vertically regardless of the body** |

---

**And the rule that makes a clothed figure read: draw the body first, then the cloth on it.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Always.** Even when the figure is fully covered | |
| **Because the cloth's shape is derived from the body's** | |
| **A garment drawn without the body under it is a shape** | and it will look like laundry |
| **On a tablet this is one layer** — construct the nude figure, drop it to 25%, draw the clothing over it | |
| **Which is the workflow from stage 6, applied again** | |

---

**The specific places cloth reveals the body**, which are the ones to get right:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The shoulders** — the garment hangs from them, so they define the whole upper silhouette | |
| **The elbows and knees** — bent joints push the cloth and create zigzag folds | |
| **The waist or belt** — a horizontal break where the cloth gathers | |
| **The hips** — the widest point under a hanging garment | |
| **The chest** | |
| **And the ground**, if the garment reaches it | |

**Six places, and if those six are correct the figure under the cloth reads even where it is invisible.**

---

**What changes with the body's movement:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A raised arm lifts the whole side of a garment** and creates tension across the back | |
| **A step forward presses cloth against the front thigh and pulls it from the back** | |
| **Sitting compresses everything at the waist and the hips** | |
| **And movement leaves the cloth BEHIND the body** — a running figure's cloak trails, and that lag is what makes motion read | |
| **Williams' *Animator's Survival Kit* has the best treatment of the lag** | since it is a timing problem as much as a drawing one |

---

**And the thickness of the cloth, which is the detail people miss:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A garment has an edge, and the edge has thickness** | |
| **At a hem, a cuff, a collar or an opening, you see the cloth's inside** | |
| **Which is usually darker, and which states that the garment is a shell rather than a painted surface** | |
| **Drawing a hem as a single line** | **makes the clothing look painted on** |
| **One extra line at every opening fixes it** | |

**Practice.** Draw 50 clothed figures with the nude construction underneath on its own layer, kept. Then 50 marking the three zones in different colours before drawing any fold. Then 30 figures in motion with the cloth lagging behind. Then draw 30 garments showing their thickness at every hem, cuff and collar.
Material, and what it does:
Why linen, wool, leather and silk fold differently, and the four properties that decide a fold's character.

**Different fabrics make different folds, and the differences are predictable from four properties.**

| | Property | Effect on folds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Weight** | **heavy cloth makes few large folds; light cloth makes many small ones** |
