| **Matte, opaque** — cloth, unglazed clay, chalk | **smooth gradation from light to shadow, soft terminator, no highlight.** The textbook sphere |
| **Semi-gloss** — skin, polished wood, leather | **a soft broad highlight, gentle gradation, visible reflected light** |
| **Gloss** — glazed ceramic, wet surfaces, plastic | **a small sharp highlight, high contrast, dark reflections** |
| **Metal** | **extreme contrast, no mid-tones, reflects the environment** — **it has almost no local value of its own** |
| **Translucent** — skin at the edges, wax, leaves, thin cloth | **light passes through and glows where the material is thin**, often at the edges |
| **Transparent** — glass, water | **what you see is behind it, distorted, plus reflections** |

---

**Metal deserves the detail**, because it is the one people render as grey:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A metal surface reflects its surroundings almost entirely** | |
| **So its values are the values of what is around it** — sky above, ground below | |
| **Which gives the characteristic dark-light-dark banding** on a cylinder: dark ground reflection at the bottom, light sky at the top | |
| **The contrast is extreme** — near-black beside near-white, with no gradual transition | |
| **And the highlight is tiny and intense** | |
| **Rendering metal as smooth grey gradation** | **produces plastic, every time** |

---

**Skin**, which is the one that matters most and is the most complicated:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Semi-gloss, and translucent at the edges and in thin areas** | |
| **So: a soft broad highlight; a soft terminator; and warmth where light passes through** — ears, fingers, the nose's edge | |
| **The reflected light in skin's shadows is unusually strong** because of subsurface scattering | |
| **Which is why skin's shadows look warm and luminous** | and why rendering them as flat grey kills them |
| **At small sizes none of this survives** | and skin becomes two or three flat values, which Shepherds' §10.1 assumes |

---

**And the general rule for drawing a material: get the highlight's size and the contrast's range right, and the material reads.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A small sharp highlight plus high contrast = hard shiny** | |
| **A broad soft highlight plus moderate contrast = soft semi-gloss** | |
| **No highlight plus gentle gradation = matte** | |
| **Two decisions, and the material is stated** | before any texture is drawn |

**Practice.** Render the same sphere as each of the six materials, 10 times each. Then 30 metal cylinders with the dark-light-dark environmental banding. Then 30 skin studies with warm translucent edges. Then render 20 objects where you decide only the highlight size and the contrast range, and check that each material reads.
Rendering, and when to stop:
Taking a drawing to finish: the order, the three levels of finish, and the question that decides when it is done.

**Rendering is applying the value plan to the drawing.** It is the last stage of a picture and the one where most pictures are ruined.

---

**The order:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Separate light from shadow** — one hard decision per area, no gradation yet. **Two values** |
| **2** | **Check the two shapes** — the light shape and the shadow shape, as shapes. This is the notan |
| **3** | **Add the mid values within the light** — halftones |
| **4** | **Add reflected light within the shadow**, staying within the shadow's range |
| **5** | **Cast shadows**, with their contact points darkest |
| **6** | **Highlights**, last, and few |
| **7** | **Edge control** — hardest at the focus, softest elsewhere |

**Step 1 is the whole foundation.** **A drawing whose light and shadow shapes are decided and checked before any gradation cannot go badly wrong.** One that starts with gradation almost always does.

---

**The three levels of finish:**

| | Level | What it is | When |
| --- | --- | --- | |
| **1** | **Block-in** | **two or three flat values, no gradation** | **a study, a thumbnail, a sprite reference** |
| **2** | **Modelled** | **the six light elements, soft terminators, controlled edges** | **most illustration** |
| **3** | **Rendered** | **full tonal range, material description, texture** | **a finished portrait or a showcase piece** |

**And the decision is made before starting, not discovered.** **A drawing that drifts from level 1 to level 3 has no plan and usually stops at an awkward level 2.**

---

**When to stop**, which is the hardest judgement in the subject:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The test: does the next mark serve the picture's intention?** | |
| **Not "is there more I could render" — there always is** | |
| **Signs you have passed it** | **the focal point is no longer the most interesting area; the drawing is evenly detailed; you are rendering things you cannot name a reason for** |
| **The practical habit** | **decide the level of finish before starting, and stop there** |
| **And the second habit** | **stop while you still want to continue.** You can always resume; you cannot unrender |

---

**The three ways rendering ruins a drawing:**

| | Failure | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Even detail everywhere** | **no focal hierarchy.** The eye has nowhere to go |
| **2** | **Value drift** | **judging each area locally.** The structure dissolves |
| **3** | **Over-blending** | **the smudge tool, or too many values.** The forms soften into fog |

---

**And the one habit that prevents all three: step back constantly.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Zoom to fit, every few minutes** | |
| **Flip, every few minutes** | |
| **Posterise occasionally, to check the value groups** | |
| **All three are one keystroke on a tablet** | and the discipline is remembering to use them |
| **Which is stage 1's lesson, arriving where it finally matters most** | |

**Practice.** Render 30 studies stopping deliberately at level 1, 30 at level 2 and 10 at level 3. Then take 20 drawings and render each until you think it is finished, then look the next day and mark where you should have stopped. Then render 20 using only steps 1 and 2, and judge how many need anything more.
The value checklist:
The stage closed as a list: the order, the checks, and the counts.

**The order:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The value plan, from stage 13** — 3 to 5 values, decided at thumbnail stage |
| **2** | **The light source** — one, plus ambient; its size, direction and distance |
| **3** | **Light and shadow separated**, in two values |
| **4** | **The darkest and lightest anchors placed** |
| **5** | **Halftones within light, reflected light within shadow** |
| **6** | **Cast shadows, darkest at contact** |
| **7** | **Highlights, few** |
| **8** | **Edges controlled, hardest at the focus** |

---

**The checks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Is any shadow value lighter than any light value?** It must not be |
| **2** | **Is the darkest point in the picture a cast shadow's contact?** |
| **3** | **Does the terminator's shape describe the form's geometry?** |
| **4** | **Is reflected light kept inside the shadow's range?** |
| **5** | **Does posterising to 4 values give coherent shapes?** |
| **6** | **Are values 1 and 5 occupying very little area?** |
| **7** | **Are the hardest edges at the focal point?** |
| **8** | **Is there at least one lost edge?** |
| **9** | **Do the highlight size and contrast range state the material?** |
| **10** | **Did you stop at the level of finish you decided on?** |

---

**The counts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **200 light-logic studies** — spheres, cubes, cylinders with all six elements | |
| **50 value scales and 50 four-value renders** | |
| **150 edge studies**, including 50 with lost edges | |
| **120 material studies** across the six types | |
| **70 rendered studies** across the three levels of finish | |
| **Plus 30 posterised checks of existing work** | |

**Four to six weeks.**

---

**And the four ideas to carry:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Light values and shadow values are two separate ranges, and nothing crosses between them.** The single most important rule in shading |
| **2** | **The cast shadow is darker than the form shadow, darkest at the contact** |
| **3** | **Value is relative.** Set the darkest and lightest first and place everything by comparison |
| **4** | **Edge variation is what makes rendering read.** Hardest at the focus, lost where it does not matter |

---

**What this enables.** With value, the drawings become pictures that can be lit, and **the whole of stage 15's colour work sits on top of it** — because **colour without correct value is decoration, and value without colour is already a complete picture.** Which is why this stage comes first and why a grayscale study is always a legitimate finished work.

**Practice.** Run the ten checks on 20 rendered studies. Then total the counts and finish what is short. Then take one composition from stage 13 and render it fully in value alone, as the stage's finished piece — and keep it, because stage 15 will colour it.
Hue, value and chroma:
The three independent controls: what each one is, why separating them is the whole skill, and the one that does the work.

**A colour has three properties, and treating them as three separate decisions is the single most useful idea in colour.**

| | Property | Also called | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Hue** | **colour** | **where it sits on the wheel** — red, yellow, blue |
| **2** | **Value** | **lightness, tone** | **how light or dark** |
| **3** | **Chroma** | **saturation, intensity** | **how pure or grey** |

---

**Why separating them matters:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Beginners think in hue** — "I need a brown for the wood" | |
| **And then cannot work out why the picture is wrong** | |
| **Because the problem is almost always value or chroma**, not hue | |
| **A picture whose values are right and whose hues are wrong still reads** | |
| **A picture whose values are wrong does not**, whatever its hues | |
| **So: value first, chroma second, hue last** | |

**That ordering is the whole stage in one line.**

---

**Value, restated for colour**, because it is where most colour problems live:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Every colour has a value**, and it is what stage 14's work applies to | |
| **Yellow is intrinsically light; violet is intrinsically dark** | |
| **Which means a saturated yellow cannot be dark and a saturated violet cannot be light** without losing chroma | |
| **And the greyscale check is the test** — **desaturate and see whether the picture still works** | |
| **If it does not, the colours have been chosen by hue** | |

---

**Chroma, which is the one people never think about:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Most of the real world is low chroma** — greys, browns, muted greens | |
| **High chroma is rare and therefore attracts attention** | |
| **Which makes chroma a focal device** — the most saturated area draws the eye | |
| **And the commonest beginner failure in colour is everything at full chroma** | which produces a picture with no focus and no air |
| **The rule** | **most of the picture low chroma, with high chroma used where you want attention** |

---

**The practical consequence: a limited chroma range beats a limited hue range.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A picture using every hue but mostly low chroma reads as coherent** | |
| **A picture using two hues at full chroma reads as garish** | |
| **So the discipline that matters is restraint in chroma**, not in hue | |
| **Which is also what makes an observed colour study look real** | — reality is mostly grey |

---

**And the digital trap, which is specific and important:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A colour picker's default is a square of hue at full chroma** | |
| **So the easy colours to pick are the saturated ones** | |
| **And the ones you want are mostly in the corner nobody clicks** | |
| **The habit** | **pick a value first using the greyscale slider, then add chroma deliberately** |
| **Or work in a HSV/HSL picker where the three are separate sliders** | which is what makes them separate decisions in practice |

**Practice.** Make 30 colour studies where you pick values first in greyscale and add hue afterwards. Then take 30 photographs and sample 10 colours from each, recording their chroma — the lowness will surprise you. Then paint 20 studies with the whole picture below 30% chroma except one area. Then desaturate 30 of your colour works and see which survive.
Colour in light and shadow:
What light does to colour: the two-colour model, why shadows are not just darker, and the single rule that makes a painting glow.

**The model: a lit scene has two light sources — the key light, and the ambient light that fills the shadows.** They are usually different colours, and **the difference between them is where colour's life comes from.**

---

**The standard case — sunlight outdoors:**

| | Source | Colour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Key** | **the sun** | **warm — yellow to orange** |
| **Ambient** | **the sky** | **cool — blue** |

**Which gives the rule: warm light, cool shadow.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Lit surfaces take the sun's warmth** | |
| **Shadowed surfaces are lit only by the blue sky, so they are cool** | |
| **And the contrast between them is a temperature contrast as well as a value one** | |
| **Which is why a sunny day's shadows are blue and not grey** | |

---

**And the inverse case, which is just as common:**

| | Situation | Key | Ambient |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Overcast** | **the whole sky** — cool and diffuse | **cool shadows too** — the contrast nearly vanishes | |
| **Indoors by a window** | **cool daylight** | **warm bounced light from the room** — **cool light, warm shadow**, the reverse of the sunny rule | |
| **Firelight** | **very warm, small, close** | **cool or dark** | |
| **Moonlight** | **cool and dim** | **very dark** | |

**So "warm light, cool shadow" is not a law — it is the most common case.** **The law is: the key and the ambient differ in temperature, and that difference is the picture's colour structure.**

---

**What this means for drawing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A shadow is not the lit colour made darker** | |
| **It is the surface lit by a different light** | |
| **So it changes hue and chroma, not only value** | |
| **And "darker" is only the beginning of it** | |
| **The commonest colour failure** | **shadows made by adding black**, which lowers value and chroma and changes nothing else — producing dead, grey, lifeless shadow |

---

**The practical method:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Decide the key light's colour and the ambient's** |
| **2** | **For every surface, decide whether it is in light or in shadow** — the stage 14 split |
| **3** | **Lit surfaces: local colour shifted towards the key's hue** |
| **4** | **Shadowed surfaces: local colour shifted towards the ambient's hue, and lowered in value and usually in chroma** |
| **5** | **Reflected light: shifted towards whatever is bouncing into it** |

---

**And the one rule that makes a painting glow: chroma peaks at the light-shadow transition.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The brightest-lit surfaces are often washed out towards white** — losing chroma | |
| **The deepest shadows are dark and low in chroma** | |
| **The most saturated colour is in the halftones**, just before the terminator | |
| **Which is why skin looks ruddiest at the edge of the light**, and why a painted apple's reddest point is not its brightest | |
| **Getting this right is most of the difference between a flat colour study and a luminous one** | |

**Practice.** Paint 30 studies of one object under sunlight, overcast, window light and firelight, changing only the key and ambient colours. Then 30 studies where every shadow is made by shifting hue rather than adding black. Then 20 where chroma peaks at the terminator. Then photograph the same object in four lights and sample the shadow colours in each.
Temperature, and the limited palette:
Warm against cool as a structural device, and the discipline that makes colour coherent: fewer colours, mixed.

**Temperature is a relative judgement**, not an absolute one. **A colour is warm or cool compared with its neighbours** — a "cool red" is cool beside a warm red and warm beside any blue.

---

**What temperature does:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It separates planes** — warm advances, cool recedes | |
| **It separates light from shadow**, as the previous lesson showed | |
| **It carries mood** — warm reads as comfort, energy, life; cool as distance, calm, cold | |
| **And it is independent of value** | so it is a second channel for stating the same structure |

---

**The practical device: temperature contrast within a value.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Two areas at the same value, one warm and one cool, separate clearly** | |
| **Without any value contrast at all** | |
| **Which lets you separate forms where the values must stay close** | |
| **And it is how a picture can have subtle values and still read** | |
| **This is the most useful single colour technique**, and it has no equivalent in value work | |

---

**Now the limited palette**, which is the discipline that makes colour cohere:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Choose three or four colours plus white, and mix everything from them** | |
| **Every colour in the picture then shares pigment with every other** | |
| **Which produces harmony automatically** | |
| **And it forces mixing, which teaches colour relationships far faster than picking does** | |

**The classical choice is the Zorn palette: yellow ochre, ivory black, vermilion and white.** Four colours, and it produces a remarkable range — including convincing skin and a surprising blue-grey from the black.

---

**On a tablet**, a limited palette has to be imposed deliberately:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The picker offers 16 million colours** | |
| **So the discipline must be a rule rather than a constraint** | |
| **The method** | **make a palette swatch on its own layer, 4 to 8 colours, and pick only from it** |
| **Krita's palette docker holds a saved palette** | and it is what makes this practical |
| **And mixing can be done by sampling between two swatches** | which is the digital equivalent of mixing on a palette |

---

**And this is exactly what Shepherds' Palette v0.1 is:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **132 entries in 33 ramps of four** — a limited palette, imposed project-wide | |
| **With the ramps running Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light** | |
| **So each ramp is a value sequence of one material's colour** | |
| **Which is the structure this lesson describes, built into a game's art contract** | |
| **And the reason it works** | **everything in the game shares the same colour relationships** |

**So a pixel-art palette and a painter's limited palette are the same idea**, and understanding either one explains the other.

**Practice.** Paint 30 studies with the four-colour Zorn palette, mixing everything. Then 30 with your own 6-colour palette. Then 20 studies using temperature contrast at equal value to separate forms. Then take Shepherds' Palette v0.1, pick three ramps, and paint 10 studies using only those twelve colours.
Local colour and the colour of light:
The distinction that resolves most colour confusion: what a thing is, against what it looks like under this light.

**Local colour is an object's colour in neutral light** — the red of an apple, the brown of wood. **What you actually see is the local colour modified by every light falling on it.**

---

**The confusion this resolves:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **"What colour is that wall?" — white** | |
| **"What colour is it in this picture?" — warm grey in the light, blue-violet in shadow, orange where the lamp hits it** | |
| **Both answers are correct** | |
| **And the drawing records the second** | |
| **While your knowledge insists on the first** — which is the symbol problem from stage 2, in colour | |

---

**The practical consequence: a white object is rarely white in a painting.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Its lit side is the colour of the light** | |
| **Its shadow is the colour of the ambient** | |
| **And pure white appears only at a specular highlight, if at all** | |
| **Painting a white shirt white** | **flattens it completely** |
| **Which is also true of black** | — a black coat's lit side is a mid grey of the light's hue |

---

**How much the light overrides the local colour** depends on two things:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The light's intensity** | **strong light overrides local colour; dim light preserves it** |
| **The surface's chroma** | **a saturated local colour resists; a near-neutral one takes the light's hue entirely** |
| **So in bright sunlight, everything shifts warm** | and in dim ambient light, local colours dominate |
| **Which is why midday scenes read as unified and overcast ones as varied** | |

---

**The method for getting it right: squint and compare.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Compare the colour you are judging against another in the same picture** | |
| **"Is it warmer or cooler than that?" "Lighter or darker?" "More or less saturated?"** | |
| **Three comparative questions**, which the eye answers reliably | |
| **Rather than "what colour is it", which the eye answers badly** | |
| **Stage 2's sighting, in colour** | and it is the same principle for the third time |

---

**And the thing that makes a colour study look observed rather than invented: colour variation within one object.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A real surface is not one colour** | |
| **It picks up bounced light from everything around it** | |
| **A face beside a red wall has red in its shadow; a figure on grass has green in its underside** | |
| **These bounced colours are subtle and they are what make a painting feel like a place** | |
| **The failure** | **filling an object with one hue and varying only the value** — which reads as coloured-in |

**Practice.** Paint 30 white objects under coloured light, with no pure white anywhere. Then 30 studies where every object picks up bounce from its neighbours. Then take 20 photographs and sample the same surface in light and shadow, recording how far the hue shifts. Then paint 20 studies by comparison only — judging each colour against another in the picture rather than absolutely.
Colour schemes, and restraint:
How to choose a picture's colours: the classical schemes, what each is for, and the argument for using very few.

**A colour scheme is a rule limiting which hues appear.** Its purpose is coherence, and its cost is variety.

---

**The schemes:**

| | Scheme | Hues | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Monochrome** | **one hue, varied in value and chroma** | **unified, calm, and very hard to make interesting** | |
| **Analogous** | **three neighbouring hues** | **harmonious, natural — most landscapes are this** | |
| **Complementary** | **two opposite hues** | **maximum contrast, vibrant.** Needs one dominant and one as accent | |
| **Split-complementary** | **one hue plus the two beside its opposite** | **the contrast without the harshness** | |
| **Triadic** | **three evenly spaced** | **balanced, lively, hard to control** | |

---

**The rule that makes any of them work: one dominant, one subordinate, one accent.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Roughly 70% / 25% / 5% by area** | |
| **The accent is the smallest and the most saturated** | |
| **And it goes at the focal point** | |
| **An even split between two hues is the commonest scheme failure** | — it reads as indecision |

---

**And the argument for restraint, which is this lesson's point:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Most pictures that look good use fewer colours than you think** | |
| **Most pictures that look amateur use more** | |
| **Because variety is easy and coherence is hard** | |
| **And the eye reads a limited scheme as deliberate** | |
| **The practical test** | **can you name the picture's colour scheme in one phrase?** If not, there probably is not one |

---

**Colour as a narrative device**, which is where this connects to the project:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A restricted palette can carry meaning** — a place, a time, a mood, a faction | |
| **And a colour reserved for one purpose becomes a signal** | |
| **Which is exactly what `colour-palette.md`'s violet rule is** | — *"violet may be used only for Shepherd, sacred, or deliberately dissonant content"* |
| **A colour that appears decoratively stops signalling** | |
| **So the discipline of reserving a hue is a storytelling device, not only an aesthetic one** | |

---

**The method for choosing a picture's colours:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Decide the value plan first** — stage 13 and 14 |
| **2** | **Decide the key light and ambient colours** |
| **3** | **Decide the scheme and the dominant hue** |
| **4** | **Decide where the accent goes** — the focal point |
| **5** | **Build a palette of 6 to 8 swatches** |
| **6** | **Paint only from it** |

---

**And the honest gap in this curriculum, stated plainly.** **Gurney's *Color and Light* is the modern standard on this subject and it is not on the shelf.** What is here — Edwards' *Color* for mixing, Famous Artists 16 for practice, Loomis' *The Eye of the Painter* for seeing — covers the ground but less systematically. **The free video resources carry more of this stage than any other.**

**Practice.** Paint 20 studies in each of the five schemes, 100 in total. Then 30 with a strict 70/25/5 distribution. Then take 30 paintings you admire and name each one's scheme and its accent's position. Then paint 10 studies where one reserved colour carries a meaning, and see whether a viewer notices it.
The colour checklist:
The stage closed as a list: the order, the checks, and the counts.

**The order:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The value plan**, already done |
| **2** | **The key light's colour and the ambient's** |
| **3** | **The scheme, the dominant hue, and the accent's position** |
| **4** | **A palette of 6 to 8 swatches, saved** |
| **5** | **Block in the light and shadow masses in colour** |
| **6** | **Local colours shifted by their light** |
| **7** | **Bounce and reflected colour** |
| **8** | **The accent, last and smallest** |

---

**The checks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Does it work desaturated?** The greyscale check |
| **2** | **Do the key and ambient differ in temperature?** |
| **3** | **Was any shadow made by adding black?** It should not have been |
| **4** | **Is the most saturated colour at the terminator rather than in the light?** |
| **5** | **Is most of the picture low chroma?** |
| **6** | **Is the highest chroma at the focal point?** |
| **7** | **Is there a nameable colour scheme?** |
| **8** | **Is the distribution roughly 70/25/5?** |
| **9** | **Is any white pure white, or any black pure black?** Usually neither should be |
| **10** | **Does each object pick up bounce from its neighbours?** |

---

**The counts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **60 value-first colour studies** | |
| **100 light-and-shadow studies** across four lighting conditions | |
| **80 limited-palette studies**, including 30 Zorn | |
| **70 local-colour studies**, including white and black objects | |
| **100 scheme studies**, 20 of each | |
| **Plus 60 analyses of photographs and paintings** | |

**Four to six weeks.**

---

**And the four ideas to carry:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Value first, chroma second, hue last.** Most colour problems are value problems |
| **2** | **A shadow is a surface lit by a different light**, not a darker version of the lit colour |
| **3** | **Chroma peaks at the terminator**, not in the brightest light |
| **4** | **Restraint reads as deliberate.** Fewer colours, mixed from a limited set |

---

**And the connection to the pixel-art work this curriculum serves.** **Shepherds' Palette v0.1 — 132 entries in 33 four-step ramps running Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light — is a limited palette with its value structure pre-built.** Everything in this stage explains why that structure works: **each ramp is one material's local colour at four values, and the hue shifts between a ramp's steps are the light-and-shadow logic, frozen into a palette.** Understanding this stage is what lets you use that palette rather than merely obey it.

**Practice.** Run the ten checks on 20 colour studies. Then total the counts and finish what is short. Then take the value render from stage 14's finished piece and colour it, as this stage's finished piece. Then take Shepherds' Palette v0.1, pick one ramp, and work out which lighting situation its four steps describe.
Taking a piece to finish:
The whole pipeline in one lesson: from idea to finished illustration, and the stage at which most pieces die.

**Everything in this curriculum has been a part. This is the sequence that uses all of them.**

| | Stage | From |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The idea, stated in a sentence** | — |
| **2** | **20 thumbnails; pick one** | **stage 13** |
| **3** | **Notan and value plan** | **stages 13, 14** |
| **4** | **Reference gathering** | — |
| **5** | **The drawing** — gesture, construction, anatomy | **stages 5 to 12** |
| **6** | **The value render** | **stage 14** |
| **7** | **Colour** | **stage 15** |
| **8** | **Finish and edge control** | **stage 14** |

---

**Step 1 deserves more weight than it gets.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **"A shepherd finds something in a field at dusk"** is an idea | |
| **"A character" is not** | |
| **The sentence decides the thumbnails, the composition, the light and the colour** | |
| **And a picture made without one drifts** | — it is the commonest reason a piece is abandoned half-finished |

---

**Step 4, reference, is where discipline matters:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Gather before drawing, not during** | |
| **Because stopping mid-drawing to find a reference breaks the drawing's momentum** | |
| **And gather MORE than you need** — several angles, several lighting conditions | |
| **Reference is for checking and for information**, never for copying | |
| **And §2.1's rule applies** — **what the documents state governs, and reference fills in only what they do not** | |

---

**The stage at which most pieces die: between 5 and 6.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The drawing is done, the piece looks unfinished, and the next step is large and uncertain** | |
| **So it gets abandoned, or over-rendered, or endlessly adjusted** | |
| **The fix is the value plan from step 3** | — **if the values were decided at thumbnail stage, step 6 is execution rather than decision** |
| **Which is the whole argument for planning** | **it converts judgement into work, and work can be finished** |

---

**The three failure modes of a finished piece:**

| | Failure | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Tight and lifeless** | **the gesture was lost in construction, and never recovered** |
| **2** | **Loose and unresolved** | **no value plan; rendering by feel** |
| **3** | **Even and unfocused** | **no focal hierarchy; everything rendered equally** |

---

**And the single most useful habit: finish things.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The last 20% of a piece teaches more than the first 80%** | |
| **Because it is where all the decisions interact** | |
| **And it is the part most people never practise**, because studies are easier and more satisfying | |
| **The rule worth adopting** | **one finished piece for every twenty studies** |
| **Which is a small proportion and far more than most people manage** | |

**Practice.** Take one idea through all eight steps to a finished piece. Then do it four more times. Then take 20 abandoned pieces and identify at which step each one stopped. Then adopt the one-in-twenty rule for a year, and count.
Sequential art:
Eisner and McCloud: the panel, the gutter, and what a drawn sequence can do that a single picture cannot.

**Shepherds' register 3 is *"illustrated graphic-novel tableaux"***, which makes this a working requirement rather than an aside.

---

**The panel, and the gutter:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A panel is a moment, framed** | |
| **The gutter is the space between panels** | |
| **And the reader supplies what happens in the gutter** — **McCloud's central argument: closure** | |
| **Which means the reader does most of the storytelling**, and the artist's job is to give them enough and not more | |
| **So what you leave out between panels is as designed as what you put in them** | |

---

**McCloud's panel transitions**, which is the practical vocabulary:

| | Transition | Gutter contains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Moment to moment** | **almost nothing** — a small time step | |
| **Action to action** | **one action's completion** | |
| **Subject to subject** | **a change of focus within a scene** | |
| **Scene to scene** | **a jump in place or time** | |
| **Aspect to aspect** | **no time at all** — wandering around a place or mood | |
| **Non-sequitur** | **no connection** | |

**Western comics use action-to-action and subject-to-subject most; aspect-to-aspect is the one that creates atmosphere and is used least in the West.**

---

**Eisner's contribution: the page as a unit.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A page is read as a whole before it is read panel by panel** | |
| **So the page's composition matters as much as each panel's** | |
| **A large panel dominates and slows the reading** | |
| **A row of small ones accelerates it** | |
| **And the panel's shape carries meaning** — tall and narrow compresses, wide expands | |
| **Which makes panel layout a pacing device** | and it is the thing that distinguishes comics from illustrated prose |

---

**The reading path:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Left to right, top to bottom — in Western convention** | |
| **The eye enters the page at the top left and exits at the bottom right** | |
| **So the last panel on a page is an emphasis position**, and the first is an establishing one | |
| **And any layout that makes the reading order ambiguous has failed**, whatever it looks like | |

---

**What a sequence does that a single picture cannot:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Time** — before, during, after | |
| **Cause** — one thing leading to another | |
| **Contrast** — two moments juxtaposed | |
| **Pace** — slow and fast passages | |
| **And interiority** — showing a character's attention by what is shown next | |

---

**For the project specifically:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A tableau is usually a single large image rather than a page of panels** | |
| **But it uses the same vocabulary** — the moment chosen, what is implied before and after, and the reading order within the frame | |
| **And a sequence of tableaux is a sequence of panels with very large gutters** | |
| **So McCloud's closure applies**, and choosing which moments to show is the design | |

**Practice.** Draw 20 three-panel sequences using each of McCloud's six transitions. Then 10 full pages, designing the layout before the panels. Then take one Prologue scene and tell it in 6 tableaux, choosing the moments. Then redraw it in 3 and in 12, and compare what each can carry.
Character and creature design sheets:
The deliverable this curriculum has been building towards: what a design sheet contains, and the standard it must meet.

**A design sheet is the document that lets somebody else — or you, six months later — draw the same character correctly.** It is the practical output of everything in stages 6 to 12.

---

**What it contains:**

| | Element | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The character in a neutral pose, front, side and back** | **the base, with proportions established on shared guide lines** |
| **2** | **Three-quarter views** | **the most-seen angles** |
| **3** | **The head, larger, from several angles** | **features are too small on the full figure** |
| **4** | **Expressions** — four or six | |
| **5** | **Costume details, drawn separately and larger** | **fastenings, equipment, how things attach** |
| **6** | **Signature equipment, alone** | **the crook, the satchel, the sling** |
| **7** | **A silhouette, in black** | **the recognisability test** |
| **8** | **Notes** — height in heads, materials, colours, anything stated by the documents | |

---

**The standard it must meet: consistency.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Every view is the same person** | |
| **Every proportion aligns across the views, on shared horizontals** | |
| **The costume is identical in every view, including which side things are on** | |
| **And a reader can draw a new pose from it without guessing** | |
| **Which is a far higher standard than a single good drawing** | and it is what makes it a design rather than an illustration |

---

**The common failures:**

| | Failure | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Views that are different heights** | **no shared guide lines** |
| **2** | **Costume details that move between views** | **drawn from imagination each time rather than from the design** |
| **3** | **A design that cannot be drawn from another angle** | **it was designed as a silhouette rather than as a form** |
| **4** | **A design that is unrecognisable in black** | **no distinctive shape** |
| **5** | **Detail that cannot survive the production size** | **designed at 20 cm for use at 80 pixels** |

**Failure 5 is the one this project cares about most**, and the test is the reduction exercise from stages 9 and 10: **draw the design at its production size and see what survives.**

---

**For a creature, the same with three additions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The skeleton**, or at least the body plan it is built on | |
| **Scale against a human figure** | |
| **And its characteristic poses** — how it stands, moves and rests, since a creature's attitude is less obvious than a person's | |

---

**And the project's constraint on all of it**, which is where this curriculum and the Aseprite one meet:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **§2.1** — nothing invented to fill a gap | |
| **§5.4** — eight authored directions, no mirroring, so asymmetry is free | |
| **§9's silhouette test** — identity is silhouette, equipment and value structure at 80 px | |
| **And Timon has final say on design** | |
| **So a design sheet made here is a proposal**, and its job is to be clear enough to be approved or corrected | |

**Practice.** Produce complete design sheets for 5 characters and 3 creatures, to the eight-element standard. Then test each by drawing a new pose from the sheet alone, without the original reference. Then reduce each to its production size and check what survives. Then take one sheet to the standard a collaborator could work from, and have someone try.
The illustration checklist:
The stage closed as a list: the pipeline, the checks, and the counts.

**The pipeline:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **The idea, in a sentence** |
| **2** | **20 thumbnails, pick 1** |
| **3** | **Notan and value plan** |
| **4** | **Reference, gathered before drawing** |
| **5** | **The drawing — gesture, construction, anatomy** |
| **6** | **Value render** |
| **7** | **Colour** |
| **8** | **Edge control and finish** |

---

**The checks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Can you say what the picture is about in one sentence?** |
| **2** | **Does it work as a 3 cm thumbnail?** |
| **3** | **Does it work in two values?** |
| **4** | **Is there one focal point, with its devices concentrated?** |
| **5** | **Is the gesture still alive in the finished figures?** |
| **6** | **Does the finish match the value plan?** |
| **7** | **Are the edges hardest at the focus?** |
| **8** | **Is the colour scheme nameable?** |
| **9** | **Did you stop at the planned level of finish?** |
| **10** | **For a design sheet: can someone else draw a new pose from it?** |

---

**The counts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **5 complete illustrations**, through all eight steps | |
| **20 three-panel sequences** and 10 pages | |
| **One Prologue scene told three ways** | |
| **5 character design sheets and 3 creature sheets** | |
| **Plus the one-in-twenty finishing ratio**, applied from here on | |

**Open-ended — this stage is a practice rather than a syllabus.**

---

**And the three ideas to carry:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Plan converts judgement into work.** A picture with a value plan can be finished; one without is a series of judgements that never end |
| **2** | **The reader supplies the gutter.** What you leave out is designed |
| **3** | **A design sheet's standard is consistency**, which is much harder than a good drawing and is the actual deliverable |

---

**What this stage is for, stated once plainly.** Everything before it was capability. **This is the stage where the capability produces something somebody else can use** — an illustration, a sequence, or a design sheet that Timon can approve or correct. **Which is the point at which this curriculum starts paying into the project rather than preparing for it.**

**Practice.** Run the ten checks on your 5 illustrations. Then total the counts and finish what is short. Then produce one complete design sheet for a Shepherds character, to the standard a collaborator could work from, and show it.
Volume, forever:
What to do after the stages run out: the practice that continues, and the numbers that matter.

**There is no end to this curriculum.** The stages cover the knowledge; **the skill is built by repetition that continues indefinitely.**

---

**The daily practice, which is the whole of it:**

| | Element | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Warm-up** — dot targeting, lines, ellipses, boxes | **10 minutes** |
| **2** | **Gesture** — timed reference, 30 seconds each | **10 minutes** |
| **3** | **One study** — whatever the current weakness is | **20–40 minutes** |
| **4** | **Something for its own sake** | **the 50% rule, below** |

**An hour a day, indefinitely, is what this looks like.** The Drawing habit on the dashboard is daily for this reason.

---

**The 50% rule**, from Drawabox, and it is the most important thing in this lesson:

> **Half your drawing time must be spent drawing for fun, with no instructional goal, no correction, and no analysis.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Why** | **because the purpose of learning to draw is to draw**, and a practice that is entirely exercises forgets that |
| **And practically** | **people who only do exercises stop.** Enjoyment is what sustains a decade-long practice |
| **What counts** | **anything you want to draw, drawn badly or well, with no requirement to improve** |
| **What does not** | **studies, exercises, or anything you are judging** |
| **And it is not optional** | — it is half |

---

**The numbers that matter:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Days drawn, not hours** — consistency beats intensity, and a daily 30 minutes beats a weekly four hours | |
| **Finished pieces** — one in twenty | |
| **Gestures** — they never stop being the warm-up | |
| **And the count log from stage 1** | which is what makes any of this measurable |

---

**What to work on, which is the recurring question:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The thing that is worst** | |
| **Found by** | **drawing something complete and seeing what fails** |
| **Not by** | **picking a topic because it is interesting** |
| **The method** | **every month, draw five finished-ish pieces, list what went wrong, and make the most common failure next month's study subject** |
| **Which keeps the practice directed without requiring a curriculum** | |

---

**Copying masters, deliberately**, which is the oldest study method there is:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Pick a drawing you admire and copy it, carefully** | |
| **Then analyse what the artist did that you would not have** | |
| **The gap is the lesson** | |
| **And the library holds Michelangelo's drawings**, which is as good a place to start as exists | |
| **The rule** | **copy to learn, never to publish** |

---

**And the honest statement about time.** **Drawing takes years.** The stages in this curriculum represent perhaps eighteen months of serious work to pass through once, and **passing through once is the beginning.** The people who draw well have drawn for a decade or more, most days.

**That is not discouraging. It is the reason to start the daily hour now rather than to plan a better approach.**

**Practice.** Set up the daily hour and keep it for 30 days without exception, logging each one. Then apply the 50% rule honestly and measure whether you are meeting it. Then do the monthly five-pieces-and-a-failure-list review, and let it choose the next month's study.
Measuring progress:
How to tell whether you are improving: four methods, and the comparison this curriculum set up in its first lesson.

**The problem: improvement in drawing is invisible day to day.** Your standards rise at the same rate as your ability, so your work always looks equally inadequate. **This is universal and it drives people to quit.**

---

**The four methods:**

| | Method | Interval |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The dated comparison** — the same subject, drawn months apart | **3 to 6 months** |
| **2** | **The old-work review** — look at work from a year ago | **annually** |
| **3** | **The failure list** — what goes wrong, tracked over time | **monthly** |
| **4** | **The count log** | **continuously** |

---

**Method 1, which is the one this curriculum set up in stage 1:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The three pre-instruction drawings — a self-portrait, your own hand, a chair** | |
| **Dated, kept, and not looked at** | |
| **Now draw them again, under the same conditions** | |
| **And compare** | |
| **This is the single most convincing evidence of improvement available** | and it is why Edwards' course begins with it |

**Do it now if you have worked through the stages. Then date the new set and do it again in a year.**

---

**Method 3, the failure list, is the most useful for direction:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Every month, note what went wrong in your finished pieces** | |
| **Over a year, the list changes** | |
| **"Proportions wrong" becomes "hands weak" becomes "value structure unclear" becomes "compositions static"** | |
| **And the progression of the failures IS the progression of your ability** | |
| **Which is a far better measure than how the drawings look** | because it is specific |

---

**What does not measure progress:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **How you feel about your current work** — always negative, by design | |
| **Comparison with other artists** — different training, different years, different goals | |
| **Social reception** | — it measures appeal, not ability |
| **And the number of hours** | — hours of unfocused repetition measure nothing |

---

**The one honest sign that you are improving: you can see more errors than you could.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A beginner cannot see what is wrong with their drawing** | |
| **An improving artist can see exactly what is wrong and cannot yet fix it** | |
| **A competent one can see it and fix it** | |
| **So the frustrating middle stage — seeing the errors without the ability — is the evidence of progress** | |
| **And it is where most people stop**, believing the increased dissatisfaction means they are getting worse | |

**Practice.** Redraw the three pre-instruction drawings from stage 1 and compare them against the originals. Then build a failure list from your last 10 finished pieces. Then set a calendar reminder to repeat both in 6 months. Then look at your work from a year ago, if you have any.
Where this goes:
The curriculum's end: what has been covered, what has not, and the two routes out of it.

**What seventeen stages covered:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The instrument** — a tablet, configured, with the no-undo discipline that replaces paper's | |
| **The mark** — line, aim, confidence, economy | |
| **Space** — form, construction, perspective, both freehand and built | |
| **The figure** — gesture, construction, anatomy, hands, head, clothing | |
| **Animals and creatures** | |
| **The picture** — composition, value, colour | |
| **And production** — illustration, sequence, design sheets | |

**Which is the whole of representational drawing, from zero.**

---

**What it did not cover, honestly:**

| | | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Painting as a medium** — brushwork, surface, impasto | **a different subject** | |
| **Digital painting craft beyond one stage** | **Ctrl+Paint carries it** | |
| **Abstraction and non-representational design** | **a different tradition** | |
| **Typography and graphic design** | **Famous Artists 17–20, excluded** | |
| **Animation** | **Williams' book, and the Godot and Aseprite curriculums** | |
| **Pixel art** | **the Aseprite curriculum, which defers portraits and design to this one** | |
| **Life drawing from a model** | **not available; named as better throughout** | |

---

**The two routes out:**

**Route 1 — depth.** Pick one area and go much further than this curriculum does.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The head** — portraiture is a lifetime on its own | |
| **Colour and light** — and **this is where to buy Gurney**, the one real gap | |
| **Perspective and environments** — and **Scott Robertson**, the other gap | |
| **Animation** — Williams, and the project needs it | |

**Route 2 — application.** Stop studying and make things.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Which is what the project wants** | |
| **§11's open art work is eight asset classes, all of them unmade** | |
| **And the Prologue's requirement is a finite, written list** | |
| **So the application is specified** — which is unusually fortunate | |
| **And the honest advice** | **route 2, with route 1 applied to whatever route 2 reveals as weakest** |

---

**The relationship to Timon, restated, because it is the frame for all of it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **He has final say on design and draws by hand** | |
| **This curriculum exists so that you can contribute and understand what he is doing** | |
| **Not to replace him** | |
| **And the most useful thing it produces is not a finished illustration** — **it is the ability to have a real conversation about a design**, and to make a proposal that is worth responding to | |

---

**And the last thing worth saying.** This is the eighth and final curriculum in the route. **It is also the only one whose subject cannot be finished** — there is no point at which drawing is learned. **Which makes it the right one to end on**, because the route was never meant to terminate: *"we never stop if possible, ad astra."*

**Practice.** Write down which of the two routes you are taking and why. Then, if route 1, pick the area and find its next resource. If route 2, pick the first asset from §11's open work and make it. Then set the daily hour, and begin.
